docs.title: Lesson M01.L03: Random Variables & Probability Distributions
docs.text: Field Value Module M01 — Probability & Statistics Review Level Graduate (ECMT5001) Duration ~75 minutes Learning Objective Characterise random variables by their distributions, expected values, and variances; standardise normal random variables; and identify when the \(t\), \(\chi^2\), and \(F\) distributions arise in econometric testing. Provenance Wooldridge Appendices B & C; ECMT1020 Weeks 1–3 (R.2–R.4, R.8–R.9)

docs.title: 1. Random Variables
docs.text:
A random variable (RV) \(X\) is a function that assigns a real number to each outcome in a sample space. We distinguish two types:

Discrete Continuous Values Countable set \(\{x_1, x_2, \ldots\}\) Uncountable interval (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}\)) Distribution Probability mass function (PMF) Probability density function (PDF) Probability of exact value \(P(X = x_i) > 0\) possible \(P(X = x) = 0\) always Economic example Number of workers laid off Wage rate (AUD/hr)

docs.title: 2. Probability Mass Function (Discrete)
docs.text:
The PMF \(p(x_i) = P(X = x_i)\) satisfies:

\[p(x_i) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } i, \qquad \sum_{i} p(x_i) = 1\]

Example (Bernoulli): A firm wins a government contract with probability \(\theta = 0.3\).

\[X = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{(win)} \\ 0 & \text{(no win)} \end{cases}, \qquad P(X=1) = 0.3,\; P(X=0) = 0.7\]

docs.title: 3. Probability Density Function (Continuous)
docs.text:
For continuous \(X\), the PDF \(f(x)\) gives the density of probability (not the probability itself):

\[f(x) \geq 0, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\]

Probabilities are areas under the curve:

\[P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\]

Note: \(P(X = c) = 0\) for any single point \(c\) — this is not a contradiction; it means exact values have zero measure.

docs.title: 4. Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
docs.text:
The CDF applies to both discrete and continuous RVs:

\[F(x) = P(X \leq x)\]

Key properties: - \(F\) is non-decreasing. - \(F(-\infty) = 0\); \(F(+\infty) = 1\). - For continuous \(X\): \(P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)\). - For continuous \(X\): \(f(x) = F'(x)\) (the PDF is the derivative of the CDF).

docs.title: 5. Expected Value
docs.text:
The expected value (population mean) \(\mu = E(X)\) is the probability-weighted average of all possible values.

Discrete: $\(E(X) = \sum_{i} x_i\, p(x_i)\)$

Continuous: $\(E(X) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x\, f(x)\, dx\)$

Both are weighted averages — the weights are probabilities (discrete) or probability densities (continuous).

docs.title: Expectation Rules
docs.text:
For constants \(a\), \(b\) and random variables \(X\), \(Y\):

Rule Formula Linearity \(E(aX + b) = a\,E(X) + b\) Additivity \(E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y)\) Constant \(E(b) = b\) Independence \(E(XY) = E(X)\,E(Y)\) if \(X \perp Y\)

docs.title: 6. Variance
docs.text:
The variance \(\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2\) measures the average squared deviation from the mean:

\[\text{Var}(X) = E\!\left[(X - \mu)^2\right]\]

Computational shortcut (expand and simplify using linearity of \(E\)):

\[\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \left[E(X)\right]^2\]

docs.title: Variance Rules
docs.text: Rule Formula Intuition Scalar \(\text{Var}(aX) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X)\) Doubling \(X\) quadruples spread Shift \(\text{Var}(X + b) = \text{Var}(X)\) Adding a constant shifts but doesn't stretch Linear combo \(\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X)\) Combines the two rules above Sum \(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)\) Spreads add, with covariance correction Independent sum \(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)\) When \(X \perp Y\), \(\text{Cov}=0\)

docs.title: 7. The Normal Distribution
docs.text:
The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the workhorse of econometrics. If \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\):

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad x \in (-\infty, +\infty)\]

Key properties: - Symmetric, bell-shaped, centred at \(\mu\). - Fully characterised by just two parameters: mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). - \(E(X) = \mu\), \(\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2\).

docs.title: The 68–95–99.7 Rule
docs.text: \[P(\mu - \sigma < X < \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.683$$ $$P(\mu - 2\sigma < X < \mu + 2\sigma) \approx 0.954$$ $$P(\mu - 3\sigma < X < \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.997\]

docs.title: Standardisation
docs.text:
Any \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) random variable can be transformed to the standard normal \(Z \sim N(0,1)\):

\[Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\]

This is why z-scores from Lesson M01.L01 appear here: standardising a sample observation is the sample-level analogue of this population-level transformation. Standard normal probabilities are tabulated in every econometrics textbook.

docs.title: 8. The \(t\)-Distribution
docs.text:
When \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) but \(\sigma^2\) is unknown and must be estimated from data, we can no longer use the \(Z\) statistic. Instead:

\[t = rac{ ar{X} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}\]

The \(t\)-distribution with \( u\) degrees of freedom is: - Symmetric and bell-shaped like the normal, but with heavier tails. - As \( u o \infty\), \(t_ u o N(0,1)\). - Used for all OLS coefficient hypothesis tests: \(t = \hat{ eta}/ ext{se}(\hat{ eta})\).

In practice with econometric samples (\(n > 120\)), the \(t\) and \(Z\) critical values are nearly identical.

docs.title: 9. The Chi-Squared Distribution (\(\chi^2\))
docs.text:
If \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_k \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)\), then:

\[W = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2 \sim \chi^2_k\]

The \(\chi^2_k\) distribution: - Is right-skewed (always \(\geq 0\)). - Has mean \(k\) and variance \(2k\). - Arises naturally when estimating variance: \((n-1)s^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\). - Used for Breusch–Pagan heteroskedasticity tests and goodness-of-fit tests.

docs.title: 10. The F-Distribution
docs.text:
If \(W_1 \sim \chi^2_{d_1}\) and \(W_2 \sim \chi^2_{d_2}\) are independent:

\[F = rac{W_1/d_1}{W_2/d_2} \sim F_{d_1, d_2}\]

The F-distribution with numerator degrees of freedom \(d_1\) and denominator \(d_2\): - Is right-skewed, always \(\geq 0\). - Arises when testing multiple hypotheses simultaneously in OLS. - The overall F-test in regression: "Are any regressors jointly significant?"

Key relationship: \(t_ u^2 = F_{1, u}\). A squared \(t\)-statistic with \( u\) df equals an F-statistic with \((1, u)\) df.

docs.title: Standardising a Normal Variable & Finding Probabilities
docs.text:
The hourly wage of a randomly selected Australian full-time worker is normally distributed with mean \(\mu = \$38\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = \$12\).

Question: What proportion of workers earn between $26 and $56 per hour?

Step 1 — Standardise the bounds:

\[Z_1 = \frac{26 - 38}{12} = \frac{-12}{12} = -1\] \[Z_2 = \frac{56 - 38}{12} = \frac{18}{12} = 1.5\]

Step 2 — Find probabilities using the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\):

\[P(26 \leq W \leq 56) = P(-1 \leq Z \leq 1.5) = \Phi(1.5) - \Phi(-1)\]

From tables (or R: pnorm(1.5) - pnorm(-1)):

\[\Phi(1.5) = 0.9332, \qquad \Phi(-1) = 1 - \Phi(1) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587\] \[P(26 \leq W \leq 56) = 0.9332 - 0.1587 = \mathbf{0.7745}\]

Interpretation: About 77.5% of Australian full-time workers earn between $26 and $56 per hour under this model.

Step 3 — Variance property check:

If we double all wages (\(V = 2W\)): $\(E(V) = 2 \times 38 = \$76, \qquad \text{Var}(V) = 4 \times 144 = 576 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sigma_V = \$24\)$

The standard deviation also doubled — confirming \(\text{Var}(aX) = a^2\text{Var}(X)\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Economic variables are normally distributed — or if not, I should use a different method."

The normal distribution is central to econometric theory because of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT): as sample size \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) and OLS estimators \(\hat{\beta}\) converge to normal, regardless of the distribution of the underlying data.

This means: 1. You do not need wages, prices, or GDP to be normally distributed. 2. Inference (t-tests, F-tests) is justified in large samples even when residuals are skewed or heavy-tailed. 3. In small samples, however, the CLT has not kicked in, and non-normal residuals can distort inference. This is why residual diagnostics matter.

Many economic variables are inherently skewed (income, house prices, firm sizes follow Pareto or log-normal distributions). The log transformation \(\ln(Y)\) often produces a more symmetric variable and is used extensively in econometrics — not to "fix" normality, but because log-linear models have natural economic interpretations (elasticities).

docs.title: Prompt 1
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be the annual return (%) on an Australian equity fund, with \(X \sim N(8, 25)\) (mean 8%, variance 25, so \(\sigma = 5\%\)).

(a) What is the probability of a negative return in any given year? (b) What return corresponds to the 95th percentile?

Answer **(a)** $P(X < 0)$: standardise: $$Z = \frac{0 - 8}{5} = -1.6$$ $$P(X < 0) = \Phi(-1.6) = 1 - \Phi(1.6) = 1 - 0.9452 = \mathbf{0.0548}$$ About 5.5% chance of a negative return each year. **(b)** The 95th percentile of $N(0,1)$ is $z_{0.95} = 1.645$. $$X_{0.95} = \mu + z_{0.95} \cdot \sigma = 8 + 1.645 \times 5 = 8 + 8.225 = \mathbf{16.225\%}$$ A return of approximately 16.2% is at the 95th percentile. *In R:* `qnorm(0.95, mean=8, sd=5)` gives the same answer.

docs.title: Prompt 2
docs.text:
A discrete random variable \(X\) represents the number of Reserve Bank of Australia rate cuts in a given year, with the following distribution:

\(x\) 0 1 2 3 \(P(X=x)\) 0.30 0.40 0.20 0.10

(a) Compute \(E(X)\). (b) Compute \(\text{Var}(X)\) using the formula \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\). (c) If each rate cut reduces the mortgage rate by 0.25%, and \(Y = 0.25X\) represents the total rate reduction, find \(E(Y)\) and \(\text{Var}(Y)\).

Answer **(a) Expected value:** $$E(X) = 0(0.30) + 1(0.40) + 2(0.20) + 3(0.10) = 0 + 0.40 + 0.40 + 0.30 = \mathbf{1.10}$$ **(b) Variance:** First compute $E(X^2) = 0^2(0.30) + 1^2(0.40) + 2^2(0.20) + 3^2(0.10) = 0 + 0.40 + 0.80 + 0.90 = 2.10$. $$\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 2.10 - (1.10)^2 = 2.10 - 1.21 = \mathbf{0.89}$$ **(c) Linear transformation $Y = 0.25X$:** $$E(Y) = 0.25 \times E(X) = 0.25 \times 1.10 = \mathbf{0.275\%}$$ $$\text{Var}(Y) = (0.25)^2 \times \text{Var}(X) = 0.0625 \times 0.89 = \mathbf{0.0556}$$ The expected total mortgage rate reduction is 0.275%, with standard deviation $\sqrt{0.0556} \approx 0.236\%$.

docs.title: Prompt 3
docs.text:
Explain in your own words: (a) Why does the \(t\)-distribution have heavier tails than the standard normal? (b) In a regression with \(n = 50\) observations and \(k = 4\) regressors (including the intercept), what are the degrees of freedom for the \(t\)-test on each coefficient? For the overall \(F\)-test?

Answer **(a)** The $t$-statistic is $(\bar{X} - \mu) / (s/\sqrt{n})$. Unlike the $Z$-statistic, the denominator $s$ is itself a random variable — it varies from sample to sample. When $s$ happens to be small (underestimating $\sigma$), the $t$-statistic is inflated. This additional uncertainty from estimating $\sigma$ makes extreme values of $t$ more probable than extreme values of $Z$, producing heavier tails. As $n \to \infty$, $s \to \sigma$ and the extra uncertainty vanishes — so $t_\nu \to N(0,1)$. **(b)** With $n = 50$ observations and $k = 4$ parameters (including intercept): - **$t$-test degrees of freedom:** $n - k = 50 - 4 = \mathbf{46}$ df. Each individual coefficient is tested against $t_{46}$. - **$F$-test degrees of freedom:** The overall $F$-test has numerator df $= k - 1 = 3$ (the 3 slope coefficients, excluding the intercept) and denominator df $= n - k = 46$. So $F \sim F_{3, 46}$. *Practical note:* With 46 df, the $t_{46}$ critical value at the 5% level is approximately 2.013, very close to the normal critical value of 1.960.

docs.title: Lesson M01.L04: Joint Distributions, Conditional Expectation, and Covariance
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 01 — Probability & Statistics Review Level Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD) Duration 30–35 minutes Learning Objective Understand joint and conditional distributions; compute covariance and correlation; correctly interpret the relationship between independence and zero covariance Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Appendix B.2–B.4

docs.title: Joint Distributions
docs.text:
When two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are observed together, their behaviour is described by a joint distribution.

Discrete case — Joint PMF:

\[f(x, y) = P(X = x,\ Y = y)\]

The joint PMF satisfies \(\sum_x \sum_y f(x,y) = 1\).

Continuous case — Joint PDF:

\[f(x,y) \geq 0 \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y)\, dx\, dy = 1\]

Marginal distributions recover the behaviour of each variable alone by summing (or integrating) over the other:

\[f_X(x) = \sum_y f(x, y) \qquad \text{(discrete)}\] \[f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y)\, dy \qquad \text{(continuous)}\]

In economics, a joint distribution is natural whenever two outcomes are simultaneously determined — for example, an individual's wage and their years of schooling both emerge from the same labour-market process.

docs.title: Conditional Distributions and Conditional Expectation
docs.text:
The conditional PMF/PDF of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is:

\[f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)}, \qquad f_X(x) > 0\]

The conditional expectation \(E(Y \mid X = x)\) is the expected value of \(Y\) once we fix \(X\) at the value \(x\):

\[E(Y \mid X = x) = \sum_y y \cdot f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) \qquad \text{(discrete)}\] \[E(Y \mid X = x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \cdot f_{Y|X}(y \mid x)\, dy \qquad \text{(continuous)}\]

Economic interpretation: \(E(\text{wage} \mid \text{education} = 16)\) is the average wage we would expect for a worker with exactly 16 years of schooling — the conditional mean of wages within that schooling group.

docs.title: Law of Iterated Expectations
docs.text:
One of the most useful results in probability theory:

\[E\bigl[E(Y \mid X)\bigr] = E(Y)\]

The "outer" expectation is taken over the distribution of \(X\). In words: if we first compute the conditional mean of \(Y\) for each value of \(X\), and then average those conditional means using the distribution of \(X\), we recover the unconditional mean of \(Y\).

Why it matters in econometrics: The law of iterated expectations underpins the zero conditional mean assumption \(E(u \mid x) = 0\) in regression — if the error has zero conditional mean for every value of \(x\), it also has unconditional mean zero: \(E(u) = E[E(u \mid x)] = 0\).

docs.title: Covariance
docs.text:
Covariance measures the direction and degree to which \(X\) and \(Y\) move together:

\[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E\bigl[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)\bigr]\]

Computational shortcut (USYD notation):

\[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)\]

Sample covariance (used in estimation):

\[\widehat{\text{Cov}}(X, Y) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{n - 1}\]

Key properties:

Property Formula Symmetry \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \text{Cov}(Y,X)\) Cov with constant \(\text{Cov}(X, a) = 0\) Cov with itself \(\text{Cov}(X, X) = \text{Var}(X)\) Scaling \(\text{Cov}(aX, bY) = ab\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)\) Linearity \(\text{Cov}(X + Z, Y) = \text{Cov}(X, Y) + \text{Cov}(Z, Y)\)

Variance of a sum (crucial for regression asymptotics):

\[\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)\]

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated, \(\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)\).

docs.title: Correlation Coefficient
docs.text:
Covariance is scale-dependent. The Pearson correlation coefficient standardises it to the range \([-1, 1]\):

\[\rho_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}\]

where \(\sigma_X = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\) and \(\sigma_Y = \sqrt{\text{Var}(Y)}\).

  • \(\rho = +1\): perfect positive linear relationship
  • \(\rho = -1\): perfect negative linear relationship
  • \(\rho = 0\): no linear relationship (but see the common misconception below)

Sample correlation (USYD formula):

\[r_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} = \frac{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \sum(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]

docs.title: Independence and Zero Covariance
docs.text:
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(E(XY) = E(X)E(Y)\), which implies:

\[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y) = 0 \implies \rho_{XY} = 0\]

Independence \(\Rightarrow\) zero covariance (always).

Zero covariance \(\not\Rightarrow\) independence (in general).

The exception: if \((X, Y)\) follow a bivariate normal distribution, then \(\rho_{XY} = 0\) does imply independence. This is a special property of the normal distribution, not a general rule.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"If Cov(X, Y) = 0 (or ρ = 0), then X and Y are independent."

This is false in general. Zero covariance means there is no linear relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\), but a nonlinear relationship can still exist.

Classic counterexample: Let \(X \sim N(0,1)\) and \(Y = X^2\). Then:

\[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E(X \cdot X^2) - E(X)E(X^2) = E(X^3) - 0 = 0\]

(since \(E(X^3) = 0\) for a symmetric distribution). Yet \(Y\) is completely determined by \(X\) — they are maximally dependent. Covariance and correlation only capture linear association.

The one valid exception: For the bivariate normal distribution, \(\rho = 0 \Leftrightarrow\) independence. This is a special property of the normal family and does not extend to other distributions.

Econometric relevance: The assumption \(\text{Cov}(u, x) = 0\) in OLS is weaker than the assumption \(E(u \mid x) = 0\). The latter (zero conditional mean) implies the former (zero covariance), but not vice versa. OLS unbiasedness requires the stronger condition.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1

Consider the joint distribution of \(X\) (hours studied per week) and \(Y\) (exam score, out of 100):

\(Y = 60\) \(Y = 80\) \(Y = 95\) \(P(X=x)\) \(X = 5\) 0.15 0.10 0.05 0.30 \(X = 10\) 0.10 0.25 0.10 0.45 \(X = 20\) 0.05 0.10 0.10 0.25

(a) Compute \(E(X)\), \(E(Y)\), and \(E(XY)\). (b) Compute \(\text{Cov}(X, Y)\). (c) Compute \(\rho_{XY}\).

Answer **(a)** $$E(X) = 5(0.30) + 10(0.45) + 20(0.25) = 1.50 + 4.50 + 5.00 = 11.00$$ $$E(Y) = 60(0.30) + 80(0.45) + 95(0.25) = 18 + 36 + 23.75 = 77.75$$ $$E(XY) = 5(60)(0.15) + 5(80)(0.10) + 5(95)(0.05)$$ $$+ 10(60)(0.10) + 10(80)(0.25) + 10(95)(0.10)$$ $$+ 20(60)(0.05) + 20(80)(0.10) + 20(95)(0.10)$$ $$= 45 + 40 + 23.75 + 60 + 200 + 95 + 60 + 160 + 190 = 873.75$$ **(b)** $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 873.75 - (11.00)(77.75) = 873.75 - 855.25 = 18.50$$ **(c)** Compute variances: $$E(X^2) = 25(0.30)+100(0.45)+400(0.25) = 7.5+45+100=152.5; \quad \text{Var}(X)=152.5-121=31.5; \quad \sigma_X \approx 5.612$$ $$E(Y^2) = 3600(0.30)+6400(0.45)+9025(0.25) = 1080+2880+2256.25=6216.25; \quad \text{Var}(Y)=6216.25-6045.0625=171.19; \quad \sigma_Y \approx 13.084$$ $$\rho_{XY} = \frac{18.50}{5.612 \times 13.084} \approx \frac{18.50}{73.43} \approx 0.252$$ A moderate positive correlation — more study hours is associated with higher scores.

Prompt 2

Let \(X \sim U\{-1, 0, 1\}\) (discrete uniform) and \(Y = X^2\).

(a) Find the joint distribution of \((X, Y)\). (b) Compute \(\text{Cov}(X, Y)\). (c) Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent? Explain.

Answer **(a)** Since $Y$ is a deterministic function of $X$: | $X$ | $Y$ | $P(X=x, Y=y)$ | |---|---|---| | $-1$ | 1 | 1/3 | | 0 | 0 | 1/3 | | 1 | 1 | 1/3 | **(b)** $$E(X) = (-1)(1/3) + 0(1/3) + 1(1/3) = 0$$ $$E(Y) = 1(1/3) + 0(1/3) + 1(1/3) = 2/3$$ $$E(XY) = (-1)(1)(1/3) + (0)(0)(1/3) + (1)(1)(1/3) = -1/3 + 0 + 1/3 = 0$$ $$\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y) = 0 - 0 \cdot (2/3) = 0$$ **(c)** $X$ and $Y$ are **not independent** — knowing $X$ completely determines $Y = X^2$. This is the classic counterexample to "zero covariance implies independence."

Prompt 3

A portfolio holds two assets with returns \(R_1\) and \(R_2\): - \(E(R_1) = 0.08\), \(\text{Var}(R_1) = 0.04\) - \(E(R_2) = 0.12\), \(\text{Var}(R_2) = 0.09\) - \(\text{Cov}(R_1, R_2) = -0.02\)

The portfolio return is \(R_P = 0.5 R_1 + 0.5 R_2\).

(a) Find \(E(R_P)\). (b) Find \(\text{Var}(R_P)\). (c) Interpret the effect of the negative covariance on portfolio risk.

Answer **(a)** $$E(R_P) = 0.5 E(R_1) + 0.5 E(R_2) = 0.5(0.08) + 0.5(0.12) = 0.10$$ **(b)** $$\text{Var}(R_P) = 0.5^2 \text{Var}(R_1) + 0.5^2 \text{Var}(R_2) + 2(0.5)(0.5)\text{Cov}(R_1, R_2)$$ $$= 0.25(0.04) + 0.25(0.09) + 0.5(-0.02)$$ $$= 0.01 + 0.0225 - 0.01 = 0.0225$$ **(c)** Without diversification, a naïve average of individual variances would be $0.25(0.04)+0.25(0.09) = 0.0325$. The negative covariance reduces portfolio variance to 0.0225, illustrating the diversification benefit: assets that tend to move in opposite directions lower total portfolio risk.

docs.title: Lesson M01.L05: Sampling Distributions and Sample Statistics
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 01 — Probability & Statistics Review Level Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD) Duration 30–35 minutes Learning Objective Define and distinguish population vs sample; understand the sampling distribution of the sample mean; apply the Central Limit Theorem; compute standard errors; articulate why the CLT justifies large-sample inference in econometrics Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Appendix C.1–C.3

docs.title: Population vs Sample
docs.text:
In econometrics we almost always want to know something about a population — the complete set of units (individuals, firms, countries) to which our conclusions are meant to apply. Because populations are typically unobservable or too large to measure fully, we work with a sample — a subset drawn from the population.

Concept Population Sample Size \(N\) (often unknown/infinite) \(n\) (known, finite) Mean \(\mu\) (parameter, unknown) \(\bar{X}\) (statistic, computed) Variance \(\sigma^2\) (parameter, unknown) \(s^2\) (statistic, computed) Correlation \(\rho\) \(r\)

Random sampling is the process of drawing observations such that each unit has a known probability of selection, and draws are independent. The standard econometric framework assumes simple random sampling (SRS): each unit is equally likely to be selected, and draws are i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed).

docs.title: Sample Mean as an Estimator
docs.text:
Given a random sample \(\{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\}\) where each \(X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} (\mu, \sigma^2)\), the sample mean is:

\[\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\]

The sample mean is an estimator of the population mean \(\mu\). It is a random variable — its value changes from sample to sample.

docs.title: Properties of Estimators
docs.text:
An estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) of a parameter \(\theta\) is evaluated on three criteria:

1. Unbiasedness

\[E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\]

An estimator is unbiased if its expected value (averaging over all possible samples) equals the true parameter. The sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu\):

\[E(\bar{X}) = E\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} E(X_i) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot n\mu = \mu \checkmark\]

The sample variance \(s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\) (the \(n-1\) denominator corrects for the degrees of freedom used to estimate \(\bar{X}\)).

2. Efficiency (Minimum Variance)

Among all unbiased estimators of \(\theta\), the efficient estimator has the smallest variance. A more efficient estimator wastes less information from the data. The Cramér–Rao lower bound gives the theoretical minimum variance for an unbiased estimator.

3. Consistency

An estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is consistent if it converges in probability to the true value as \(n \to \infty\):

\[\hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \theta \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty\]

The sample mean is consistent for \(\mu\) by the Law of Large Numbers (LLN): as the sample grows, \(\bar{X}\) gets arbitrarily close to \(\mu\).

Mnemonic for graduate study: Unbiasedness is a finite-sample property (holds for any \(n\)). Consistency is an asymptotic property (holds as \(n \to \infty\)). An estimator can be biased but consistent (e.g., MLE of \(\sigma^2\) divides by \(n\) but still converges to \(\sigma^2\)), or unbiased but inconsistent (theoretically possible, though rare in practice).

docs.title: Sampling Distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
docs.text:
Because \(\bar{X}\) is a random variable, it has its own distribution — the sampling distribution. Its mean and variance follow directly from the properties of \(X_i\):

\[E(\bar{X}) = \mu\] \[\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \text{Var}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Var}(X_i) = \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]

(The cross terms vanish because the \(X_i\) are independent.)

Standard error of the mean:

\[SE(\bar{X}) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(\bar{X})} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown, so we replace it with the sample standard deviation \(s\):

\[\widehat{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Key observation: \(SE(\bar{X})\) shrinks at rate \(1/\sqrt{n}\). Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.

docs.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
docs.text:
The Central Limit Theorem is arguably the most important result in applied statistics:

Theorem: Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\). Then as \(n \to \infty\):

\[\bar{X} \xrightarrow{d} N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\]

Equivalently, the standardised sample mean converges in distribution to a standard normal:

\[Z_n = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)\]

What the CLT says: No matter what shape the underlying population distribution has (uniform, exponential, skewed, multimodal — as long as it has finite variance), the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as the sample size grows.

What the CLT does NOT say: The individual observations \(X_i\) are not normally distributed. Only the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is approximately normal. Many students confuse these — see the Common Misconception section.

In practice: The approximation is generally good for \(n \geq 30\) with symmetric populations, and may require \(n \geq 100\)–\(200\) for heavily skewed distributions.

docs.title: Why the CLT Matters for Econometrics
docs.text:
The CLT provides the large-sample (asymptotic) justification for the t-tests and F-tests used throughout econometrics:

  1. OLS estimators \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\) can be written as weighted sums of the \(Y_i\) (hence weighted sums of i.i.d. observations). By the CLT, their sampling distributions are approximately normal in large samples.

  2. t-tests for regression coefficients: the test statistic \(t = \hat{\beta}_1 / SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\) follows (approximately) a \(t\)-distribution in finite samples and converges to \(N(0,1)\) as \(n \to \infty\).

  3. Without the CLT, we would need to assume the error term \(u\) is normally distributed (Wooldridge's Assumption MLR.6) to justify exact finite-sample t and F tests. With the CLT, normality of \(u\) is only needed for small samples — large samples let the CLT do the work.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Scenario: A USYD researcher samples hourly wages (in AUD) from 64 casual workers. The sample yields \(\bar{X} = \$32.50\) and \(s = \$8.00\).

Step 1: Compute the standard error.

\[\widehat{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{8.00}{\sqrt{64}} = \frac{8.00}{8} = \$1.00\]

Step 2: Apply the CLT.

Since \(n = 64 \geq 30\) and wages are roughly symmetric, the CLT guarantees:

\[\bar{X} \approx N(32.50,\ 1.00^2)\]

Step 3: Compute a probability.

What is the probability that a sample mean from repeated samples of size 64 would be at least \(\$34.00\)?

\[P(\bar{X} \geq 34.00) = P\!\left(Z \geq \frac{34.00 - 32.50}{1.00}\right) = P(Z \geq 1.50) \approx 0.0668\]

So there is about a 6.7% chance of observing a sample mean this high or higher if the true population mean is \(\$32.50\).

Step 4: Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\).

\[\bar{X} \pm 1.96 \times SE(\bar{X}) = 32.50 \pm 1.96(1.00) = [30.54,\ 34.46]\]

We are 95% confident the population mean hourly wage lies between $30.54 and $34.46.

Interpretation: The CLT transforms a point estimate ($32.50) into an interval that quantifies our uncertainty about the population mean, even though wages are not normally distributed in the population.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"The CLT says that the data is approximately normally distributed in large samples."

This is false. The CLT says that the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is approximately normal — not the individual observations.

Illustration: Suppose individual wages follow a highly right-skewed distribution (many low-wage workers, a few very high earners). Even with \(n = 1000\):

  • A histogram of the raw wage data will still look right-skewed.
  • A histogram of sample means (each computed from 1000 draws, repeated across many simulated datasets) will look approximately normal.

These are completely different objects. The CLT applies to the second, not the first.

Why this matters: - For inference: t-tests on \(\bar{X}\) are valid in large samples even if individual wages are skewed (CLT justifies normality of \(\bar{X}\)). - For modelling: If you assume individual wages are normal for some modelling purpose (e.g., MLE), you need to verify this separately — the CLT does not help you there.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1

Weekly household incomes in a city have population mean \(\mu = \$2{,}500\) and population standard deviation \(\sigma = \$600\). A random sample of \(n = 100\) households is drawn.

(a) What is \(E(\bar{X})\) and \(SE(\bar{X})\)? (b) Using the CLT, what is the probability that the sample mean exceeds \(\$2{,}600\)? (c) What sample size would be needed to halve the standard error?

Answer **(a)** $$E(\bar{X}) = \mu = \$2{,}500$$ $$SE(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{600}{\sqrt{100}} = \frac{600}{10} = \$60$$ **(b)** By CLT, $\bar{X} \approx N(2500, 60^2)$. $$P(\bar{X} > 2600) = P\!\left(Z > \frac{2600 - 2500}{60}\right) = P(Z > 1.667) \approx 0.0478$$ About a 4.8% chance. **(c)** We need $SE(\bar{X}) = 60/2 = 30$, so: $$\frac{600}{\sqrt{n}} = 30 \implies \sqrt{n} = 20 \implies n = 400$$ Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error (the $1/\sqrt{n}$ relationship).

Prompt 2

An economist estimates a sample variance \(s^2 = 25\) from \(n = 36\) observations.

(a) Compute the estimated standard error of the mean. (b) Explain in one sentence why the denominator of \(s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) uses \(n-1\) instead of \(n\). (c) Suppose a colleague uses \(\tilde{s}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) instead. Is \(\tilde{s}^2\) unbiased for \(\sigma^2\)? Is it consistent?

Answer **(a)** $$\widehat{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{25}}{\sqrt{36}} = \frac{5}{6} \approx 0.833$$ **(b)** Using $n-1$ (Bessel's correction) corrects for the fact that $\bar{X}$ was estimated from the same data — the deviations $X_i - \bar{X}$ sum to zero by construction, so only $n-1$ of them are "free", leaving one degree of freedom consumed. **(c)** - $\tilde{s}^2$ is **biased**: $E(\tilde{s}^2) = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2$. - $\tilde{s}^2$ is **consistent**: as $n \to \infty$, $\frac{n-1}{n} \to 1$, so $\tilde{s}^2 \xrightarrow{p} \sigma^2$. This is an example of a biased but consistent estimator.

Prompt 3

Three different estimators of the population mean \(\mu\) are proposed from a sample of size \(n\):

\[\hat{\mu}_1 = \bar{X} \qquad \hat{\mu}_2 = X_1 \qquad \hat{\mu}_3 = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{2}\]

(a) Is each estimator unbiased for \(\mu\)? (Assume i.i.d. data with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).) (b) Compute \(\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_1)\), \(\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_2)\), \(\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_3)\) for general \(n\). (c) Which estimator is most efficient for \(n > 2\)? Which is least efficient? (d) Is \(\hat{\mu}_2\) consistent?

Answer **(a)** All three are unbiased: - $E(\bar{X}) = \mu$ ✓ - $E(X_1) = \mu$ ✓ - $E\!\left(\frac{X_1+X_2}{2}\right) = \frac{\mu + \mu}{2} = \mu$ ✓ **(b)** - $\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_1) = \sigma^2/n$ - $\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_2) = \sigma^2$ - $\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_3) = \frac{1}{4}(\sigma^2 + \sigma^2) = \sigma^2/2$ **(c)** For $n > 2$: $\hat{\mu}_1$ is most efficient (smallest variance $\sigma^2/n$); $\hat{\mu}_2$ is least efficient (variance $\sigma^2$, independent of $n$). **(d)** $\hat{\mu}_2$ is **not consistent**: $\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}_2) = \sigma^2$ for all $n$ — adding more data never reduces the variance of an estimator that ignores all data except the first observation.

docs.title: Lesson M01.L06: Hypothesis Testing
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 01 — Probability & Statistics Review Level Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD) Duration 30–35 minutes Learning Objective Set up and execute a formal hypothesis test; interpret the p-value correctly; distinguish Type I and Type II errors; connect confidence intervals to hypothesis tests; avoid the most common conceptual errors about "accepting" the null Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Appendix C.6

docs.title: The Framework
docs.text:
Hypothesis testing is a formal procedure for deciding, on the basis of sample data, whether a claim about a population parameter is plausible.

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): The maintained claim, assumed true until evidence overturns it. Usually a specific value:

\[H_0 : \mu = \mu_0 \qquad \text{(e.g., } H_0 : \mu = 50{,}000 \text{)}\]

Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\): The claim we would accept if \(H_0\) is rejected. Can be:

Type Form When to Use Two-sided \(H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0\) No prior directional belief One-sided (upper) \(H_1: \mu > \mu_0\) Theory predicts parameter is larger One-sided (lower) \(H_1: \mu < \mu_0\) Theory predicts parameter is smaller

Significance level \(\alpha\): The maximum tolerated probability of incorrectly rejecting a true \(H_0\). Common choices: \(\alpha = 0.05\) (5%) or \(\alpha = 0.01\) (1%).

docs.title: Errors in Hypothesis Testing
docs.text:
\(H_0\) is TRUE \(H_0\) is FALSE Reject \(H_0\) Type I Error (probability = \(\alpha\)) Correct Decision (power = \(1-\beta\)) Fail to reject \(H_0\) Correct Decision Type II Error (probability = \(\beta\))
  • Type I error (false positive): Rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true. Controlled by choosing \(\alpha\).
  • Type II error (false negative): Failing to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_1\) is true. Its probability \(\beta\) depends on the true parameter value, sample size, and \(\alpha\).
  • Power \(= 1 - \beta\): the probability of correctly rejecting a false \(H_0\). A good test has high power.

There is an inherent trade-off: lowering \(\alpha\) (stricter standard for rejection) reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors (lower power).

docs.title: Test Statistic
docs.text:
For testing \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) with a sample of size \(n\), the test statistic is:

\[t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]
  • Numerator: observed distance of the sample mean from the null value
  • Denominator: \(SE(\bar{X}) = s/\sqrt{n}\), the standard error (estimated standard deviation of \(\bar{X}\))

Under \(H_0\) and either (a) normality of \(X_i\), or (b) large \(n\) (CLT), this statistic follows a \(t\)-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom:

\[t \sim t_{n-1} \qquad \text{under } H_0\]

As \(n \to \infty\), \(t_{n-1} \to N(0,1)\).

docs.title: The p-value
docs.text:
The p-value is the probability, computed assuming \(H_0\) is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed:

\[\text{p-value} = P(|T| \geq |t_{\text{obs}}| \mid H_0 \text{ true}) \qquad \text{(two-sided)}\] \[\text{p-value} = P(T \geq t_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0 \text{ true}) \qquad \text{(one-sided upper)}\]

Decision rule: Reject \(H_0\) if:

\[\text{p-value} < \alpha\]

Equivalently, using critical values: reject \(H_0\) if \(|t_{\text{obs}}| > t_{n-1,\, \alpha/2}\) (two-sided) or \(t_{\text{obs}} > t_{n-1,\, \alpha}\) (one-sided upper).

A small p-value means the data would be very unlikely if \(H_0\) were true — this is evidence against \(H_0\).

docs.title: Two-sided vs One-sided Tests
docs.text:
For a two-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) with large \(n\):

  • Critical value: \(\pm 1.96\) (from \(N(0,1)\); for \(t_{n-1}\), use the appropriate table value)
  • Rejection region: \(|t| > 1.96\)

For a one-sided upper test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) with large \(n\):

  • Critical value: \(+1.645\)
  • Rejection region: \(t > 1.645\)

Use one-sided tests only when there is a strong a priori theoretical reason to believe the parameter can only deviate in one direction. Otherwise, use two-sided tests to avoid inflating the apparent significance.

docs.title: Confidence Intervals as the Dual of Hypothesis Tests
docs.text:
A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is:

\[\bar{X} \pm t_{n-1,\, 0.025} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

For large \(n\), \(t_{n-1,\, 0.025} \approx 1.96\):

\[\bar{X} \pm 1.96 \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Duality result: A two-sided test at significance level \(\alpha\) rejects \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) if and only if \(\mu_0\) falls outside the \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval.

The confidence interval is therefore the set of all parameter values that would not be rejected by the data. It gives richer information than a simple reject/fail-to-reject decision.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Economic question: Is the average annual wage of economics graduates equal to $50,000?

Setup:

Value Sample size \(n = 49\) Sample mean \(\bar{X} = \$52{,}500\) Sample std dev \(s = \$10{,}500\) Null value \(\mu_0 = \$50{,}000\) Significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\)

Step 1: State hypotheses.

\[H_0: \mu = 50{,}000 \qquad H_1: \mu \neq 50{,}000\]

Two-sided, because we are simply asking whether the true mean differs from $50,000 in either direction.

Step 2: Compute the test statistic.

\[SE(\bar{X}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{10{,}500}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{10{,}500}{7} = 1{,}500\] \[t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{SE(\bar{X})} = \frac{52{,}500 - 50{,}000}{1{,}500} = \frac{2{,}500}{1{,}500} \approx 1.667\]

Step 3: Find the p-value.

With \(df = 48\), the critical value at \(\alpha = 0.05\) (two-sided) is approximately \(t_{48,\, 0.025} \approx 2.011\).

Using tables or software: \(P(|T| \geq 1.667) \approx 0.102\).

\[\text{p-value} \approx 0.102\]

Step 4: Make the decision.

\[0.102 > 0.05 \implies \text{Fail to reject } H_0\]

Step 5: Interpret.

At the 5% significance level, we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude that the average wage of economics graduates differs from $50,000. The sample mean of $52,500 is about 1.67 standard errors above the null value — this could reasonably occur by chance even if \(\mu = \$50,000\).

Confidence interval check:

\[52{,}500 \pm 2.011 \times 1{,}500 = 52{,}500 \pm 3{,}017 = [49{,}483,\ 55{,}517]\]

Since $50,000 lies inside the interval, we confirm: fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). ✓

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
There are two critical conceptual errors, both extremely common even among researchers:

Misconception 1: "Fail to reject \(H_0\)" means "Accept \(H_0\)".

This is wrong. When we fail to reject \(H_0\), we are saying: "The data are not inconsistent with \(H_0\) at this significance level." This is a fundamentally weaker claim than saying \(H_0\) is true. We simply do not have enough evidence to rule it out.

The hypothesis-testing framework is asymmetric by design: we set up \(H_0\) as the default, and reject only when the evidence is strong. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Analogy: A not-guilty verdict in court means "not proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt" — it does not mean the defendant is innocent.

Misconception 2: "The p-value is the probability that \(H_0\) is true."

This is wrong. The p-value is a statement about the data conditional on \(H_0\) being true. In the frequentist framework, \(H_0\) is either true or false — it does not have a probability. The p-value answers: "If \(H_0\) were true, how surprising would it be to see data as extreme as ours?"

Correct interpretations: - ✅ "The p-value of 0.102 means that, if the true mean wage were $50,000, there would be a 10.2% chance of observing a sample mean at least $2,500 away from $50,000." - ❌ "There is a 10.2% probability that \(H_0\) is true."

Econometric relevance: These errors lead to overconfidence (treating failure to reject as confirmation) and misreporting (describing p-values as posterior probabilities). At the graduate level, precision in language is essential.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1

A researcher tests whether the return on a portfolio is zero (no abnormal returns). From 100 monthly observations: \(\bar{R} = 0.8\%\), \(s = 4.5\%\).

(a) State \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) (two-sided). (b) Compute the test statistic. (c) At \(\alpha = 0.05\), use the critical value \(\pm 1.984\) (\(df = 99\)). Make a decision. (d) Compute the 95% confidence interval for the population mean return.

Answer **(a)** $$H_0: \mu = 0\% \qquad H_1: \mu \neq 0\%$$ **(b)** $$SE = \frac{4.5}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.45$$ $$t = \frac{0.8 - 0}{0.45} \approx 1.778$$ **(c)** Since $|1.778| < 1.984$, we **fail to reject $H_0$** at $\alpha = 0.05$. There is insufficient evidence of abnormal returns. **(d)** $$0.8\% \pm 1.984 \times 0.45\% = 0.8\% \pm 0.893\% = [-0.093\%,\ 1.693\%]$$ The interval contains 0%, confirming failure to reject. The researcher cannot claim statistically significant abnormal returns.

Prompt 2

A government economist claims that a new training programme raises average weekly earnings by more than $100. A sample of 36 programme participants yields \(\bar{X} = \$120\) gain, \(s = \$180\).

(a) Set up a one-sided hypothesis test appropriate for this question. (b) Compute the test statistic. (c) At \(\alpha = 0.05\), the critical value is \(t_{35,\, 0.05} \approx 1.690\). What is the conclusion? (d) Would the conclusion change at \(\alpha = 0.10\) (critical value \(\approx 1.306\))?

Answer **(a)** We want to test whether the gain exceeds \$100, so: $$H_0: \mu = 100 \qquad H_1: \mu > 100 \qquad \text{(one-sided upper)}$$ **(b)** $$SE = \frac{180}{\sqrt{36}} = 30$$ $$t = \frac{120 - 100}{30} = \frac{20}{30} \approx 0.667$$ **(c)** Since $0.667 < 1.690$, we **fail to reject $H_0$** at $\alpha = 0.05$. The sample provides insufficient evidence that the programme raises earnings by more than \$100. **(d)** Since $0.667 < 1.306$, we still fail to reject at $\alpha = 0.10$. The result is not statistically significant at conventional levels — the \$120 observed gain is well within what we'd expect by chance under $H_0: \mu = 100$.

Prompt 3

In a sample of 25 firms, average R&D expenditure as a percentage of revenue is \(\bar{X} = 4.2\%\) with \(s = 1.8\%\). An industry report claims the true mean is 3.5%.

(a) Test \(H_0: \mu = 3.5\%\) vs \(H_1: \mu \neq 3.5\%\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) (\(df = 24\), critical value \(\approx \pm 2.064\)). (b) Compute the p-value bracket using t-tables (hint: where does \(t_{\text{obs}}\) fall between critical values for various \(\alpha\)?). (c) Construct a 99% confidence interval for \(\mu\) (\(t_{24,\, 0.005} \approx 2.797\)). Does it contain 3.5%? (d) Write a one-sentence non-technical conclusion for a policy report.

Answer **(a)** $$SE = \frac{1.8}{\sqrt{25}} = 0.36$$ $$t = \frac{4.2 - 3.5}{0.36} = \frac{0.7}{0.36} \approx 1.944$$ Since $|1.944| < 2.064$, we **fail to reject $H_0$** at $\alpha = 0.05$. **(b)** From $t_{24}$ tables, $t_{0.025} \approx 2.064$ and $t_{0.05} \approx 1.711$. Our $t_{\text{obs}} \approx 1.944$ falls between them, so the two-sided p-value is between 0.05 and 0.10. We have weak evidence against $H_0$ but not at the 5% level. **(c)** $$4.2 \pm 2.797 \times 0.36 = 4.2 \pm 1.007 = [3.193\%,\ 5.207\%]$$ The interval contains 3.5%, consistent with failure to reject at the 5% level (and also at the 1% level, since 3.5% is inside the 99% CI). **(d)** "Based on our sample of 25 firms, we cannot rule out that the true average R&D expenditure rate equals the industry benchmark of 3.5% of revenue, though the observed average of 4.2% suggests actual spending may be somewhat higher."

docs.title: Lesson M02.L01: The Simple Linear Regression Model
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 02 — Simple Regression Analysis Level Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD) Duration 30–35 minutes Learning Objective State and interpret the simple linear regression model; articulate the role of the error term and the zero conditional mean assumption; distinguish the population model from sample estimates; correctly frame regression as association rather than causation Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 2 (intro)

docs.title: The Simple Linear Regression Model
docs.text:
The simple linear regression model describes a linear relationship between a dependent variable \(y\) and a single explanatory variable \(x\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

This is the population model — it describes the true (unknown) data-generating process.

Component Name Role \(y\) Dependent variable (regressand) The outcome we want to explain \(x\) Independent variable (regressor, covariate) The explanatory variable \(\beta_0\) Intercept Expected value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\) \(\beta_1\) Slope coefficient Change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\), ceteris paribus \(u\) Error term (disturbance) Everything that affects \(y\) beyond \(x\)

USYD notation note: The ECMT1020 notes also write this as \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon\), using \(\epsilon\) or \(u\) interchangeably for the error term. At ECMT5001 level we follow Wooldridge and use \(u\) throughout.

docs.title: Interpreting the Coefficients
docs.text:
The intercept \(\beta_0\):

\[\beta_0 = E(y \mid x = 0)\]

This is the expected value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\). In many economic applications the intercept has no direct behavioural interpretation (e.g., "wage when education = 0 years"), but it is essential for the model to fit the data correctly — it ensures the regression line passes through the correct point in the \((x, y)\) plane.

The slope \(\beta_1\):

\[\beta_1 = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \qquad \text{(holding } u \text{ fixed)}\]

This is the ceteris paribus effect of \(x\) on \(y\) — the change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\), holding everything else constant.

Wage-education example: In the model $\(\text{wage} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{education} + u\)$ \(\beta_1\) is interpreted as: "One additional year of education is associated with a change of \(\beta_1\) dollars in hourly wage, holding all other factors constant." If \(\beta_1 = 2.5\), each extra year of schooling predicts a $2.50/hour higher wage.

GDP growth example: In the model $\(\text{GDP growth} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{investment rate} + u\)$ \(\beta_1\) measures how much GDP growth changes (in percentage points) for each one-percentage-point increase in the investment rate.

docs.title: The Error Term \(u\)
docs.text:
The error term \(u\) is not noise to be dismissed — it is a substantive part of the model. It captures:

  1. Omitted factors: All other variables that influence \(y\) but are not included in the model. For wages: ability, experience, industry, location, social networks, …
  2. Measurement error: If \(x\) or \(y\) is measured imperfectly, measurement error enters \(u\).
  3. Inherent randomness: Human behaviour is not fully deterministic; even a perfect model would have irreducible randomness.

Because we cannot directly observe \(u\), we must impose assumptions that make the model tractable.

docs.title: The Zero Conditional Mean Assumption
docs.text:
The single most important assumption in simple regression:

\[E(u \mid x) = 0\]

This says: the average value of the unobserved error is zero for every value of \(x\).

What it implies: - The error is uncorrelated with \(x\): \(\text{Cov}(u, x) = 0\) (a weaker condition, necessary but not sufficient) - None of the omitted factors in \(u\) are systematically related to \(x\) - The relationship between \(y\) and \(x\) is correctly specified as linear

From the law of iterated expectations: If \(E(u \mid x) = 0\), then \(E(u) = E[E(u \mid x)] = 0\). So zero conditional mean implies zero unconditional mean — but not vice versa.

Economic example of violation: In the wage-education model, if more-able workers both earn higher wages and choose more schooling, then ability (in \(u\)) is positively correlated with education (\(x\)), violating \(E(u \mid x) = 0\). This causes omitted variable bias — a central problem in empirical economics.

docs.title: Population Model vs Sample Estimates
docs.text:
The population model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\) contains the true parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), which we can never observe. From a sample \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\), we compute estimates \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (the OLS estimators, derived in M02.L02).

The fitted value for observation \(i\) is the model's predicted \(y\):

\[\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\]

The residual for observation \(i\) is the difference between the actual and fitted value:

\[\hat{u}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]

Residuals (\(\hat{u}_i\)) are the sample analogues of the unobservable error terms (\(u_i\)). They can be computed once we have estimates; the errors \(u_i\) can never be directly observed.

Population Sample Model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\) \(y_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i + \hat{u}_i\) Parameters \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) (unknown, fixed) \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\) (computed, random) Disturbances \(u_i\) (unobservable) \(\hat{u}_i\) (residuals, observable) Prediction \(E(y \mid x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) \(\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\)

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Economic question: Do countries with higher investment rates experience faster GDP growth?

Step 1: Define variables and set up the model.

Let: - \(y_i\) = average annual GDP growth rate (%) for country \(i\) over 1990–2020 - \(x_i\) = average gross fixed capital formation as % of GDP (investment rate) for country \(i\)

Population model:

\[\text{GDP growth}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{investment rate}_i + u_i\]

Step 2: Interpret \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) before estimation.

  • \(\beta_0\): the expected GDP growth rate for a country with a 0% investment rate. This is economically implausible (no real-world country has zero investment), so \(\beta_0\) serves mainly as a mathematical anchor for the line.
  • \(\beta_1\): the expected change in GDP growth (in percentage points) for each one-percentage-point increase in the investment rate, holding all else constant. Economic theory (capital accumulation, Solow model) predicts \(\beta_1 > 0\).

Step 3: What does \(u_i\) capture?

The error term \(u_i\) for country \(i\) includes: - Institutional quality (rule of law, corruption) - Human capital and education levels - Technology and productivity shocks - Political stability - Natural resource endowments - Trading partner conditions

Step 4: Assess the zero conditional mean assumption.

Is \(E(u_i \mid \text{investment rate}_i) = 0\) plausible? Potentially not — richer countries with better institutions (captured in \(u_i\)) may also have higher investment rates (\(x_i\)). If so, \(\beta_1\) would be biased upward (part of what we estimate as the "investment effect" would actually reflect institutional quality). This motivates moving to multiple regression (Module 03).

Step 5: Once data are obtained, compute fitted values and residuals.

Suppose OLS estimation yields \(\hat{\beta}_0 = 1.2\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.15\). Then for a country with an investment rate of 25%:

\[\hat{y} = 1.2 + 0.15 \times 25 = 1.2 + 3.75 = 4.95\%\]

If that country's actual GDP growth was 4.20%, its residual is:

\[\hat{u} = 4.20 - 4.95 = -0.75 \text{ pp}\]

The country grew 0.75 percentage points slower than the model predicted — meaning factors in \(u\) (perhaps poor institutions) dragged growth below its predicted level.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"The regression line shows that \(x\) causes \(y\)."

This is false. An estimated regression line shows the conditional mean of \(y\) given \(x\) — a statement about association, not causation. The model

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

describes how \(y\) tends to vary with \(x\) in the data. It does not prove that changing \(x\) would cause \(y\) to change.

Why the distinction matters: If we regress wages on education and find \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 2.5\), this reflects correlation in the data. If more-educated people are also more innately able (an omitted variable in \(u\)), then the "effect" of education is overstated — the regression captures both the true causal effect of education and the omitted ability effect.

When does correlation become causation in regression?

Only under the zero conditional mean assumption \(E(u \mid x) = 0\). If this holds (e.g., in a randomised experiment where \(x\) is randomly assigned), then \(\hat{\beta}_1\) consistently estimates the causal effect. In observational data, we cannot guarantee \(E(u \mid x) = 0\) without additional structural or experimental arguments.

Tools for establishing causation (covered in Modules 06–08): randomised experiments, instrumental variables (IV), regression discontinuity design (RDD), difference-in-differences (DiD). All of these provide ways to make \(E(u \mid x) = 0\) (or an equivalent) more credible.

Practical rule: When reporting regression results, say "a one-unit increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\hat{\beta}_1\) change in \(y\)" rather than "causes" — unless you have a credible identification strategy.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1

A researcher models house prices using the simple regression:

\[\text{price}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{sqft}_i + u_i\]

where price is in $000s and sqft is square footage.

(a) Interpret \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) in economic terms. (b) List three economic factors that would be captured in \(u_i\). (c) OLS yields \(\hat{\beta}_0 = 25.0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.12\). A house has 1,800 sqft and sold for $260,000. Compute the fitted value and the residual. (d) Is the zero conditional mean assumption \(E(u \mid \text{sqft}) = 0\) likely to hold? Why or why not?

Answer **(a)** - $\beta_0 = 25.0$: The expected price of a house with 0 square feet — not economically meaningful, but mathematically the y-intercept. - $\beta_1 = 0.12$: Each additional square foot of floor area is associated with a \$120 higher house price, holding all else constant. **(b)** Examples: neighbourhood quality/location, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, age and condition of the property, school district quality, proximity to public transport, lot size, renovation status. **(c)** $$\hat{y} = 25.0 + 0.12 \times 1{,}800 = 25.0 + 216.0 = 241.0 \quad (\$241{,}000)$$ $$\hat{u} = 260.0 - 241.0 = 19.0 \quad (\$19{,}000)$$ The house sold for \$19,000 more than predicted — likely reflecting unobserved quality (e.g., premium location, recent renovation). **(d)** Probably **not**. Larger houses are more likely to be in high-income suburbs (better schools, lower crime), which are also correlated with price. Location quality is in $u$ but correlated with sqft, violating $E(u \mid \text{sqft}) = 0$.

Prompt 2

An economist writes down the model:

\[\ln(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{educ}_i + u_i\]

where \(\ln(\text{wage})\) is the natural log of hourly wage and educ is years of schooling.

(a) If \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.08\), give the approximate percentage-change interpretation of this coefficient. (b) What does \(\hat{\beta}_0\) estimate? Is this interpretable? (c) Name two variables likely captured in \(u_i\) and explain whether each would bias \(\hat{\beta}_1\) upward or downward.

Answer **(a)** Since the dependent variable is in logs, $\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.08$ implies that one additional year of education is associated with approximately an **8% increase** in hourly wages (the exact statement is $100(\hat{\beta}_1)\%$, valid for small values of $\hat{\beta}_1$). **(b)** $\hat{\beta}_0 = \ln(\widehat{\text{wage}})$ when educ $= 0$. Exponentiating: $e^{\hat{\beta}_0}$ estimates the predicted hourly wage for a worker with zero years of schooling. In practice this is extrapolation far outside the data range and has little economic meaning. **(c)** - **Ability (IQ, non-cognitive skills):** More able people earn higher wages *and* tend to stay in school longer → positive correlation with educ → $\hat{\beta}_1$ biased **upward** (overestimates the return to schooling). - **Family background/wealth:** Wealthier families can invest more in schooling and also provide career networks → positive correlation with educ → $\hat{\beta}_1$ again biased **upward**. - (Counter-example) **Physical labour requirements:** Jobs requiring heavy physical labour may pay more but require less formal schooling → negative correlation with educ → $\hat{\beta}_1$ biased **downward**.

Prompt 3

For each scenario below, (i) write the simple regression model, (ii) interpret \(\beta_1\), and (iii) identify the most important variable likely in \(u\) that would violate \(E(u \mid x) = 0\):

(a) Modelling a firm's total cost (\(y\)) as a function of output quantity (\(x\)). (b) Modelling a country's infant mortality rate (\(y\)) as a function of per-capita healthcare spending (\(x\)). (c) Modelling student exam scores (\(y\)) as a function of hours studied (\(x\)).

Answer **(a)** $$\text{total cost}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{output}_i + u_i$$ - $\beta_1$: the marginal cost — the expected increase in total cost from producing one additional unit of output. - Key omitted variable: input prices (wages, materials costs). Firms with higher input prices face higher costs *and* may produce less (negative correlation with output) → if input prices vary across firms in the data, $E(u \mid x) \neq 0$. **(b)** $$\text{infant mortality}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{health spending}_i + u_i$$ - $\beta_1$: the expected change in infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births) for a \$1 increase in per-capita healthcare spending. Theory predicts $\beta_1 < 0$. - Key omitted variable: income per capita. Richer countries both spend more on healthcare *and* have lower infant mortality for reasons beyond healthcare (sanitation, nutrition, education) → positive omitted-variable bias, understating the true healthcare effect. **(c)** $$\text{score}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{hours}_i + u_i$$ - $\beta_1$: the expected increase in exam score (points) for each additional hour studied. - Key omitted variable: prior academic ability. Stronger students may study more efficiently (or strategically study more) *and* score higher → positive correlation with hours → $\hat{\beta}_1$ overstates the causal effect of study time.
