docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Ch 3.1–3.2 (pp. 68–85)
  • Angrist & Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch 3 (Frisch–Waugh interpretation)
  • HILDA Survey data dictionary (University of Melbourne) — for Australian wage examples

docs.title: Lesson M03.L02: OLS Estimation in Multiple Regression
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive OLS estimators in multiple regression; interpret \(R^2\) and adjusted \(\bar{R}^2\); understand why \(R^2\) alone is insufficient for model selection. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Sections 3.2–3.3)

docs.title: OLS in Multiple Regression: The Objective
docs.text:
Given the model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\), OLS chooses estimates \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1, \ldots, \hat{\beta}_k\) to minimise the sum of squared residuals (SSR):

\[\min_{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots,\hat{\beta}_k} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_{i1} - \cdots - \hat{\beta}_k x_{ik}\bigr)^2\]

In simple regression (one regressor) the first-order conditions give explicit formulas. With \(k > 1\) regressors the FOCs are a system of \(k+1\) equations — solved most cleanly in matrix notation.

docs.title: Matrix Notation (Awareness Level)
docs.text:
Stack the data into matrices:

\[\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix}_{n\times 1}, \quad \mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1k}\\\vdots & & & \vdots\\1 & x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{nk}\end{pmatrix}_{n\times(k+1)}, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_k\end{pmatrix}_{(k+1)\times 1}\]

The OLS estimator in closed form is:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}\]

Requirements for this formula to exist:

  • \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})\) must be invertible — equivalent to MLR.3 (no perfect collinearity)
  • \(n > k + 1\) — more observations than parameters

You are not expected to derive this result from scratch in ECMT5001, but you should recognise the notation and understand that the scalar formulas for \(k=1\) are a special case.

docs.title: Fitted Values and Residuals
docs.text:
Once \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is obtained:

\[\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_k x_{ik}\] \[\hat{u}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]

These definitions are identical to simple regression — the OLS residual is always the actual minus fitted value.

docs.title: Algebraic Properties of OLS
docs.text:
These properties follow mechanically from the first-order conditions and hold for any OLS regression (simple or multiple):

Property Statement Zero mean residuals \(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i = 0\) Orthogonality \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}\hat{u}_i = 0\) for each \(j = 1,\ldots,k\) Sample means on surface \((\bar{x}_1, \ldots, \bar{x}_k, \bar{y})\) lies on the OLS regression surface SST decomposition \(SST = SSE + SSR\) where \(SSE = \sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\)

The orthogonality conditions say the residuals are uncorrelated with every included regressor in the sample. This is a mechanical property — it does not imply \(E(u|x_j) = 0\) in the population (that requires Assumption MLR.4).

docs.title: \(R^2\) in Multiple Regression
docs.text:
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{SSE}{SST}\]

This is identical to the simple-regression formula. \(R^2\) is the fraction of the total variation in \(y\) explained by all regressors jointly.

Key mechanical fact: \(R^2\) never decreases when you add a regressor. Why? OLS can always set the new coefficient to zero and reproduce the old fit; any nonzero coefficient can only reduce SSR further.

This makes \(R^2\) a poor model-selection criterion — it will always favour the kitchen-sink model.

docs.title: Adjusted \(R^2\) (Penalised Fit)
docs.text:
To penalise for adding extra parameters, define:

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)} = 1 - \frac{n-1}{n-k-1}(1 - R^2)\] Component Meaning \(SSR/(n-k-1)\) Estimated residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) — penalises for each parameter used \(SST/(n-1)\) Sample variance of \(y\) — fixed

Properties of \(\bar{R}^2\):

  • Can be negative (when the regression fits worse than the intercept-only model)
  • Decreases when an added variable contributes less than its "fair share" to fit reduction
  • \(\bar{R}^2 \leq R^2\) always (equality when \(k=0\))
  • A regressor raises \(\bar{R}^2\) if and only if its \(|t\text{-stat}| > 1\) (approximately)
\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{s_y^2}\]

where \(s_y^2 = SST/(n-1)\) is the sample variance of \(y\). This framing makes clear: adding a regressor raises \(\bar{R}^2\) iff it reduces the estimated residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}^2\).

docs.title: Which to Report?
docs.text:
• \(R^2\): useful for describing how much variation is explained; always report it.
  • \(\bar{R}^2\): use for comparing models with different numbers of regressors on the same sample and same \(y\).
  • Neither is appropriate for comparing models with different transformations of \(y\) (e.g., \(\ln y\) vs \(y\)), because \(SST\) changes.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A researcher estimates two models on \(n = 100\) observations of Australian workers:

Model 1: \(\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\,\text{educ}\)

Statistic Value \(SSR_1\) 48.6 \(SST\) 72.0 \(R^2\) 0.325 \(\bar{R}^2\) ?

Model 2: \(\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\,\text{educ} + \hat{\beta}_2\,\text{exper} + \hat{\beta}_3\,\text{tenure}\)

Statistic Value \(SSR_2\) 40.3 \(SST\) 72.0 \(R^2\) 0.440 \(\bar{R}^2\) ?

Step 1: Compute \(\bar{R}^2\) for Model 1 (\(k=1\), \(n=100\))

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{48.6/98}{72.0/99} = 1 - \frac{0.4959}{0.7273} = 1 - 0.682 = 0.318\]

Step 2: Compute \(\bar{R}^2\) for Model 2 (\(k=3\), \(n=100\))

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{40.3/96}{72.0/99} = 1 - \frac{0.4198}{0.7273} = 1 - 0.577 = 0.423\]

Step 3: Compare

Model \(k\) \(R^2\) \(\bar{R}^2\) 1 (educ only) 1 0.325 0.318 2 (educ + exper + tenure) 3 0.440 0.423

Both \(R^2\) and \(\bar{R}^2\) rise from Model 1 to Model 2, confirming that experience and tenure are jointly contributing meaningfully to explained variation — they are not just soaking up degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Compute \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) for Model 2

\[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{SSR}{n-k-1} = \frac{40.3}{96} = 0.4198\]

This is the estimated variance of the error term \(u\), used in constructing standard errors for each \(\hat{\beta}_j\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
\(R^2\) increasing when you add a variable means the variable belongs

False. \(R^2\) mechanically increases with every added regressor, even noise. A variable with a \(t\)-statistic of 0.1 will still raise \(R^2\). Always check (1) \(\bar{R}^2\) — did it rise? (2) the \(t\)-statistic — is the coefficient statistically different from zero? (3) economic theory — does the variable belong in the model on substantive grounds? All three should support inclusion.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Algebraic property. Prove that \(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i = 0\) in any OLS regression that includes an intercept. (Hint: The intercept column in \(\mathbf{X}\) is a column of ones; use the orthogonality condition \(\sum x_{i0}\hat{u}_i = 0\) where \(x_{i0} = 1\).)

  2. Adjusted \(R^2\) calculation. A researcher estimates a model with \(n = 50\), \(k = 5\), and reports \(R^2 = 0.72\). Calculate \(\bar{R}^2\). Then suppose they add 5 more irrelevant regressors and \(R^2\) rises to 0.76. Calculate the new \(\bar{R}^2\) and explain whether the additional regressors improved the model.

  3. Model comparison. Two models are estimated on the same \(n=200\) sample:

  4. Model A: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + u\); \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.41\)
  5. Model B: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4 + u\); \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.39\)

Which model do you prefer and why? What does it imply about \(x_2, x_3, x_4\)?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Ch 3.2–3.3 (pp. 85–102)
  • Greene, Econometric Analysis, Ch 3 (full matrix derivation)
  • R/Python: lm() / statsmodels.OLS — both report \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\) automatically

docs.title: Lesson M03.L03: Gauss–Markov Assumptions and BLUE
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: State and interpret the six MLR assumptions; articulate the Gauss–Markov theorem and what BLUE means; identify which assumption is most likely violated in applied work and what consequence follows. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.3), Chapter 3 Appendix

docs.title: The Six MLR Assumptions
docs.text: The properties of OLS — unbiasedness, efficiency, and valid inference — depend on which assumptions hold. Wooldridge labels these MLR.1–MLR.6.

docs.title: MLR.1 — Linear in Parameters
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\]

The model is linear in the \(\beta_j\)'s. The \(x_j\)'s can be nonlinear functions of underlying variables (e.g., \(\ln(\text{wage})\), \(\text{age}^2\), \(\text{educ} \times \text{female}\)) — as long as each enters the equation multiplied by a single \(\beta_j\).

Violation: A truly nonlinear parameter structure, e.g., \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1^{\beta_2} x\). Such models require nonlinear least squares (NLLS).

docs.title: MLR.2 — Random Sampling
docs.text:
The observed data \(\{(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik},y_i) : i=1,\ldots,n\}\) constitute a random sample from the population described by MLR.1.

Consequence of violation: Survey non-response bias, cluster sampling without correction, or time-series data (where observations are autocorrelated) can all violate MLR.2. Results still hold under weaker conditions (e.g., stationarity in time-series), but require more care.

docs.title: MLR.3 — No Perfect Collinearity
docs.text:
In the sample, no independent variable is an exact linear combination of the others. Equivalently, \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) has full rank \(k+1\).

Example violation: Including both "male" and "female" dummies (each 0/1) when those are the only two groups — they sum to 1, exactly equal to the intercept column. OLS cannot be computed.

Important: MLR.3 is about perfect collinearity only. High (imperfect) multicollinearity is permitted but inflates standard errors — see M03.L05.

docs.title: MLR.4 — Zero Conditional Mean (Exogeneity)
docs.text:
\[E(u \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k) = 0\]

The error term has zero mean conditional on all values of all included regressors. This is the most important assumption for unbiasedness of OLS.

It rules out: - Omitted variables that correlate with any \(x_j\) (M03.L04) - Simultaneity / reverse causality (e.g., wages affecting education choices) - Measurement error in regressors (M10)

When MLR.4 fails, OLS is biased and inconsistent — the gold-standard fix is instrumental variables (M10).

docs.title: MLR.5 — Homoskedasticity
docs.text:
\[\text{Var}(u \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k) = \sigma^2\]

The variance of the error is constant across all covariate values. Combined with MLR.4, this gives \(E(u^2 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2\).

Consequence of violation (heteroskedasticity): OLS remains unbiased (MLR.4 intact) but is no longer BLUE — a weighted least squares (WLS) estimator has smaller variance. The standard errors reported by default OLS are also incorrect; use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (M06).

docs.title: MLR.6 — Normality of the Error
docs.text:
\[u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

Implies MLR.4 and MLR.5. Needed for exact finite-sample \(t\)- and \(F\)-tests under OLS.

In large samples: By the Central Limit Theorem, \(t\)-statistics are asymptotically standard normal even without MLR.6, so this assumption becomes less critical as \(n\) grows. For small samples (e.g., \(n < 30\)), violation of normality can distort inference.

docs.title: The Gauss–Markov Theorem
docs.text:
Gauss–Markov Theorem

Under MLR.1–MLR.5, the OLS estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is BLUE: Best Linear Unbiased Estimator.

Breaking down BLUE:

Letter Meaning B (Best) Among all linear unbiased estimators, OLS has the smallest variance for every \(\beta_j\) L (Linear) The estimator is a linear function of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) U (Unbiased) \(E(\hat{\beta}_j) = \beta_j\) for all \(j\) E (Estimator) It is a specific estimator, not a guess

"Best" in the BLUE sense means: for any other linear unbiased estimator \(\tilde{\beta}_j\),

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) \leq \text{Var}(\tilde{\beta}_j)\]

This is a minimum variance result — OLS squeezes the most information out of the data, given the constraints.

docs.title: Which Assumptions Drive What?
docs.text: Result Assumptions Required OLS is unbiased: \(E(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \boldsymbol{\beta}\) MLR.1–MLR.4 OLS is efficient (BLUE) MLR.1–MLR.5 OLS \(t\)-tests are exact in finite samples MLR.1–MLR.6 OLS \(t\)-tests are asymptotically valid MLR.1–MLR.4 + CLT (large \(n\))

docs.title: Worked Example: Economic Violations of Each Assumption
docs.text:
Context: A researcher estimates the effect of rainfall on crop yield for 200 Australian wheat farms:

\[\text{yield}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{rain}_i + \beta_2\,\text{fertiliser}_i + \beta_3\,\text{soil quality}_i + u_i\] Assumption Potential Violation Consequence MLR.1 True relationship is \(\text{yield} = \beta_0 \cdot \text{rain}^{\beta_1}\) (Cobb-Douglas) OLS fitted model is misspecified; must use NLLS or log-transform MLR.2 Farms selected because they're large (size-biased sample) Estimates may not generalise to all farms; selection bias MLR.3 Researcher includes both sand_fraction and clay_fraction where they sum to 1 (together with silt_fraction already included) OLS fails: singular matrix; drop one category MLR.4 Fertiliser use is chosen by the farmer partly in response to expected yield (reverse causality) OLS estimate of \(\beta_2\) is biased; need IV MLR.5 Variance of yield is much larger for farms with high rainfall (heteroskedasticity) OLS is unbiased but standard errors are wrong; use robust SEs MLR.6 Yield has a left-skewed distribution (bounded below at zero; catastrophic failures create a fat left tail) \(t\)-tests are approximate in small samples; large-sample CLT still applies

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
OLS is the best estimator (full stop)

The Gauss–Markov theorem says OLS is best among linear unbiased estimators — not among all possible estimators. If MLR.5 fails (heteroskedasticity), weighted least squares (WLS) is a linear estimator that is also unbiased and beats OLS on variance. If the error is known to be non-normal, some maximum likelihood estimators can dominate OLS in small samples. BLUE is not "best estimator ever" — it is "best in a specific class under specific conditions."

Multicollinearity violates MLR.3

Only perfect collinearity violates MLR.3. Imperfect multicollinearity (high \(R_j^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on other regressors) is perfectly consistent with MLR.3 — OLS remains BLUE. The problem with imperfect multicollinearity is large standard errors, not bias or breakdown of the estimator.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Assumption mapping. For each of the following scenarios, state which MLR assumption is violated and whether OLS is (a) biased, (b) inefficient, or (c) invalid for inference:
  2. (i) The error variance is three times larger for firms with revenues above $1 billion.
  3. (ii) A model of house prices omits suburb fixed effects, and suburb correlates with both price and included regressors (number of bedrooms, bathrooms).

  4. (iii) A researcher includes male (0/1) and female (0/1) as the only two gender dummies with a constant.

  5. BLUE theorem. An alternative linear estimator for \(\beta_1\) is the "split-sample estimator" \(\check{\beta}_1 = (\bar{y}_H - \bar{y}_L)/({\bar{x}_H - \bar{x}_L})\), where \(H\) and \(L\) denote the top and bottom halves of the \(x_1\) distribution. This estimator is linear in \(y\) and unbiased under MLR.1–MLR.4. What does the Gauss–Markov theorem imply about its variance relative to \(\hat{\beta}_1^{OLS}\)?

  6. MLR.4 vs MLR.5. Explain in one paragraph why MLR.4 (zero conditional mean) is more damaging to violate than MLR.5 (homoskedasticity). In what sense does heteroskedasticity "only" affect efficiency and standard errors, while endogeneity affects the coefficients themselves?

docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Ch 3.3–3.4, Appendix 3A (Gauss–Markov proof sketch)
  • Davidson & MacKinnon, Econometric Theory and Methods, Ch 2 (rigorous BLUE proof)
  • Stock & Watson, Introduction to Econometrics, Ch 6.6 (BLUE intuition)

docs.title: Lesson M03.L04: Omitted Variable Bias
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive the omitted variable bias formula; determine the direction and magnitude of bias given the sign of the omitted variable's true coefficient and its correlation with the included regressor; apply OVB reasoning to real economic examples. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.3)

docs.title: What Is Omitted Variable Bias?
docs.text:
Omitted variable bias (OVB) arises when a variable that belongs in the true regression — because it affects \(y\) and correlates with at least one included regressor — is left out. The OLS estimate of the included regressor's coefficient absorbs part of the omitted variable's effect and is therefore biased.

OVB is a violation of MLR.4: the omitted variable ends up in the error term \(u\), making \(E(u \mid x_1) \neq 0\).

docs.title: The OVB Formula (Two-Variable Case)
docs.text:
True model (population):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u, \quad E(u \mid x_1, x_2) = 0\]

Estimated model (researcher omits \(x_2\)):

\[y = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 x_1 + v, \quad v = \beta_2 x_2 + u\]

The simple-regression OLS estimator of \(\tilde{\beta}_1\) is:

\[\tilde{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2}\]

Taking expectations (using the true model):

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \tilde{\delta}_1\]

where \(\tilde{\delta}_1\) is the auxiliary regression coefficient — the slope from regressing \(x_2\) on \(x_1\):

\[\tilde{\delta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)(x_{i2} - \bar{x}_2)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)^2}\]

Key formula

\[\boxed{E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \underbrace{\beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1}_{\text{OVB}}}\]

Bias \(= \beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1\)

docs.title: Direction of Bias
docs.text:
The sign of OVB depends on the signs of \(\beta_2\) and \(\tilde{\delta}_1\):

\(\beta_2 > 0\) (omitted var ↑ \(y\)) \(\beta_2 < 0\) (omitted var ↓ \(y\)) \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) (omitted corr. positively with \(x_1\)) → Upward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) → Downward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 < 0\) (omitted corr. negatively with \(x_1\)) → Downward bias \(\tilde{\delta}_1 < 0\) → Upward bias

Mnemonic: Same signs → upward bias; opposite signs → downward bias

Note: "upward bias" means \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1) > \beta_1\) (OLS overestimates the true effect).

docs.title: Classic Example: Ability Bias in Returns to Education
docs.text:
True model:

\[\ln(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{educ} + \beta_2\,\text{ability} + u\]
  • \(\beta_2 > 0\): more able workers earn higher wages (ability raises \(y\))
  • \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\): more able individuals tend to acquire more education (ability correlates positively with educ)

OVB:

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \underbrace{\beta_2}_{>0} \cdot \underbrace{\tilde{\delta}_1}_{>0} > \beta_1\]

Conclusion: Simple OLS of log-wage on education overestimates the true return to education. Part of what we attribute to schooling is really the wage premium for ability.

docs.title: Australian Example: Family Background and Returns to Education
docs.text:
In Australia, children from wealthier family backgrounds tend to: 1. Achieve higher educational attainment (educ ↑) 2. Earn higher wages due to networks, cultural capital, and inherited advantages (wage ↑)

If a researcher regresses \(\ln(\text{wage})\) on educ without controlling for family background (SES index):

  • \(\beta_2 > 0\) (SES raises wages)
  • \(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\) (SES correlates positively with education)

→ Upward OVB on \(\hat{\beta}_1\). The estimated return to education is inflated.

This has direct policy implications: if we overestimate returns to education, we may over-invest in tertiary subsidies relative to other interventions.

docs.title: Worked Example: Calculate Direction and Magnitude
docs.text:
Setup: A researcher has data on 500 workers and estimates:

\[\widehat{\ln(\text{wage})} = 0.50 + 0.12\,\text{educ} \qquad (\text{simple regression})\]

An econometrician reveals that the true model is:

\[\ln(\text{wage}) = 0.20 + 0.08\,\text{educ} + 0.04\,\text{ability} + u\]

The auxiliary regression of ability on educ gives:

\[\widehat{\text{ability}} = -1.2 + 0.9\,\text{educ} \implies \tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.9\]

Step 1: Compute predicted OVB

\[\text{OVB} = \beta_2 \cdot \tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.04 \times 0.9 = 0.036\]

Step 2: Check against formula

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \text{OVB} = 0.08 + 0.036 = 0.116\]

This is close to the observed \(\tilde{\beta}_1 = 0.12\) (small discrepancy due to sampling variation). ✓

Step 3: Direction of bias

\(\beta_2 = 0.04 > 0\) and \(\tilde{\delta}_1 = 0.9 > 0\) → upward bias. The simple regression overestimates the return to education by roughly \(0.036\) log-wage units (≈ 3.6 percentage points).

Policy implication: A policy that raises education by 1 year would produce an approximately 8% wage increase (true \(\beta_1 = 0.08\)), not the 12% suggested by the biased estimate.

docs.title: OVB with Multiple Included Regressors
docs.text:
In the general case with multiple included regressors \(x_1, \ldots, x_k\) and omitted variable \(x_{k+1}\):

\[\text{OVB on }\hat{\beta}_j = \beta_{k+1} \cdot \tilde{\delta}_j\]

where \(\tilde{\delta}_j\) is the coefficient on \(x_j\) in the auxiliary regression of \(x_{k+1}\) on all included \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\). Every included coefficient is potentially biased if the omitted variable correlates with it.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
Adding more variables always eliminates OVB

Partially true, but dangerous. Adding the correct omitted variable eliminates OVB. However:

  1. The added variable may itself be endogenous — then you introduce a new form of bias. For example, adding job type to control for ability may be a bad control if job type is partly caused by education.

  2. Proxy variables (e.g., IQ test scores as a proxy for ability) reduce but do not eliminate OVB, because the proxy is an imperfect measure.

  3. Adding irrelevant variables does not reduce any bias but inflates variance and can induce new near-multicollinearity.

Zero correlation means no OVB

If the omitted variable is uncorrelated with \(x_1\) (\(\tilde{\delta}_1 = 0\)), then \(\text{OVB} = \beta_2 \cdot 0 = 0\) even if \(\beta_2 \neq 0\). A variable that affects \(y\) but is uncorrelated with included regressors goes into the error term without biasing any coefficient — it only increases residual variance (\(\hat{\sigma}^2\)) and hence standard errors.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. OVB direction. A researcher estimates the effect of the minimum wage (minwage) on employment (emp) without controlling for regional economic conditions (local_gdp). Suppose the true model is:

$\(\ln(\text{emp}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(\text{minwage}) + \beta_2 \ln(\text{local\_gdp}) + u\)$

with \(\beta_2 > 0\). Australian states with higher local GDP tend to set higher minimum wages (\(\tilde{\delta}_1 > 0\)). Without controlling for local_gdp, is the OLS estimate of \(\beta_1\) (the employment elasticity of the minimum wage) biased upward or downward? What does this imply about published estimates of minimum wage effects that don't control for regional conditions?

  1. Derive OVB. Start from the true model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\) and the formula \(\tilde{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_{i1}-\bar{x}_1)(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_{i1}-\bar{x}_1)^2}\). Substitute the true model for \(y_i\) and show that \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2\tilde{\delta}_1\).

  2. Numerical OVB. True model: \(y = 1 + 2x_1 + 3x_2 + u\). Auxiliary regression: \(x_2 = 0.5 + 0.4x_1 + \epsilon\). You estimate the misspecified model \(y = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 x_1 + v\). (a) Compute \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1)\). (b) Is OLS upward or downward biased? (c) How much does OLS overstate/understate the effect of \(x_1\)?

docs.text:

  • Angrist & Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch 3.2 (OVB formula in IV context)
  • Card (1995) — uses distance to college as IV to address ability bias; classic paper
  • HILDA longitudinal data — used in Australian studies of education–wage link

docs.title: Lesson M03.L05: Multicollinearity and Variance of OLS
docs.text: Module: M03 — Multiple Regression Analysis Level: Graduate (ECMT5001, USYD S1 2027) Duration: 35 min Learning Objective: Derive the variance formula for OLS in multiple regression; define the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF); distinguish perfect from imperfect multicollinearity; explain consequences for inference without confusing multicollinearity with bias. Provenance: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Chapter 3 (Section 3.4)

docs.title: Variance of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) in Multiple Regression
docs.text:
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, the sampling variance of the OLS estimator for \(\beta_j\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}\]

where:

Symbol Definition \(\sigma^2\) Population error variance (\(\text{Var}(u \mid \mathbf{x})\)) \(SST_j\) \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2\) — total sample variation in \(x_j\) \(R_j^2\) \(R^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on all other regressors \(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1},x_{j+1},\ldots,x_k\)

The standard error (square root of estimated variance) is:

\[\widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_j \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}}\]

where \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = SSR/(n-k-1)\).

docs.title: Three Ways to Get Small Variance
docs.text:
From the formula, \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) is small when:

  1. \(\sigma^2\) is small — the regression model fits well; not much unexplained variation in \(y\)
  2. \(SST_j\) is large — plenty of variation in \(x_j\) in the sample; more signal
  3. \(R_j^2\) is small — \(x_j\) is not well explained by the other regressors; no multicollinearity

The third factor is what makes multicollinearity costly.

docs.title: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
docs.text:
Define the Variance Inflation Factor for \(\hat{\beta}_j\):

\[VIF_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}\]

So:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j} \cdot VIF_j\]

The factor \(\sigma^2/SST_j\) is what the variance would be if \(x_j\) were orthogonal to all other regressors (\(R_j^2 = 0\), so \(VIF_j = 1\)). Multicollinearity inflates this baseline by the factor \(VIF_j \geq 1\).

Rule of thumb:

\(VIF_j\) Interpretation \(1\) No collinearity; baseline variance \(1\)–\(5\) Mild; generally acceptable \(5\)–\(10\) Moderate; monitor closely \(> 10\) Severe; consider remedies

Some textbooks use VIF \(> 10\) as the threshold; others use VIF \(> 5\). Judgement and context matter.

docs.title: Perfect Multicollinearity (MLR.3 Violated)
docs.text:
Perfect multicollinearity: \(R_j^2 = 1\) — one regressor is an exact linear combination of others.

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j \cdot (1 - 1)} = \frac{\sigma^2}{0} = \infty\]

OLS breaks down completely — the matrix \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) is singular and \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) does not exist. Software will drop one of the collinear columns or throw an error.

Common causes:

  • Dummy variable trap: Including \(d_{\text{male}}\) and \(d_{\text{female}}\) with an intercept (they sum to 1)
  • Exact definitional relationship: Including both total_tax and income_tax + GST + other_tax when the latter three sum exactly to the former
  • Redundant transformation: Including \(x\) and \(2x\) simultaneously

docs.title: Imperfect Multicollinearity
docs.text:
Imperfect multicollinearity: \(R_j^2\) close to (but not equal to) 1.

OLS is still computable, unbiased, and BLUE — MLR.3 is not violated. However:

  • \(VIF_j\) is large → \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) is large
  • Standard errors are large
  • \(t\)-statistics are small → it is hard to detect that \(\beta_j \neq 0\) even when it truly is (Type II error)
  • Coefficient estimates are sensitive to small changes in the sample (overfitting)

The core problem: with highly correlated regressors, the data contain insufficient independent information to precisely estimate the separate effects.

docs.title: Economic Causes of Multicollinearity
docs.text:
1. Aggregate macroeconomic variables: GDP, consumption, and investment all trend together — high pairwise correlations in time series.

  2. Overlapping demographic controls: Age, years of experience, and years since leaving school are all highly correlated life-stage variables.

  3. Physical characteristics: Height and weight are highly correlated for human subjects.

  4. Lagged variables: Including \(x_t\), \(x_{t-1}\), \(x_{t-2}\) in a time-series model creates near-perfect collinearity if \(x\) is a smooth series.

docs.title: Remedies for Multicollinearity
docs.text:
Remedy How Caution Collect more data Larger \(n\) reduces \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) directly Not always feasible; may not solve collinearity if correlation is structural Drop a variable Remove one collinear regressor Only valid if the dropped variable doesn't belong — otherwise introduces OVB Principal components Replace correlated \(x\)'s with uncorrelated linear combinations Components lose economic interpretability Ridge regression Add penalty \(\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\) to SSR Introduces bias; requires choice of tuning parameter \(\lambda\)

Note: If the collinear variable belongs in the model (non-zero \(\beta_j\)), dropping it trades multicollinearity for OVB — often a worse problem. The preferred solution is more data.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: A researcher regresses log-housing prices on three regressors: \(x_1\) = floor area (m²), \(x_2\) = number of bedrooms, \(x_3\) = number of bathrooms. All are likely correlated.

Auxiliary regressions (to compute \(R_j^2\)):

\(j\) Regress \(x_j\) on others \(R_j^2\) \(VIF_j\) 1 (floor area) \(x_2, x_3\) 0.82 \(1/(1-0.82) = 5.56\) 2 (bedrooms) \(x_1, x_3\) 0.75 \(1/(1-0.75) = 4.00\) 3 (bathrooms) \(x_1, x_2\) 0.88 \(1/(1-0.88) = 8.33\)

Baseline variance (if \(R_j^2 = 0\)):

Suppose \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 0.04\) and \(SST_3 = 200\) (variation in bathrooms). Then:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)_{\text{baseline}} = \frac{0.04}{200} = 0.0002\] \[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3) = 0.0002 \times VIF_3 = 0.0002 \times 8.33 = 0.001666\] \[SE(\hat{\beta}_3) = \sqrt{0.001666} \approx 0.0408 \quad \text{vs baseline } \sqrt{0.0002} \approx 0.0141\]

The standard error for \(\hat{\beta}_3\) is 2.89 times larger than it would be with no multicollinearity (since \(\sqrt{VIF_3} = \sqrt{8.33} \approx 2.89\)). This makes the \(t\)-statistic for \(\beta_3\) roughly 2.89 times smaller — harder to achieve statistical significance even if bathrooms genuinely affect price.

Diagnosis: \(VIF_3 = 8.33\) is in the "moderate to severe" range. The researcher should check whether floor area and bathrooms are nearly perfectly collinear, possibly because large homes always have many bathrooms. Adding the number of floors or age of building as an alternative dimension of heterogeneity may help.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
Multicollinearity biases OLS estimates

False. Under MLR.1–MLR.4, OLS is unbiased regardless of multicollinearity (as long as MLR.3 holds, i.e., no perfect collinearity). High \(R_j^2\) inflates \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) and standard errors — affecting efficiency and inference — but does not bias \(E(\hat{\beta}_j)\). Confusing multicollinearity with OVB is one of the most common errors in applied econometrics.

Dropping a correlated variable fixes multicollinearity without cost

Dropping a variable reduces multicollinearity but only "fixes" the problem costlessly if the dropped variable has \(\beta_j = 0\) in the true model. If \(\beta_j \neq 0\), you have traded a precision problem (large SE) for a bias problem (OVB) — and bias is generally worse because it cannot be fixed by collecting more data.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. VIF calculation. You have three regressors: income (\(x_1\)), consumption (\(x_2\)), savings (\(x_3\)), where by definition \(\text{savings} = \text{income} - \text{consumption}\).
  2. (a) What is \(R_3^2\) from regressing savings on income and consumption?
  3. (b) What is \(VIF_3\)?
  4. (c) What does this imply for \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)\)?

  5. (d) How would you fix this problem?

  6. Variance formula. In a regression of test scores on class size (\(x_1\)) and school funding (\(x_2\)) with \(n = 200\) Australian schools: \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 100\), \(SST_1 = 400\), \(R_1^2 = 0.65\).

  7. (a) Calculate \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)\) and \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\).

  8. (b) If the sample grew to \(n = 800\) (quadrupling), roughly how would \(SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\) change? (Hint: \(SST_1\) scales approximately with \(n\).)

  9. Remedies trade-off. A researcher finds VIF = 12 for one regressor. List two remedies and, for each, state the condition under which it is valid without introducing new bias. Then explain which remedy is theoretically preferable if the researcher has access to a much larger dataset.

docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Ch 3.4 (pp. 96–105)
  • Belsley, Kuh & Welsch, Regression Diagnostics (1980) — definitive reference on collinearity diagnostics
  • R: car::vif() computes VIF automatically after lm()
  • Python: statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence.variance_inflation_factor()

docs.title: Lesson M04.L01: Sampling Distributions of OLS Estimators
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 04 — Statistical Inference in OLS Level Graduate (ECMT5001, S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Derive the exact and asymptotic sampling distributions of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) under MLR.1–MLR.6, and correctly identify degrees of freedom for the t-distribution Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7e, Chapter 4 (pp. 117–130)

docs.title: MLR.1–MLR.6: The Classical Linear Model Assumptions
docs.text:
Recall the six assumptions of the Classical Linear Model (CLM):

Assumption Name Statement MLR.1 Linearity in parameters \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\) MLR.2 Random sampling \((x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik}, y_i)\) are i.i.d. draws from the population MLR.3 No perfect collinearity No exact linear relationship among regressors MLR.4 Zero conditional mean \(E(u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k) = 0\) MLR.5 Homoskedasticity \(Var(u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \sigma^2\) MLR.6 Normality \(u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)

MLR.1–MLR.5 give us BLUE (Gauss–Markov). MLR.6 is the additional normality assumption that pins down the exact finite-sample distribution of \(\hat{\beta}_j\).

docs.title: The Exact Sampling Distribution Under MLR.1–MLR.6
docs.text:
Under all six CLM assumptions, the OLS estimator \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is a linear combination of the \(y_i\) values. Since \(y_i\) is itself a linear function of the normally distributed error \(u_i\) (by MLR.6), \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is also normally distributed:

\[\hat{\beta}_j \sim N\!\left(\beta_j,\; Var(\hat{\beta}_j)\right)\]

where \(Var(\hat{\beta}_j) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{SST_j(1 - R_j^2)}\), with \(SST_j = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2\) and \(R_j^2\) the \(R^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on all other regressors.

Standardising to a \(N(0,1)\) variate (subtracting mean, dividing by SD):

\[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{sd(\hat{\beta}_j)} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\sigma / \sqrt{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}} \sim N(0,1)\]

This is a clean \(Z\)-statistic — but it requires knowing \(\sigma^2\), the true error variance, which is unobservable.

docs.title: Replacing \(\sigma^2\) with \(\hat{\sigma}^2\): Why We Use the t-Distribution
docs.text:
In practice we estimate \(\sigma^2\) by:

\[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{SSR}{n - k - 1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i^2}{n - k - 1}\]

where \(SSR\) is the sum of squared residuals, \(n\) is the number of observations, \(k\) is the number of slope regressors, and \(1\) accounts for the estimated intercept. The denominator \(n-k-1\) is the degrees of freedom (df).

Replacing \(\sigma\) with \(\hat{\sigma}\) (the standard error of the regression) gives the standard error of \(\hat{\beta}_j\):

\[se(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}}\]

Substituting into the standardised statistic:

\[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t_{n-k-1}\]

This follows a t-distribution with \(n - k - 1\) degrees of freedom.

Why t, not Z? Dividing by \(\hat{\sigma}\) rather than the true \(\sigma\) introduces an extra source of randomness. More precisely:

\[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{\chi^2_{n-k-1}/(n-k-1)}}\]

where \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) is independent of the \(\chi^2_{n-k-1}\) term. A standard normal divided by the square root of an independent scaled chi-squared is, by definition, a t-random variable. The t-distribution has heavier tails than \(N(0,1)\), reflecting the extra uncertainty from estimating \(\sigma^2\). Ignoring this and using \(Z\) critical values in small samples understates uncertainty and causes over-rejection of true null hypotheses.

docs.title: Degrees of Freedom: Where Does \(n - k - 1\) Come From?
docs.text:
We have \(n\) observations and are estimating \(k + 1\) parameters (\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_k\)). The residuals \(\hat{u}_i\) must satisfy \(k + 1\) constraints (the OLS first-order conditions), so there are only \(n - (k+1) = n - k - 1\) "free" pieces of information left to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

Model Parameters estimated Degrees of freedom Simple regression (\(k=1\)) 2 (\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)) \(n-2\) Multiple regression (\(k\) regressors) \(k+1\) \(n-k-1\)

docs.title: Large-Sample (Asymptotic) Justification: Dropping MLR.6
docs.text:
MLR.6 (normality of \(u\)) is a strong assumption. In large samples, the CLT provides an asymptotic justification:

  • Under MLR.1–MLR.5 only (no normality), \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is still consistent and asymptotically normal.
  • As \(n \to \infty\): \(t_{n-k-1} \to N(0,1)\) (the t and Z distributions converge).
  • For large \(n\), the t-statistics and p-values reported by regression software remain valid even without MLR.6.
  • Practical rule: for \(n \geq 120\) or so, the difference between \(t\) and \(Z\) critical values is negligible (e.g. \(t_{120, 0.025} \approx 1.980\) vs. \(z_{0.025} = 1.960\)). For \(n = 20\), \(t_{18, 0.025} = 2.101\) — meaningfully larger.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. You estimate the following model using \(n = 52\) monthly observations:

\[\text{sales}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{price}_i + \beta_2 \text{adspend}_i + \beta_3 \text{income}_i + u_i\]

Step 1 — Identify parameters. Number of slope regressors: \(k = 3\). Number of parameters including intercept: \(k + 1 = 4\).

Step 2 — Compute degrees of freedom. $\(df = n - k - 1 = 52 - 3 - 1 = 48\)$

Step 3 — Find the t critical value for a two-sided 5% test.

We need \(t_{48,\, 0.025}\) (upper 2.5% tail). From t-tables with 48 df, this is approximately \(2.011\).

(For comparison: \(z_{0.025} = 1.960\). Using Z instead would give a critical value 0.05 units smaller — underestimating uncertainty slightly.)

Step 4 — State the sampling distribution of any \(\hat{\beta}_j\).

Under MLR.1–MLR.6: $\(\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t_{48}\)$

Conclusion. With 52 observations and 3 regressors, our t-statistics follow a \(t_{48}\) distribution. A two-sided test at 5% significance rejects when \(|t| > 2.011\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"With a large sample, I can just use z = 1.96 instead of the t-critical value."

This is approximately (not exactly) correct, and only for large \(n\). The t-distribution is exact under MLR.1–MLR.6 regardless of sample size. Using \(z = 1.96\) for a sample of \(n = 25\) with \(k = 3\) regressors means using a critical value of 1.96 when the correct value is \(t_{21, 0.025} = 2.080\). At \(n = 25\), the z-based test will reject \(H_0\) too often — it has size greater than 5%.

Rule: Always use \(t_{n-k-1}\) critical values. With large \(n\) (say \(>120\)), \(t\) and \(z\) are nearly identical and the distinction is immaterial.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Q1. A researcher estimates a wage regression with \(n = 526\) workers and \(k = 5\) regressors (education, experience, experience², female, urban). What is the degrees of freedom for the t-distribution used in inference? What is the 5% two-sided t critical value? How does it compare to \(z_{0.025} = 1.960\)?

Answer $df = n - k - 1 = 526 - 5 - 1 = 520$. From t-tables (or note that for df $\geq 120$, the t-distribution is very close to normal): $t_{520, 0.025} \approx 1.964$. This is virtually identical to $z_{0.025} = 1.960$. With $n = 526$, using $z$ instead of $t$ is inconsequential.

Q2. A student estimates a model with \(n = 30\) and \(k = 4\) regressors, and quotes a t-statistic of 2.02 as significant at 5% (two-sided) using the \(z\) critical value of 1.96. Is this conclusion correct?

Answer No. With $n = 30$ and $k = 4$: $df = 30 - 4 - 1 = 25$. The correct critical value is $t_{25, 0.025} = 2.060$. Since $|t| = 2.02 < 2.060$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$ at the 5% level using the correct t critical value. The student's conclusion is wrong — using $z$ leads to over-rejection in small samples.

Q3. Explain why \(\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)}\) follows a t-distribution rather than a normal distribution, and state precisely what changes this distribution as the sample grows.

Answer The statistic is the ratio of a standard normal ($\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\sigma \cdot c_j}$ where $c_j$ is a known constant) to the square root of an independent scaled chi-squared random variable ($\hat{\sigma}^2 / \sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-k-1} / (n-k-1)$). This ratio defines a $t_{n-k-1}$ random variable by construction. As $n \to \infty$, the chi-squared term concentrates around its expectation of 1 (by the LLN), so the denominator converges in probability to 1, and the ratio converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$. Formally: $t_{n-k-1} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)$ as $n-k-1 \to \infty$.

docs.title: Lesson M04.L02: t-Tests for Individual Coefficients
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 04 — Statistical Inference in OLS Level Graduate (ECMT5001, S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Construct and interpret t-tests for OLS regression coefficients; distinguish two-sided and one-sided tests; separate statistical significance from economic significance Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7e, Chapter 4.2 (pp. 124–140)

docs.title: Setting Up the Null Hypothesis
docs.text:
The most common null hypothesis in regression inference is:

\[H_0: \beta_j = 0\]

This tests whether regressor \(x_j\) has any partial effect on \(y\) (holding the other regressors constant). But more generally, we can test any specific value:

\[H_0: \beta_j = a_j\]

for a hypothesised value \(a_j \in \mathbb{R}\). Choosing \(a_j = 0\) is by far the most common case in applied work.

docs.title: The t-Statistic
docs.text:
Under \(H_0: \beta_j = a_j\) and the CLM assumptions (MLR.1–MLR.6):

\[t_{\hat{\beta}_j} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - a_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t_{n-k-1}\]

For the standard null \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\):

\[t_{\hat{\beta}_j} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)}\]

This is what regression software reports in the "t-stat" or "t-value" column. The formula says: how many standard errors is \(\hat{\beta}_j\) away from zero?

docs.title: Two-Sided Test
docs.text:
\[H_0: \beta_j = 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_j \neq 0\]

Reject \(H_0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) if:

\[|t_{\hat{\beta}_j}| > t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2}\]

where \(t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2}\) is the upper \(\alpha/2\) critical value of the \(t_{n-k-1}\) distribution. Common values:

Significance level \(\alpha\) \(t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2}\) (large \(n\)) Stars convention 10% 1.645 * 5% 1.960 ** 1% 2.576 ***

docs.title: One-Sided Test (Upper Tail)
docs.text:
\[H_0: \beta_j \leq 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_j > 0\]

Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\) if:

\[t_{\hat{\beta}_j} > t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha}\]

(Note: upper-tail critical value, not \(\alpha/2\), since rejection is in one direction only.)

docs.title: One-Sided Test (Lower Tail)
docs.text:
\[H_0: \beta_j \geq 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_j < 0\]

Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\) if:

\[t_{\hat{\beta}_j} < -t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha}\]

Important: Always state your alternative hypothesis before looking at the data; choosing the direction of the test after seeing the sign of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is data snooping and inflates Type I error.

docs.title: p-Values
docs.text:
The p-value is the probability, under \(H_0\), of observing a t-statistic at least as extreme as the one computed:

\[p\text{-value (two-sided)} = 2 \cdot P(T > |t_{\hat{\beta}_j}|) \quad \text{where } T \sim t_{n-k-1}\]

Interpretation: the p-value is the smallest significance level \(\alpha\) at which we would reject \(H_0\) given the data.

  • \(p < 0.01\): strong evidence against \(H_0\) (*** in most software)
  • \(0.01 \leq p < 0.05\): moderate evidence against \(H_0\) (**)
  • \(0.05 \leq p < 0.10\): weak evidence against \(H_0\) (*)
  • \(p \geq 0.10\): insufficient evidence to reject \(H_0\)

docs.title: Reading Regression Output
docs.text:
A typical software output table looks like:

           Coeff    SE       t      p-value
(Intercept) 5.400   0.631   8.56   <0.001 ***
educ        0.082   0.010   8.20   <0.001 ***
exper       0.004   0.002   2.10    0.037  **
female     -0.296   0.036  -8.22   <0.001 ***

To recover the t-statistic manually: divide coefficient by SE. For example: $\(t_{\text{educ}} = \frac{0.082}{0.010} = 8.20 \checkmark\)$

docs.title: Economic Significance vs. Statistical Significance
docs.text:
A crucial distinction for applied work:

Statistically significant Not statistically significant Large effect Ideal: precise and meaningful Plausible effect, but underpowered — need more data Small effect Precisely estimated but trivially small — may not matter in practice Neither significant nor meaningful

Example. Suppose we have \(n = 50{,}000\) observations and estimate that a marketing campaign increases revenue by $0.50 on average (\(t = 12.3\), \(p < 0.001\)). The coefficient is highly statistically significant, but if the campaign costs $200 per customer, the effect is economically negligible.

Conversely, a small study (\(n = 40\)) might estimate a large wage effect of education but with \(t = 1.5\) (\(p = 0.14\)) — not statistically significant, but the effect may be economically real; we simply lack precision.

Rule for exam write-ups: Always comment on both statistical significance (t-stat, p-value, stars) AND the magnitude and economic interpretation of the coefficient.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. A researcher regresses log hourly wages on three regressors using \(n = 526\) observations from the CPS:

\[\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, \text{educ}_i + \beta_2\, \text{exper}_i + \beta_3\, \text{female}_i + u_i\]

The OLS estimation yields the following output (\(df = 526 - 3 - 1 = 522\)):

Variable \(\hat{\beta}_j\) \(se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) \(t\)-stat \(p\)-value Intercept 0.284 0.104 2.73 0.007 educ 0.092 0.007 13.14 <0.001 exper 0.004 0.001 4.00 <0.001 female −0.297 0.036 −8.25 <0.001

For large \(df \approx 522\), we use \(t_{522, 0.025} \approx 1.965\) (5% two-sided) and \(t_{522, 0.005} \approx 2.585\) (1% two-sided).

Test 1: Is education statistically significant? (\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), two-sided, \(\alpha = 0.05\))

Step 1 — Hypotheses: $\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0\)$

Step 2 — Test statistic: $\(t_{\hat{\beta}_1} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1}{se(\hat{\beta}_1)} = \frac{0.092}{0.007} = 13.14\)$

Step 3 — Distribution under \(H_0\): \(t_{522}\)

Step 4 — Decision: \(|13.14| = 13.14 > 1.965\). Reject \(H_0\).

Step 5 — Interpretation: Education has a statistically significant positive effect on log wages. Each additional year of schooling is associated with approximately a \(9.2\%\) increase in hourly wages, holding experience and gender constant.

Test 2: Is the gender gap statistically significant? (\(H_0: \beta_3 = 0\), two-sided, \(\alpha = 0.01\))

Step 1 — Hypotheses: $\(H_0: \beta_3 = 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_3 \neq 0\)$

Step 2 — Test statistic: $\(t_{\hat{\beta}_3} = \frac{-0.297}{0.036} = -8.25\)$

Step 3 — Distribution under \(H_0\): \(t_{522}\)

Step 4 — Decision: \(|-8.25| = 8.25 > 2.585\). Reject \(H_0\) at the 1% level.

Step 5 — Interpretation: Women earn statistically and economically significantly less than men: approximately \(29.7\%\) lower log wages, holding education and experience constant. The estimate is precise (small SE relative to coefficient) and economically large.

Test 3: Does experience have a positive effect? (\(H_0: \beta_2 \leq 0\), one-sided upper, \(\alpha = 0.05\))

Step 1 — Hypotheses: $\(H_0: \beta_2 \leq 0 \qquad H_1: \beta_2 > 0\)$

Step 2 — Test statistic: $\(t_{\hat{\beta}_2} = \frac{0.004}{0.001} = 4.00\)$

Step 3 — Distribution under \(H_0\): \(t_{522}\)

Step 4 — Decision: \(4.00 > t_{522, 0.05} \approx 1.645\). Reject \(H_0\).

Step 5 — Interpretation: Experience has a statistically significant positive effect on wages. However, the magnitude is small: each additional year of experience raises log wages by only \(0.4\%\) — statistically detectable but economically modest compared to education.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"A non-significant coefficient means the variable has no effect on Y."

This is incorrect. Failing to reject \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\) means we cannot detect a statistically meaningful effect with this sample. The reasons could be: 1. The true effect is genuinely zero. 2. The sample is too small (low power) to detect a real but moderate effect. 3. There is high multicollinearity, inflating \(se(\hat{\beta}_j)\). 4. The data have high variance, making all estimates imprecise.

The correct language: "We find no statistically significant evidence of an effect at the 5% level" — not "there is no effect."

Illustration. If \(\hat{\beta}_j = 5.0\) with \(se(\hat{\beta}_j) = 4.0\), then \(t = 1.25\) and \(p \approx 0.21\). We fail to reject \(H_0\), but the estimated effect is large. A 95% CI would be roughly \(5.0 \pm 2 \times 4.0 = (-3, 13)\) — very wide. We simply don't have enough precision to rule out zero, not evidence that the effect is zero.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Q1. A model of house prices (thousands of dollars) with \(n = 88\) and \(k = 4\) regressors yields: \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{sqft}} = 0.045\), \(se = 0.012\). Test \(H_0: \beta_{\text{sqft}} = 0\) against \(H_1: \beta_{\text{sqft}} > 0\) at the 5% significance level. State all steps and interpret the result in context.

Answer **Step 1:** $H_0: \beta_{\text{sqft}} \leq 0$, $H_1: \beta_{\text{sqft}} > 0$ (one-sided upper). **Step 2:** $t = 0.045 / 0.012 = 3.75$. **Step 3:** Under $H_0$, $t \sim t_{n-k-1} = t_{88-4-1} = t_{83}$. **Step 4:** $t_{83, 0.05} \approx 1.663$. Since $3.75 > 1.663$, **reject $H_0$**. **Step 5:** Each additional square foot is associated with a statistically significant \$45 increase in house price (holding other variables constant), significant at the 5% level.

Q2. From the same output: \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{pool}} = 4.5\) (thousands of dollars) with \(se = 8.2\). A colleague concludes "a pool adds $4,500 to house value." Critically evaluate this claim.

Answer $t = 4.5 / 8.2 = 0.549$. With $df = 83$, the two-sided critical value at 5% is $\approx 1.989$. Since $0.549 < 1.989$, we **fail to reject** $H_0: \beta_{\text{pool}} = 0$. The estimate suggests a positive effect, but the standard error is nearly twice the coefficient. We cannot detect a statistically significant pool premium with this sample. The colleague should not make a causal claim from a statistically insignificant estimate. The true effect could plausibly be zero (or even negative) — the data are too imprecise to tell.

Q3. A researcher tests \(H_0: \beta_j = 1\) (rather than the standard \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\)) for a coefficient \(\hat{\beta}_j = 1.38\) with \(se = 0.14\), \(n = 200\), \(k = 3\). Compute the t-statistic and state whether you reject at the 5% two-sided level.

Answer **Step 1:** $H_0: \beta_j = 1$, $H_1: \beta_j \neq 1$. **Step 2:** $t = (\hat{\beta}_j - a_j)/se = (1.38 - 1.00) / 0.14 = 0.38 / 0.14 = 2.71$. **Step 3:** $df = 200 - 3 - 1 = 196$. $t_{196, 0.025} \approx 1.972$. **Step 4:** $|2.71| > 1.972$, so **reject $H_0$** at the 5% level. **Conclusion:** The data provide statistically significant evidence that $\beta_j \neq 1$ at the 5% level.

docs.text:

  • Wooldridge (2019), §4.3: "Confidence Intervals"

docs.title: Lesson M04.L03: Confidence Intervals for OLS Coefficients
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 04 — Statistical Inference in OLS Level Graduate (ECMT5001, S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Construct 95% and 99% confidence intervals for regression coefficients; correctly interpret them; connect CIs to hypothesis tests; understand what makes intervals wider or narrower Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7e, Chapter 4.3 (pp. 140–146)

docs.title: The Confidence Interval Formula
docs.text:
From Lesson M04.L01, we know that under MLR.1–MLR.6:

\[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t_{n-k-1}\]

A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is constructed by inverting this pivotal quantity: find the values of \(\beta_j\) that are not rejected by a two-sided \(\alpha\)-level t-test:

\[\boxed{\hat{\beta}_j \pm t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2} \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_j)}\]

where \(t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2}\) is the upper \(\alpha/2\) critical value of the \(t_{n-k-1}\) distribution.

Common confidence levels and their critical values (large \(n\)):

Confidence level \(\alpha\) \(\alpha/2\) \(t^*\) (large \(n\)) 90% 0.10 0.05 1.645 95% 0.05 0.025 1.960 99% 0.01 0.005 2.576

For finite samples, always use the exact \(t_{n-k-1, \alpha/2}\) value from tables.

docs.title: Correct Interpretation
docs.text:
The correct frequentist interpretation of a 95% CI is:

If we were to repeat the sampling and estimation procedure many times, 95% of the intervals constructed this way would contain the true value \(\beta_j\).

This is a statement about the procedure, not about any single realised interval.

The parameter \(\beta_j\) is a fixed (non-random) unknown constant. It does not have a probability distribution. Once a specific interval \([L, U]\) has been computed from data, it either contains \(\beta_j\) or it does not — there is no probability in between. The randomness lives entirely in \(\hat{\beta}_j\) (and hence in \(L\) and \(U\)), not in \(\beta_j\).

docs.title: Relationship Between CIs and Hypothesis Tests
docs.text:
There is a direct duality between a two-sided t-test and a confidence interval:

\[\text{Reject } H_0: \beta_j = a_j \text{ at level } \alpha \iff a_j \notin \text{ } 100(1-\alpha)\% \text{ CI for } \beta_j\]

This means: - If \(0\) lies outside the 95% CI, we reject \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\) at the 5% level. - If \(0\) lies inside the 95% CI, we fail to reject \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\) at the 5% level.

The CI provides richer information than the hypothesis test — it tells you not just whether to reject, but also the range of values consistent with the data at the specified confidence level.

docs.title: What Makes a CI Wider or Narrower?
docs.text:
The width of a CI is \(2 \cdot t_{n-k-1,\, \alpha/2} \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_j)\).

Since \(se(\hat{\beta}_j) = \dfrac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}}\), the CI is wider when:

Factor Effect on CI width Why Smaller \(n\) Wider Less data → less precision; also larger \(t^*\) with fewer df Larger \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) (noisier data) Wider Regression errors are large Less variation in \(x_j\) (small \(SST_j\)) Wider Can't pin down slope without variation in regressor High multicollinearity (large \(R_j^2\)) Wider \(x_j\) is nearly explained by other regressors; little unique information Higher confidence level (99% vs 95%) Wider Larger \(t^*\) to capture more of the distribution

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. A graduate student estimates the following model of log earnings using \(n = 935\) workers with \(k = 4\) regressors (\(df = 935 - 4 - 1 = 930\)):

\[\log(\text{earnings}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ}_i + \beta_2 \text{exper}_i + \beta_3 \text{exper}^2_i + \beta_4 \text{female}_i + u_i\]

The OLS output is:

Variable \(\hat{\beta}_j\) \(se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) Intercept 0.316 0.085 educ 0.078 0.006 exper 0.033 0.006 exper² −0.0005 0.0001 female −0.252 0.028

With \(df = 930\), we use \(t^* \approx 1.963\) for 95% CIs and \(t^* \approx 2.581\) for 99% CIs (approximately equal to \(z\) critical values given large \(n\)).

95% CI for \(\beta_1\) (return to education):

\[\hat{\beta}_1 \pm t^* \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_1) = 0.078 \pm 1.963 \times 0.006$$ $$= 0.078 \pm 0.012$$ $$= (0.066,\; 0.090)\]

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true return to an additional year of education lies between 6.6% and 9.0% (log-point change in earnings), holding other variables constant.

Since 0 is far outside this interval, we reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) at the 5% level (consistent with \(t = 0.078/0.006 = 13.0\), which is very large).

99% CI for \(\beta_4\) (gender gap):

\[\hat{\beta}_4 \pm t^* \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_4) = -0.252 \pm 2.581 \times 0.028$$ $$= -0.252 \pm 0.072$$ $$= (-0.324,\; -0.180)\]

Interpretation: We are 99% confident that the female earnings penalty lies between \(-32.4\%\) and \(-18.0\%\) log earnings, controlling for education and experience. The entire interval lies below zero, confirming the gender gap is significant at the 1% level.

Comparing 95% vs 99%: The 99% CI for \(\beta_4\) would be:

\[-0.252 \pm 2.581 \times 0.028 = (-0.324, -0.180)\]

vs the 95% CI:

\[-0.252 \pm 1.963 \times 0.028 = (-0.307, -0.197)\]

The 99% interval is wider by \(2 \times (2.581 - 1.963) \times 0.028 = 2 \times 0.017 = 0.035\) — a modest widening given the large sample.

CI for \(\beta_2\) (experience, where \(0\) might plausibly be inside):

\[\hat{\beta}_2 \pm 1.963 \times 0.006 = 0.033 \pm 0.012 = (0.021,\; 0.045)\]

Zero is outside the interval, so we reject \(H_0: \beta_2 = 0\) at 5%. But also note: zero is very far from 0.033 relative to \(se = 0.006\). The experience effect is precisely estimated.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"There is a 95% probability that \(\beta_j\) lies in the interval \((L, U)\)."

This is a common but incorrect statement. In the frequentist framework:

  • \(\beta_j\) is a fixed unknown constant, not a random variable.
  • The interval endpoints \(L = \hat{\beta}_j - t^* \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) and \(U = \hat{\beta}_j + t^* \cdot se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) are random — they depend on the random sample.
  • Once we observe the data and compute, say, \(L = 0.066\) and \(U = 0.090\), the probability that \(\beta_1 \in (0.066, 0.090)\) is either 0 or 1 (it either does or doesn't). We just don't know which.

The correct statement: "The interval was constructed by a procedure that, in repeated samples, would contain the true \(\beta_j\) in 95% of cases."

Bayesian note: A statement like "95% probability that \(\beta_j \in (L, U)\)" has a precise meaning in Bayesian statistics (it would be a 95% credible interval). But under frequentist OLS, this language is incorrect.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Q1. A model of city crime rates has \(n = 46\) cities, \(k = 3\) regressors, \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{unemployment}} = 0.82\), \(se = 0.41\). Construct a 95% CI and a 90% CI. Does the 95% CI include zero? What does this imply for a two-sided test at 5%?

Answer $df = 46 - 3 - 1 = 42$. From t-tables: $t_{42, 0.025} \approx 2.018$ (95%), $t_{42, 0.05} \approx 1.682$ (90%). **95% CI:** $0.82 \pm 2.018 \times 0.41 = 0.82 \pm 0.828 = (-0.008,\; 1.648)$. **90% CI:** $0.82 \pm 1.682 \times 0.41 = 0.82 \pm 0.690 = (0.130,\; 1.510)$. The 95% CI barely includes zero (lower bound $\approx -0.008$), so we **fail to reject** $H_0: \beta_{\text{unemployment}} = 0$ at the 5% level. However, the 90% CI excludes zero, so we **would reject** at the 10% level. The result is marginally insignificant at 5%: $t = 0.82/0.41 = 2.00 < t_{42,0.025} = 2.018$.

Q2. For the same regression, a colleague claims: "Because the 95% CI is \((-0.008, 1.648)\), there is only a 5% chance that the true effect is negative." Correct this statement.

Answer The statement is incorrect. The parameter $\beta_{\text{unemployment}}$ is a fixed unknown — it is either positive or negative; there is no probability attached to its sign under frequentist inference. The correct interpretation: the interval $(-0.008, 1.648)$ was produced by a procedure that yields intervals containing the true $\beta$ in 95% of repeated samples. We do not know whether this particular realised interval is one of the 95% that contain the truth, or one of the 5% that do not. The fact that 95% of the interval lies in the positive region reflects the distribution of $\hat{\beta}$, not a probability over $\beta$.

Q3. A researcher reports: \(\hat{\beta} = 0.120\), \(se = 0.048\), \(n = 80\), \(k = 2\). Construct the 95% CI and verify that the result is consistent with the t-test outcome at the 5% level.

Answer $df = 80 - 2 - 1 = 77$. $t_{77, 0.025} \approx 1.991$. **95% CI:** $0.120 \pm 1.991 \times 0.048 = 0.120 \pm 0.096 = (0.024,\; 0.216)$. Zero is **outside** the interval, so we **reject** $H_0: \beta = 0$ at 5%. **Verification via t-test:** $t = 0.120 / 0.048 = 2.50 > 1.991$. Reject $H_0$. ✓ Both approaches yield the same decision, confirming the duality between CIs and hypothesis tests.

docs.text:
• Wooldridge (2019), §4.3: "Confidence Intervals" (pp. 140–146)
  • Wooldridge (2019), Appendix B.4: "Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing"
  • Stock & Watson (2020), Introduction to Econometrics, §7.3: "Confidence Intervals for a Single Coefficient"
  • Freedman, Pisani & Purves (2007), Statistics, Ch. 26: for intuition on what confidence intervals do and don't mean

docs.title: Lesson M04.L04: F-Tests and Joint Hypotheses
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 04 — Statistical Inference in OLS Level Graduate (ECMT5001, S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Formulate and execute F-tests for joint hypotheses; relate the F-statistic to restricted and unrestricted SSR/R²; test the overall significance of a regression; understand why individual t-tests cannot replace joint tests Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7e, Chapter 4.5 (pp. 153–168)

docs.title: Why We Need Joint Tests
docs.text:
Suppose we want to know whether education and experience are together relevant predictors of wages. We might think: just check whether both have \(|t| > 1.96\). But this is wrong.

If the t-tests for \(\hat{\beta}_1\) and \(\hat{\beta}_2\) are correlated (which they are whenever the regressors are correlated), then: - Two individually insignificant variables can be jointly significant. - Two individually significant variables can (in principle) be jointly redundant.

The correct tool for testing multiple restrictions simultaneously is the F-test.

docs.title: Setting Up the Hypotheses
docs.text:
A joint hypothesis imposes \(q\) linear restrictions on the \(\beta\) vector. The most common case is testing that \(q\) specific coefficients are all zero:

\[H_0: \beta_1 = 0,\; \beta_2 = 0,\; \ldots,\; \beta_q = 0$$ $$H_1: \text{at least one of } \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_q \neq 0\]

For example, in a model with 5 regressors, we might test whether the last two are jointly irrelevant: \(H_0: \beta_4 = 0, \beta_5 = 0\) (\(q = 2\) restrictions).

docs.title: Restricted vs. Unrestricted Models
docs.text:
The F-test compares two regressions:

Unrestricted model (UR): includes all regressors (k total); has \(SSR_{ur}\) and \(R^2_{ur}\).

Restricted model (R): imposes \(H_0\) by dropping the \(q\) restricted regressors; has \(SSR_r\) and \(R^2_r\).

Imposing restrictions always increases SSR (or at best leaves it unchanged). The question is: does the increase in SSR from imposing \(H_0\) represent more than we'd expect by chance?

docs.title: The F-Statistic
docs.text:
\[\boxed{F = \frac{(SSR_r - SSR_{ur})\,/\,q}{SSR_{ur}\,/\,(n-k-1)}}\]

where: - \(SSR_r - SSR_{ur}\) = increase in residual sum of squares from imposing restrictions - \(q\) = number of restrictions (numerator df) - \(n - k - 1\) = degrees of freedom of the unrestricted model (denominator df)

Under \(H_0\) (and CLM assumptions MLR.1–MLR.6):

\[F \sim F_{q,\; n-k-1}\]

An F-distribution with \(q\) and \(n-k-1\) degrees of freedom. Since larger F means larger deterioration in fit under \(H_0\), we always use a right-tailed test:

\[\text{Reject } H_0 \text{ at level } \alpha \iff F > F_{q,\; n-k-1,\; \alpha}\]

docs.title: Equivalent \(R^2\) Form
docs.text:
Since \(SSR = SST(1 - R^2)\) and \(SST\) is the same in restricted and unrestricted models (when the restricted model still includes an intercept):

\[\boxed{F = \frac{(R^2_{ur} - R^2_r)\,/\,q}{(1 - R^2_{ur})\,/\,(n-k-1)}}\]

This form is convenient when software reports \(R^2\) rather than \(SSR\).

docs.title: Overall Significance of the Regression
docs.text:
A special case: the null hypothesis that all slope coefficients are zero (none of the \(k\) regressors help explain \(y\)):

\[H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0 \qquad (q = k \text{ restrictions})\]

Under \(H_0\), the restricted model is just \(y_i = \beta_0 + u_i\), so \(R^2_r = 0\), and the F-statistic simplifies to:

\[F = \frac{R^2_{ur}/k}{(1 - R^2_{ur})/(n-k-1)}\]

This is the overall F-statistic reported by regression software. Rejecting this \(H_0\) means the regression has some explanatory power beyond just the mean of \(y\).

docs.title: Why Individual t-Tests Are Not Sufficient for Joint Hypotheses
docs.text:
Suppose we test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) and \(H_0: \beta_2 = 0\) individually at 5% each. With two independent tests, the probability of making at least one Type I error (false rejection) is:

\[1 - (1 - 0.05)^2 = 1 - 0.9025 = 9.75\%\]

For correlated tests (which is typical in regression), the size distortion can be even worse or better depending on the correlation direction. The F-test controls the joint size at exactly \(\alpha\).

Moreover, even if both t-statistics are individually below their critical values, the F-statistic can exceed its critical value if both estimators are simultaneously pushed in the same direction by the data.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. We estimate a log-wage regression with \(n = 526\) workers and two potential regressors beyond education and gender: \(\text{exper}\) and \(\text{exper}^2\).

Unrestricted model (\(k = 4\) regressors: educ, exper, exper², female): $\(\log(\hat{\text{wage}}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{educ} + \beta_2\,\text{exper} + \beta_3\,\text{exper}^2 + \beta_4\,\text{female} + u\)$ $\(SSR_{ur} = 97.34, \quad R^2_{ur} = 0.3625, \quad df_{ur} = 526 - 4 - 1 = 521\)$

Restricted model (\(k^* = 2\) regressors: educ, female — drops exper and exper²): $\(\log(\hat{\text{wage}}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{educ} + \beta_4\,\text{female} + v\)$ $\(SSR_r = 103.79, \quad R^2_r = 0.3201\)$

Joint hypothesis: \(H_0: \beta_2 = 0,\, \beta_3 = 0\) (\(q = 2\) restrictions).

Step 1 — State hypotheses: $\(H_0: \beta_2 = 0 \text{ and } \beta_3 = 0 \qquad H_1: \text{at least one } \neq 0\)$

Step 2 — Compute F-statistic (SSR form): $\(F = \frac{(SSR_r - SSR_{ur})\,/\,q}{SSR_{ur}\,/\,(n-k-1)} = \frac{(103.79 - 97.34)\,/\,2}{97.34\,/\,521}\)$

\[= \frac{6.45\,/\,2}{97.34\,/\,521} = \frac{3.225}{0.1868} = 17.26\]

Verification via R² form: $\(F = \frac{(0.3625 - 0.3201)\,/\,2}{(1 - 0.3625)\,/\,521} = \frac{0.0424\,/\,2}{0.6375\,/\,521} = \frac{0.0212}{0.001224} = 17.32\)$

(Small rounding difference; both \(\approx 17.3\).)

Step 3 — Distribution under \(H_0\): \(F \sim F_{2,\, 521}\)

Step 4 — Critical value: At \(\alpha = 1\%\), \(F_{2,\, 521, 0.01} \approx 4.62\). At \(\alpha = 5\%\), \(F_{2,\, 521, 0.05} \approx 3.00\).

Step 5 — Decision: \(17.3 \gg 4.62\). Strongly reject \(H_0\) at any conventional significance level.

Step 6 — Interpretation: Experience and experience-squared are jointly highly significant. Despite experience and \(\text{exper}^2\) being correlated (which can inflate individual SEs), together they explain substantial variation in log wages beyond education and gender.

docs.title: Connecting to Individual t-Tests
docs.text:
For context, individual t-statistics from the unrestricted model might be: - \(t_{\text{exper}} = 0.033 / 0.008 = 4.13\) (significant at 1%) - \(t_{\text{exper}^2} = -0.0005 / 0.0001 = -5.00\) (significant at 1%)

Here individual t-tests also indicate significance, consistent with the F-test. But this won't always be the case: see the misconception section below.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Two individually insignificant t-tests mean the variables are jointly insignificant."

Consider a model where \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are highly positively correlated. The individual standard errors of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) and \(\hat{\beta}_2\) are inflated by multicollinearity. Individually, neither may pass the threshold \(|t| > 1.96\). Yet the F-test may strongly reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0, \beta_2 = 0\).

Numerical illustration. Suppose:

\(\hat{\beta}_j\) \(se\) \(t\) \(x_1\) 1.0 0.8 1.25 \(x_2\) 0.9 0.8 1.13

Both t-statistics are below 1.96 — individually insignificant at 5%. Yet if \(\hat{\beta}_1\) and \(\hat{\beta}_2\) are negatively correlated (induced by positive correlation between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)), the F-statistic for their joint significance may exceed the critical value \(F_{2, n-k-1, 0.05} \approx 3.0\).

Conversely: two individually significant coefficients could (in principle) be jointly just significant, though in practice this is less common.

Rule: Always use the F-test when testing joint hypotheses. Individual t-tests are correct only for single-coefficient tests.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Q1. A model of house prices has \(n = 148\) observations and \(k = 5\) regressors. You want to test whether the three neighbourhood characteristic variables (school quality, crime rate, pollution) are jointly significant. The unrestricted model has \(SSR_{ur} = 12{,}450\) and the restricted model (dropping those three variables) has \(SSR_r = 14{,}200\). Compute the F-statistic, state its null distribution, find the 5% critical value, and give your conclusion.

Answer **Step 1:** $H_0: \beta_{\text{school}} = \beta_{\text{crime}} = \beta_{\text{pollution}} = 0$; $q = 3$ restrictions. **Step 2:** $$F = \frac{(14{,}200 - 12{,}450)\,/\,3}{12{,}450\,/\,(148-5-1)} = \frac{1{,}750\,/\,3}{12{,}450\,/\,142} = \frac{583.33}{87.68} = 6.66$$ **Step 3:** Under $H_0$: $F \sim F_{3,\, 142}$. **Step 4:** $F_{3,\, 142,\, 0.05} \approx 2.67$. **Step 5:** $6.66 > 2.67$. **Reject $H_0$** at 5%. The neighbourhood variables are jointly significant.

Q2. In the same house price regression, the individual t-statistics are: \(t_{\text{school}} = 1.45\), \(t_{\text{crime}} = -1.50\), \(t_{\text{pollution}} = 1.60\) (all with \(df = 142\)). The two-sided 5% critical value is \(t_{142, 0.025} \approx 1.976\). All three fail individual significance tests. Is this contradictory with the F-test result in Q1? Explain.

Answer No contradiction. This is the classic case where multicollinearity inflates individual standard errors, making each coefficient appear imprecise on its own, while the variables collectively provide substantial explanatory power. The F-test accounts for the joint distribution of the estimators — including their covariances — and correctly identifies that the three variables together significantly improve fit. Individual t-tests ignore the correlations between $\hat{\beta}_{\text{school}}$, $\hat{\beta}_{\text{crime}}$, and $\hat{\beta}_{\text{pollution}}$, and can fail to detect genuine joint significance. Conclusion: individual t-tests are not valid substitutes for the F-test when testing joint restrictions.

Q3. A model has \(R^2_{ur} = 0.48\) with \(k = 6\) regressors and \(n = 200\). The restricted model (dropping the last 3 regressors) has \(R^2_r = 0.42\). Compute the F-statistic for the joint significance of those 3 variables at the 5% level.

Answer $q = 3$, $n - k - 1 = 200 - 6 - 1 = 193$. $$F = \frac{(0.48 - 0.42)\,/\,3}{(1 - 0.48)\,/\,193} = \frac{0.06\,/\,3}{0.52\,/\,193} = \frac{0.020}{0.002694} = 7.42$$ Under $H_0$: $F \sim F_{3,\, 193}$. Critical value $F_{3,\, 193,\, 0.05} \approx 2.65$. Since $7.42 > 2.65$, **reject $H_0$**: the three variables are jointly significant at 5%.
