docs.title: Lesson M04.L05: Reporting Regression Results
docs.text: Field Detail Module Module 04 — Statistical Inference in OLS Level Graduate (ECMT5001, S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Write up regression results in correct academic style; read and produce standard output tables; avoid common reporting errors; apply asymptotic justifications for dropping MLR.6 in large samples Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 7e, Chapters 4–5 (pp. 117–200)

docs.title: Standard Regression Output Table
docs.text:
Software such as R, Stata, and Python (statsmodels) produces a standard output format. Here is a representative table with annotations:

Dependent variable: log(wage)
Observations (n): 526
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                 Coeff.    Std. Err.    t-stat    p-value
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Intercept        0.284      0.104        2.73     0.007   **
educ             0.092      0.007       13.14    <0.001  ***
exper            0.004      0.001        4.00    <0.001  ***
female          −0.297      0.036       −8.25    <0.001  ***
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R²:             0.316
Adjusted R²:    0.312
F-statistic:    80.7  (df = 3, 522)   p-value: <0.001
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Significance: * p<0.10   ** p<0.05   *** p<0.01

Column guide: | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | Coeff. | OLS estimate \(\hat{\beta}_j\) | | Std. Err. | \(se(\hat{\beta}_j) = \hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}\) | | t-stat | \(\hat{\beta}_j / se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) | | p-value | Two-sided: \(2 \times P(T > |t|)\) where \(T \sim t_{n-k-1}\) | | Stars | Summary indicator of evidence against \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\) |

docs.title: The Adjusted \(R^2\)
docs.text:
The standard \(R^2 = 1 - SSR/SST\) always increases (weakly) when you add regressors, even irrelevant ones. The adjusted \(R^2\) penalises for additional regressors:

\[\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)} = 1 - \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{s_y^2}\]

where \(s_y^2 = SST/(n-1)\) is the sample variance of \(y\). \(\bar{R}^2\) can decrease when you add a regressor if its contribution to fit is outweighed by the loss of one degree of freedom. Use \(\bar{R}^2\) (not \(R^2\)) when comparing models with different numbers of regressors.

docs.title: The Overall F-Statistic
docs.text:
The overall F-statistic tests \(H_0: \beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0\) (all slope coefficients jointly zero). From Lesson M04.L04:

\[F = \frac{R^2/k}{(1-R^2)/(n-k-1)} \sim F_{k,\, n-k-1} \text{ under } H_0\]

A large F (with small p-value) tells you the regression explains significantly more variation than a model with only the intercept. This is a minimum bar for any regression model — if overall \(F\) is insignificant, the model as a whole adds nothing.

docs.title: How to Write Up Results: Academic Style
docs.text:
The standard form for reporting a single coefficient in text is:

"A one-unit increase in \(X_j\) is associated with a \(\hat{\beta}_j\)-unit change in \(Y\) (SE \(= se(\hat{\beta}_j)\), \(t = t_j\), \(p \leq \alpha\)), holding all other variables constant."

For log-transformed dependent variables (where coefficients are approximate percentage changes):

"An additional year of education is associated with an approximately 9.2% increase in hourly wages (SE \(= 0.007\), \(t = 13.14\), \(p < 0.001\)), controlling for experience and gender."

Key elements of a complete write-up: 1. State the dependent variable and its units (or log units). 2. Report \(\hat{\beta}_j\), its SE, t-statistic, and p-value (or CI). 3. Interpret the coefficient in context: direction, magnitude, units. 4. State what is held constant (ceteris paribus). 5. Comment on economic significance — not just statistical significance. 6. Report overall model fit: \(n\), \(R^2\) (or \(\bar{R}^2\)), and overall F-statistic.

docs.title: Common Reporting Errors to Avoid
docs.text: Error Why it's wrong Correct practice Reporting stars without SEs or t-stats Stars alone give no sense of precision Always report \(\hat{\beta}_j\) and \(se(\hat{\beta}_j)\) Omitting sample size \(n\) Effect sizes and precision are meaningless without \(n\) Always state \(n\) Confusing log-coefficient interpretation \(\hat{\beta}_j\) in log-level model is not a "unit change" State it as "approximately \(100\hat{\beta}_j\%\)" Using \(R^2\) to compare models with different \(k\) \(R^2\) always rises with more regressors Use \(\bar{R}^2\) for model comparison Claiming causality from observational OLS OLS identifies association, not causation, unless exogeneity holds Use "associated with" or "predicts", not "causes" Over-reporting stars: "more stars = more important" Stars only measure evidence against \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\), not magnitude Discuss coefficient size and economic relevance separately

docs.title: Asymptotic Justification: Large Samples Without MLR.6
docs.text:
MLR.6 (normality of \(u\)) is required for the exact t and F distributions to hold. In practice, most economic data (wages, prices, returns) do not have normally distributed errors.

The asymptotic justification (MLR.1–MLR.5 only):

Under MLR.1–MLR.5 (no normality required), as \(n \to \infty\):

\[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{se(\hat{\beta}_j)} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)\]

by the CLT (since \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is a sample average of terms involving \(u_i\), which have finite variance by MLR.5). Therefore, for large \(n\):

  • t-statistics are asymptotically standard normal → t-critical values are approximately valid.
  • F-statistics divided by \(q\) are asymptotically chi-squared → F-critical values are approximately valid.
  • The normal approximation improves as \(n\) grows.

Practical implication: The \(t\) and \(F\) inference tools you learned are valid for large samples even without the normality assumption. For small samples (say \(n < 50\)), the validity of inference depends more heavily on whether errors are approximately normal — check residual plots.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. A researcher estimates a wage regression on \(n = 526\) CPS workers. Write up the results in academic report style.

The model: $\(\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{educ}_i + \beta_2\,\text{exper}_i + \beta_3\,\text{female}_i + u_i\)$

OLS output:

Variable \(\hat{\beta}_j\) \(se\) \(t\) \(p\) Intercept 0.284 0.104 2.73 0.007 educ 0.092 0.007 13.14 <0.001 exper 0.004 0.001 4.00 <0.001 female −0.297 0.036 −8.25 <0.001

\(n = 526\), \(R^2 = 0.316\), \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.312\), \(F_{3,\,522} = 80.7\) (\(p < 0.001\)).

Academic write-up:

Table 1 presents OLS estimates of the determinants of log hourly wages for \(n = 526\) workers from the 2019 Current Population Survey. The overall model is statistically significant (\(F_{3,\,522} = 80.7\), \(p < 0.001\)) and explains approximately 31.6% of the variation in log wages (\(R^2 = 0.316\); adjusted \(R^2 = 0.312\)).

Education has a precisely estimated positive return: each additional year of schooling is associated with approximately a 9.2% increase in hourly wages (SE \(= 0.007\), \(t = 13.14\), \(p < 0.001\)), holding experience and gender constant. This estimate is both statistically significant at the 1% level and economically meaningful — a four-year university degree is associated with roughly a 37% wage premium over a high school diploma (\(\approx 4 \times 9.2\%\)).

Experience also has a significant positive effect: each additional year of experience is associated with approximately a 0.4% increase in wages (SE \(= 0.001\), \(t = 4.00\), \(p < 0.001\)). While statistically significant, the magnitude is small relative to education, suggesting diminishing economic importance of raw experience after controlling for schooling.

Gender has a large and statistically significant coefficient: female workers earn approximately 29.7% lower log wages than male workers with equivalent education and experience (SE \(= 0.036\), \(t = -8.25\), \(p < 0.001\)). This is both statistically significant at the 1% level and economically substantial, representing a sizeable unexplained wage gap after controlling for observable human capital characteristics.

What this write-up does well: - Reports \(\hat{\beta}_j\), SE, \(t\), \(p\) for each coefficient. - Interprets log coefficients as approximate percentage changes. - States the ceteris paribus condition explicitly. - Comments on economic significance (magnitude, not just stars). - Reports \(n\), \(R^2\), \(\bar{R}^2\), and overall F. - Avoids causal language (uses "associated with", not "causes").

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Three asterisks () means the variable is more important than one asterisk ()."**

Stars indicate statistical significance — the strength of evidence against \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\). They are primarily driven by sample size and precision, not by the economic importance or magnitude of the effect.

Example. Suppose a study with \(n = 100{,}000\) observations finds that a firm's energy efficiency rating is associated with 0.1% higher stock returns (\(t = 6.2\), \(p < 0.001\), ***). Meanwhile, a study with \(n = 80\) finds that a CEO's previous industry experience is associated with 15% higher returns (\(t = 1.9\), \(p = 0.06\), not significant at 5%).

The first finding gets three stars; the second gets none. But the second effect (if real) is 150 times larger. Stars measure evidence, not magnitude.

Correct practice: Interpret coefficients by their magnitude and economic meaning, not their star count. A coefficient can be precisely estimated as trivially small (many stars, no economic importance) or imprecisely estimated as large (few stars, potentially large economic importance).

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Q1. A regression of house prices (\(000s) on square footage, number of bedrooms, distance to CBD, and a dummy for pool (\)k = 4$, \(n = 148\), \(df = 143\)) gives:

Variable \(\hat{\beta}\) SE sqft 0.110 0.014 bedrooms 8.200 4.100 dist_CBD −3.500 0.850 pool 5.100 8.200 Intercept 32.5 18.3

\(R^2 = 0.682\), \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.673\), \(F_{4,143} = 76.8\) (\(p < 0.001\)).

Write a brief academic-style paragraph reporting these results, including comments on statistical and economic significance.

Answer Table 1 presents OLS estimates of house prices for $n = 148$ observations ($df = 143$). The model explains 68.2% of price variation ($R^2 = 0.682$; $\bar{R}^2 = 0.673$) and is highly significant overall ($F_{4,143} = 76.8$, $p < 0.001$). Square footage has a positive and statistically significant effect: each additional square foot is associated with \$110 higher price (SE $= 14$, $t = 7.86$, $p < 0.001$), a large and economically meaningful effect. Distance to CBD has a significant negative effect: each additional kilometre from the city reduces price by approximately \$3,500 (SE $= 850$, $t = -4.12$, $p < 0.001$). Number of bedrooms shows a positive coefficient of \$8,200 (SE $= 4,100$, $t = 2.00$, $p \approx 0.047$), marginally significant at 5%. The pool premium is positive (\$5,100) but not statistically significant at conventional levels (SE $= 8,200$, $t = 0.62$, $p \approx 0.53$); the sample is likely underpowered to detect this effect.

Q2. A researcher reports: "Education is highly significant () while experience is only marginally significant (). Therefore education matters more for wages than experience." Identify the flaw in this reasoning and explain what additional information would be needed.

Answer The flaw is conflating statistical significance (which measures evidence against $H_0: \beta = 0$) with economic magnitude. The stars reflect the precision of the estimate relative to zero — not the size of the effect. To assess which variable matters more economically, the researcher should: 1. Compare the **magnitude** of the coefficients, standardised to a common scale (e.g., a one standard-deviation change in each variable: $\hat{\beta}_j \times sd(x_j)$). 2. Consider the realistic range of variation in each variable. If most workers have similar experience levels but widely varying education, education's total contribution to wage variation would be larger regardless of which coefficient is more "significant." Stars alone cannot determine economic importance.

Q3. A student estimates a model with \(n = 800\) workers and reports that the model has \(R^2 = 0.44\) and \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.43\). They add three more regressors and find \(R^2 = 0.45\) but \(\bar{R}^2 = 0.42\). Should they prefer the extended model? What does this tell you about the three new variables?

Answer No, they should prefer the original model. The rise in $R^2$ from 0.44 to 0.45 is mechanical — $R^2$ always weakly increases with additional regressors. The fall in $\bar{R}^2$ from 0.43 to 0.42 indicates the three new regressors do not contribute enough explanatory power to justify their cost in degrees of freedom. In other words, the improvement in fit is smaller than what one would expect by chance from adding three arbitrary variables. This also suggests that the three new regressors are likely jointly insignificant — a formal F-test for their joint significance would help confirm this. If $F < F_{3,\,794,\, 0.05} \approx 2.61$, we cannot reject that their true coefficients are all zero.

docs.title: Lesson M05.L01: Log Transformations in Regression
docs.text: Field Detail Module 05 — Functional Forms & Dummy Variables Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand the four log/level functional forms, interpret coefficients correctly in each case, and know when to apply logarithmic transformations. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 6.2

docs.title: Why Functional Form Matters
docs.text:
OLS assumes the relationship between \(y\) and \(x\) is linear in parameters — but it does not require linearity in the original variables. By transforming variables before estimating, we can capture a wide range of non-linear economic relationships while keeping the machinery of OLS intact.

Logarithmic transformations are by far the most common such device in applied econometrics.

Convention: In econometrics, \(\log\) always means the natural logarithm \(\ln\) (base \(e \approx 2.718\)). It never means \(\log_{10}\). Software commands like log() in Stata and R also default to the natural log.

docs.title: 1. Level-Level
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

Interpretation: A one-unit increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\beta_1\)-unit change in \(y\).

\[\Delta y = \beta_1 \,\Delta x\]

Use when both variables are naturally measured in levels and the relationship is approximately linear (e.g. test score on class size).

docs.title: 2. Log-Level (Semi-Elasticity)
docs.text:
\[\log(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

Interpretation: A one-unit increase in \(x\) is associated with an approximate \(100\beta_1\) percent change in \(y\).

\[\% \Delta y \approx 100 \beta_1 \,\Delta x\]

This is called a semi-elasticity — \(x\) is in levels, \(y\) is in logs. Use when \(y\) is right-skewed (wages, income, prices) and the effect of \(x\) is proportional rather than additive.

Example: If \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.082\) in a log-wage regression on years of education, then each additional year of education is associated with approximately an 8.2% increase in wages.

docs.title: 3. Level-Log
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(x) + u\]

Interpretation: A 1% increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\beta_1/100\) unit change in \(y\).

\[\Delta y \approx \frac{\beta_1}{100}\,\% \Delta x\]

Use when \(x\) exhibits diminishing marginal impact — each extra unit of \(x\) matters less than the previous (e.g. \(y\) = test score, \(x\) = expenditure per student).

docs.title: 4. Log-Log (Constant Elasticity)
docs.text:
\[\log(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(x) + u\]

Interpretation: A 1% increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\beta_1\)% change in \(y\). Here \(\beta_1\) is the elasticity of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).

\[\% \Delta y \approx \beta_1 \,\% \Delta x\]

This is the workhorse model for demand equations and production functions. The elasticity is constant across all values of \(x\).

Example: If \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.5\) in a log-log demand equation, the price elasticity of demand is \(-0.5\) (inelastic).

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Model Dep. Var. Indep. Var. Interpretation of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) Level-level \(y\) \(x\) \(\Delta y = \hat{\beta}_1 \Delta x\) (units) Log-level \(\log(y)\) \(x\) \(\% \Delta y \approx 100\hat{\beta}_1 \Delta x\) (semi-elasticity) Level-log \(y\) \(\log(x)\) \(\Delta y \approx (\hat{\beta}_1/100)\% \Delta x\) Log-log \(\log(y)\) \(\log(x)\) \(\% \Delta y \approx \hat{\beta}_1 \% \Delta x\) (elasticity)

docs.title: When to Use Logs
docs.text:
Use logarithmic transformations when:

  1. The variable is right-skewed — wages, income, housing prices, firm revenues all tend to have long right tails. Taking logs compresses the distribution and makes OLS better behaved.
  2. You want an elasticity interpretation — log-log gives a clean, scale-free elasticity.
  3. The marginal effect is proportional rather than additive — if a $1 increase in \(x\) has a larger absolute effect at low values of \(y\) than at high values, a log-level model is more appropriate.
  4. To reduce heteroskedasticity — log transformations often stabilise variance across observations.

docs.title: Limitations: What You Cannot Log
docs.text:
The natural log is undefined for zero and negative values:

\[\log(0) = -\infty, \quad \log(x) \text{ undefined for } x < 0\]

Alternatives when \(y \geq 0\) with zeros:

  • \(\log(1 + y)\): Adds 1 before taking logs. Simple, but coefficient interpretation is non-standard; the approximation \(\%\Delta y \approx 100\hat{\beta}_1\Delta x\) holds only when \(y\) is large.
  • Inverse Hyperbolic Sine (IHS): \(\text{arcsinh}(y) = \log(y + \sqrt{y^2 + 1})\). Behaves like \(\log(2y)\) for large \(y\), equals 0 at \(y=0\), and is defined for negative values. Increasingly preferred in modern applied work.
  • Two-part (Tobit-type) models: Separate models for the zero/non-zero decision and the level conditional on being positive.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Dataset: Cross-sectional sample of \(n = 526\) workers (Wooldridge WAGE1).

Equation estimated:

\[\log(\widehat{wage}_i) = 0.584 + 0.082\, educ_i + 0.029\, exper_i - 0.0006\, exper_i^2\]

Coefficient on education: \(\hat{\beta}_{educ} = 0.082\)

Interpretation: Each additional year of education is associated with approximately 8.2% higher wages, holding experience constant.

This is a log-level model. The dependent variable is \(\log(wage)\); education is measured in years (a level).

Why log wages? Wages are right-skewed: a few very high earners pull the distribution. Taking logs produces a more symmetric distribution and stabilises variance. The percentage interpretation is also more economically natural ("a 10% wage premium") than an additive one ("$0.82/hour more").

Exact vs approximate interpretation: The exact percentage effect of a one-unit change in \(x\) in a log-level model is:

\[\% \Delta y = 100 \left(e^{\hat{\beta}_1} - 1\right)\]

For \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.082\): \(100(e^{0.082} - 1) = 100(1.0854 - 1) = 8.54\%\). The approximation (\(8.2\%\)) is close enough for small coefficients but use the exact formula for coefficients above \(\approx 0.2\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Log in a regression means log base 10."

Correction: In econometrics, \(\log\) universally refers to the natural logarithm (base \(e\)), not \(\log_{10}\). When Wooldridge writes \(\log(wage)\), he means \(\ln(wage)\). Stata's gen lwage = log(wage) and R's log(wage) both compute natural logs. If you use \(\log_{10}\) by accident, your coefficients will be off by a factor of \(\ln(10) \approx 2.303\) and your interpretations will be wrong. Always double-check which base your software uses (hint: it's always \(e\) by default in econometrics packages).

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Identification A researcher estimates:

\[\widehat{price} = 12.3 + 0.95\,\log(sqft)\]

where \(price\) is in thousands of dollars and \(sqft\) is house size in square feet. What functional form is this? Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.95\). If house size increases by 10%, what is the predicted change in price (in dollars)?

Prompt 2 — Model choice You are studying the effect of advertising expenditure on firm sales. Sales range from $50,000 to $50 million across firms. Advertising expenditure ranges from $1,000 to $500,000. Which functional form would you choose and why? What does your choice imply about the marginal return to advertising?

Prompt 3 — Zero values A researcher wants to estimate the effect of government transfers on household savings. Savings takes the value zero for 35% of households in the sample. Why is \(\log(savings)\) problematic here? Name two alternatives and briefly explain each.

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §6.2 — Functional Forms Involving Logarithms
  • Bellemare & Wichman (2020), "Elasticities and the Inverse Hyperbolic Sine Transformation", Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
  • Stata: gen lnwage = log(wage) then reg lnwage educ exper
  • R: lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = wage1)

docs.title: Lesson M05.L02: Quadratic and Interaction Terms
docs.text: Field Detail Module 05 — Functional Forms & Dummy Variables Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Specify and interpret quadratic regression models and interaction terms; compute partial effects that vary with the level of a regressor; identify turning points; understand why main effects must always accompany interaction terms. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 6.2

docs.title: Beyond Linearity
docs.text: The classical linear regression model is linear in parameters — not necessarily in the variables themselves. We can introduce non-linearity in the relationship between \(y\) and \(x\) while preserving OLS validity by including polynomial terms or interaction terms as additional regressors.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + u\]

This is just a standard multiple regression with two regressors: \(x\) and \(x^2\). OLS estimation proceeds identically to the linear case.

docs.title: Partial Effect (Marginal Effect)
docs.text:
The effect of \(x\) on \(y\) is no longer constant — it depends on the current level of \(x\):

\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \beta_1 + 2\beta_2 x\]

To evaluate the partial effect, you must plug in a specific value of \(x\) (commonly \(\bar{x}\), the sample mean).

docs.title: Turning Point
docs.text:
If \(\beta_2 \neq 0\), the parabola has a turning point (maximum or minimum) at:

\[x^* = -\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}\]
  • If \(\beta_2 < 0\): the parabola is inverted-U-shaped — marginal effect starts positive and eventually turns negative. Turning point is a maximum. Example: productivity first rises then falls with age.
  • If \(\beta_2 > 0\): the parabola is U-shaped — marginal effect starts negative and eventually turns positive. Turning point is a minimum. Example: costs as a function of output.

Important: You should check whether \(x^*\) lies within the support of the data. A turning point outside the observed range of \(x\) means the parabola is effectively monotone within the sample, and the quadratic may just be capturing curvature at the boundaries.

docs.title: Economic Motivation
docs.text:
The experience-wage profile is the canonical example:

  • Early in a career, additional experience sharply raises wages (learning, promotions).
  • Later in a career, the gains diminish (skill depreciation, physical limits).
  • This generates an inverted-U shape: \(\beta_1 > 0\), \(\beta_2 < 0\).

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \cdot x_2) + u\]

The term \(x_1 \cdot x_2\) is the interaction (or cross product) of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).

docs.title: Marginal Effect of \(x_1\)
docs.text:
\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_1} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 x_2\]

The effect of \(x_1\) on \(y\) now depends on the level of \(x_2\). This is the defining feature of an interaction model: the relationship between \(y\) and \(x_1\) is moderated by \(x_2\).

Similarly:

\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_2} = \beta_2 + \beta_3 x_1\]

docs.title: The Main Effects Rule
docs.text:
Never include an interaction term without also including both of the main effects it interacts.

If you include \(x_1 x_2\) but omit \(x_1\), you are imposing the restriction \(\beta_1 = 0\) — which is a testable hypothesis, not a modelling convenience. Omitting main effects distorts the coefficient on the interaction and produces misleading estimates. This is one of the most common specification errors in applied work.

docs.title: Economic Examples
docs.text:
• Education × Gender: Does the return to an additional year of education differ between men and women? Include \(educ \cdot female\) as an interaction.
  • Advertising × Market size: Does the effect of advertising on sales scale with the size of the market?
  • Income × Price: Do higher-income households respond less to price changes?

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Dataset: Wooldridge WAGE1, \(n = 526\).

Equation:

\[\log(\widehat{wage}_i) = 0.416 + 0.094\,educ_i + 0.041\,exper_i - 0.00071\,exper_i^2\]

Step 1 — Partial effect of experience at the mean

Sample mean experience: \(\bar{exper} = 17.0\) years.

\[\left.\frac{\partial \log(wage)}{\partial exper}\right|_{\bar{exper}} = 0.041 + 2(-0.00071)(17) = 0.041 - 0.024 = 0.017\]

At the mean level of experience, one more year is associated with approximately a 1.7% wage increase.

Step 2 — Turning point (peak earnings year)

\[exper^* = -\frac{0.041}{2 \times (-0.00071)} = \frac{0.041}{0.00142} \approx 28.9 \text{ years of experience}\]

Wages are predicted to peak at about 29 years of experience, after which additional experience is associated with slightly declining wages. The sample range of experience is 0–51 years, so the turning point is comfortably within the data.

Step 3 — Sign check

\(\hat{\beta}_{exper} = 0.041 > 0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_{exper^2} = -0.00071 < 0\): inverted-U shape, consistent with the expected diminishing returns profile.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"The coefficient on \(x^2\) tells you the effect of \(x\) on \(y\)."

Correction: The coefficient \(\hat{\beta}_2\) on \(x^2\) is not the marginal effect of \(x\). It is not even a standalone effect — it only has meaning in conjunction with \(\hat{\beta}_1\). The correct marginal effect is:

\[\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial x} = \hat{\beta}_1 + 2\hat{\beta}_2\, x\]

This expression varies with \(x\). Reporting \(\hat{\beta}_2\) alone, or treating it as "the effect of \(x\) on \(y\)," is incorrect. Always compute and report the full partial effect at a meaningful value of \(x\) (e.g. \(\bar{x}\), or several percentiles).

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Partial effect and turning point A researcher estimates the following equation for job satisfaction scores (0–100):

\[\widehat{satisf} = 42 + 3.2\,tenure - 0.08\,tenure^2\]

where \(tenure\) is years with the current employer (range: 0–35 years).

(a) What is the partial effect of tenure on satisfaction at \(tenure = 10\)? (b) At what tenure does satisfaction peak? (c) Is the turning point in the sample range? What does that imply about the shape of the relationship within the data?

Prompt 2 — Interaction term A researcher estimates:

\[\widehat{\log(sales)} = 2.1 + 0.4\,\log(advert) + 0.6\,bigmarket + 0.3\,\log(advert) \times bigmarket\]

where \(bigmarket \in \{0,1\}\) indicates a large metropolitan market.

(a) What is the marginal effect of advertising (in elasticity terms) for firms in small markets? (b) What is the marginal effect for firms in large markets? (c) Interpret the coefficient 0.3 on the interaction term.

Prompt 3 — Specification error A student estimates:

\[\widehat{gpa} = 1.8 + 0.12\,study \times sleep\]

omitting \(study\) and \(sleep\) as separate regressors. Explain why this specification is problematic. What would you estimate instead?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §6.2
  • Stata: gen expersq = exper^2 then reg lwage educ exper expersq
  • R: lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2), data = wage1)
  • For marginal effects at the mean in Stata: margins, dydx(exper) atmeans

docs.title: Lesson M05.L03: Dummy Variables
docs.text: Field Detail Module 05 — Functional Forms & Dummy Variables Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Construct and interpret binary dummy variables; understand the intercept-shift interpretation; correctly encode multi-category variables using G−1 dummies; interpret the base category. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 7.1–7.2

docs.title: What Is a Dummy Variable?
docs.text:
A dummy variable (also called an indicator variable or binary variable) takes only two values:

\[D_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if observation } i \text{ belongs to the group of interest} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

Dummy variables allow us to include qualitative information — gender, region, marital status, industry, treatment status — as regressors in a linear regression model.

docs.title: Regression with a Single Dummy
docs.text:
Consider the model:

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 x_i + u_i\]

Interpretation of \(\beta_1\):

The conditional expected value of \(y\) for each group:

\[E[y_i \mid D_i = 1, x_i] = (\beta_0 + \beta_1) + \beta_2 x_i$$ $$E[y_i \mid D_i = 0, x_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_2 x_i\]

The difference:

\[E[y_i \mid D_i = 1, x_i] - E[y_i \mid D_i = 0, x_i] = \beta_1\]

\(\hat{\beta}_1\) estimates the difference in the mean of \(y\) between the \(D=1\) group and the \(D=0\) group, controlling for \(x\).

This is an intercept shift: both groups share the same slope \(\beta_2\) (parallel regression lines), but the group with \(D=1\) has its regression line shifted up (or down) by \(\beta_1\).

docs.title: The Base/Reference Category
docs.text:
The group with \(D = 0\) is called the base category or reference group. All dummy coefficients are interpreted relative to this base.

Choosing the base category is a matter of convenience and interpretability — there is no statistical reason to prefer one choice over another, though the one with the largest sample size or the most natural comparison point is often chosen.

docs.title: Multiple Dummies from One Categorical Variable
docs.text:
Suppose a categorical variable has \(G\) mutually exclusive groups (e.g. \(G = 4\) geographic regions: North, South, East, West). You need \(G - 1\) dummy variables, omitting one group as the base.

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_{North,i} + \beta_2 D_{South,i} + \beta_3 D_{East,i} + \beta_4 x_i + u_i\]

Here West is the omitted base region. Interpretations:

  • \(\hat{\beta}_1\): estimated difference in mean \(y\) between North and West, controlling for \(x\)
  • \(\hat{\beta}_2\): estimated difference in mean \(y\) between South and West, controlling for \(x\)
  • \(\hat{\beta}_3\): estimated difference in mean \(y\) between East and West, controlling for \(x\)

The intercept \(\hat{\beta}_0\) is the predicted value of \(y\) for the West group when \(x = 0\).

Why \(G-1\) and not \(G\)? Including all \(G\) dummies creates perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap — see Lesson M05.L04). OLS cannot be computed with all \(G\) dummies included alongside an intercept.

docs.title: Example: Gender Wage Gap
docs.text:
Model:

\[\log(wage_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, female_i + \beta_2\, educ_i + \beta_3\, exper_i + u_i\]

Estimated:

\[\log(\widehat{wage_i}) = 0.417 - 0.297\, female_i + 0.080\, educ_i + 0.029\, exper_i\]

Interpretation:

\(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.297\): Holding education and experience constant, female workers earn approximately \(100 \times 0.297 = 29.7\%\) less than male workers. (Exact: \(100(e^{-0.297}-1) \approx -25.7\%\).)

This is the conditional gender gap — the portion that remains after controlling for education and experience. It does not capture the full unconditional gap, nor does it explain why the gap exists.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Dataset: Wooldridge WAGE1, \(n = 526\).

Step 1 — Create dummy variable: \(female_i = 1\) if worker is female, 0 if male.

Step 2 — Estimate model:

\[\log(\widehat{wage_i}) = 0.417 - 0.297\, female_i + 0.080\, educ_i + 0.029\, exper_i\] Variable Coefficient SE t-stat Intercept 0.417 0.099 4.21 female −0.297 0.036 −8.25 educ 0.080 0.007 11.43 exper 0.029 0.005 5.80

\(R^2 = 0.364\), \(n = 526\)

Step 3 — Interpret:

  • The coefficient on \(female\) is statistically significant (\(t = -8.25\), very far from zero).
  • The parallel-lines interpretation: male and female log-wage profiles are parallel (same returns to education and experience), but the female line lies 0.297 units below the male line.
  • The intercept 0.417 is the predicted \(\log(wage)\) for a male worker with zero education and zero experience — not economically meaningful but mathematically well-defined.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"The intercept is the mean of \(y\) for the base group."

Correction: The intercept \(\hat{\beta}_0\) is the predicted value of \(y\) for the base group when all continuous regressors equal zero. This is rarely the mean of \(y\) for the base group, and it may not even be a meaningful quantity (no worker has zero education and zero experience). The mean of \(y\) for the base group is estimated by evaluating the regression at the mean values of the continuous regressors, not at zero. To get the predicted \(y\) for the base group at meaningful covariate values, plug in specific \(x\) values:

\[\hat{y}_{base} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2 \bar{x}\]

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Interpretation A researcher estimates:

\[\widehat{health} = 3.8 + 0.6\, married + 0.15\, age - 0.12\, smoke\]

where \(health\) is a self-reported health score (1–5), \(married \in \{0,1\}\), \(age\) is in years, and \(smoke \in \{0,1\}\) indicates daily smoking.

(a) Interpret the coefficient on \(married\). (b) Who is the base category when both \(married\) and \(smoke\) are included? (c) What is the predicted health score for a 40-year-old married non-smoker?

Prompt 2 — Multi-category dummies A dataset contains workers classified into four industries: Manufacturing, Services, Finance, and Agriculture (the base). Dummies are created for Manufacturing, Services, and Finance.

(a) How would you interpret the coefficient on the Manufacturing dummy? (b) A student wants to test whether Manufacturing and Services workers earn the same average wage (controlling for other factors). How would you set up this test? (c) What would happen if the researcher also included an Agriculture dummy?

Prompt 3 — Parallel slopes Explain in your own words what the "parallel regression lines" interpretation of a dummy variable means. Under what circumstances would you expect this assumption to be violated, and how would you modify the model to allow for non-parallel lines?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §7.1–7.2
  • Stata: gen female = (sex == 2) then reg lwage female educ exper
  • R: wage1$female <- as.numeric(wage1$female) then lm(log(wage) ~ female + educ + exper, data = wage1)
  • For factor variables in R: lm(log(wage) ~ factor(industry) + educ, data = d) — R automatically drops one category

docs.title: Lesson M05.L04: The Dummy Variable Trap
docs.text: Field Detail Module 05 — Functional Forms & Dummy Variables Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand why including all G dummies for a G-category variable creates perfect multicollinearity; identify and correct the dummy variable trap; apply the rule to seasonal dummies and dummy interactions. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 7.1

docs.title: The Dummy Variable Trap: What It Is
docs.text: When a categorical variable has \(G\) mutually exclusive and exhaustive groups, we need exactly \(G - 1\) dummy variables in the regression. Including all \(G\) dummies causes perfect multicollinearity — a violation of the OLS rank assumption (MLR.3).

docs.title: Why Perfect Multicollinearity Arises
docs.text:
Suppose we have \(G = 4\) seasonal quarters: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4. Define dummies \(D_{Q1}, D_{Q2}, D_{Q3}, D_{Q4}\) where each is 1 in the corresponding quarter, 0 otherwise.

For every observation in the dataset:

\[D_{Q1,i} + D_{Q2,i} + D_{Q3,i} + D_{Q4,i} = 1 \quad \text{for all } i\]

But the intercept column in the design matrix is also a column of ones:

\[\mathbf{1} = D_{Q1} + D_{Q2} + D_{Q3} + D_{Q4}\]

This means the intercept column is an exact linear combination of the four dummy columns. The design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) does not have full column rank: \(\text{rank}(\mathbf{X}) < k+1\), and therefore \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) is singular (non-invertible).

OLS requires \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) to exist. With perfect multicollinearity, this inverse does not exist, and OLS breaks down entirely. Your software will either drop one variable automatically (Stata) or throw an error.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Drop one dummy (the base/reference category). With \(G - 1\) dummies:

\[\mathbf{1} \neq D_{Q1} + D_{Q2} + D_{Q3}\]

because the Q4 observations contribute 0 to the left-hand side but 1 to \(\mathbf{1}\). The perfect linear combination is broken, full rank is restored, and OLS can proceed.

docs.title: Seasonal Dummies Example
docs.text:
Model (annual data disaggregated by quarter):

\[\log(sales_t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_{Q1,t} + \beta_2 D_{Q2,t} + \beta_3 D_{Q3,t} + \beta_4 t + u_t\]

Q4 is the base quarter. Interpretations:

  • \(\hat{\beta}_0\): predicted log-sales in Q4, at time \(t = 0\)
  • \(\hat{\beta}_1\): difference in log-sales between Q1 and Q4, holding trend constant (\(\approx \hat{\beta}_1 \times 100\%\) seasonal effect)
  • \(\hat{\beta}_2\): Q2 vs Q4 seasonal effect
  • \(\hat{\beta}_3\): Q3 vs Q4 seasonal effect

To test whether there are any seasonal effects: F-test \(H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = 0\).

docs.title: Interaction of Two Dummy Variables
docs.text:
Sometimes we want to interact two binary dummies. Suppose:

  • \(female \in \{0,1\}\): gender indicator
  • \(graduate \in \{0,1\}\): indicator for having a graduate degree

We can create an interaction dummy:

\[female\_graduate_i = female_i \times graduate_i\]

Full model:

\[wage_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, female_i + \beta_2\, graduate_i + \beta_3\, (female_i \times graduate_i) + u_i\]

This creates four groups with the following predicted wages:

Group female graduate Predicted wage Male, non-graduate (base) 0 0 \(\hat{\beta}_0\) Female, non-graduate 1 0 \(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1\) Male, graduate 0 1 \(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2\) Female, graduate 1 1 \(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_2 + \hat{\beta}_3\)

Here \(\hat{\beta}_3\) captures whether the graduate premium is different for women than for men. If \(\hat{\beta}_3 > 0\), graduate women earn more relative to non-graduate women than the corresponding gap among men.

Note: this is equivalent to using 4 dummies from the 2×2 cross-classification, with one (male non-graduate) as the base.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Illustrating the Trap

Suppose we have \(n = 6\) observations and one categorical variable (season: Summer, Winter) with dummies \(D_S\) and \(D_W\).

Obs \(D_S\) \(D_W\) Intercept 1 (Summer) 1 0 1 2 (Summer) 1 0 1 3 (Summer) 1 0 1 4 (Winter) 0 1 1 5 (Winter) 0 1 1 6 (Winter) 0 1 1

The design matrix with intercept, \(D_S\), and \(D_W\) has three columns. But column 1 = column 2 + column 3 exactly. So \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) is:

\[\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\]

The determinant of this matrix equals \(6(9) - 3(9) - 3(9) = 54 - 27 - 27 = 0\). Singular: OLS fails.

Solution: Drop \(D_W\) (Winter becomes the base):

Design matrix now has intercept and \(D_S\) only — full rank, OLS proceeds.

\[\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 D_{S,i}\]

\(\hat{\beta}_0\) = predicted \(y\) in Winter; \(\hat{\beta}_1\) = Summer vs Winter difference.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"It doesn't matter which dummy you drop — they're all equivalent."

Correction: It matters a great deal for interpretation, though not for fit. Whichever category you drop becomes the base/reference group. Every dummy coefficient is interpreted as a difference from that base. If you drop North, coefficients measure South-vs-North, East-vs-North, West-vs-North. If you drop West, you get South-vs-West, East-vs-West, North-vs-West. The \(t\)-statistics on individual dummies change with the base choice. However, the fitted values, residuals, \(R^2\), SSE, and F-tests for joint significance are all identical regardless of which category you omit. Choose the base category that produces the most interpretable comparisons for your research question.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Identifying the trap A researcher has monthly data and creates 12 monthly dummy variables (\(Jan, Feb, \ldots, Dec\)) then estimates:

\[y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Jan_t + \beta_2 Feb_t + \cdots + \beta_{12} Dec_t + \gamma_1 x_t + u_t\]

(a) Why will OLS fail here? (b) What is the fix? (c) If the researcher runs this in Stata, what will Stata do automatically?

Prompt 2 — Seasonal dummies You have quarterly GDP growth data from 2000 Q1 to 2022 Q4. You include Q1, Q2, Q3 dummies (Q4 is base) plus a linear time trend.

(a) Interpret the coefficient on Q1. (b) To test whether Q1 and Q2 have the same seasonal effect, what test would you use? Write the null hypothesis formally. (c) To test whether there are any seasonal effects at all, write the null hypothesis and describe the test statistic.

Prompt 3 — Dummy interaction Consider the interaction model:

\[wage_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, union_i + \beta_2\, black_i + \beta_3\, (union_i \times black_i) + u_i\]

(a) Write out the predicted wage for each of the four groups (non-union/white; union/white; non-union/black; union/black), treating "white non-union" as the base. (b) Interpret \(\hat{\beta}_3 = -1.2\). (c) A researcher omits \(black_i\) from the model but includes \(union_i \times black_i\). Why is this a mistake?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §7.1
  • Stata: i.quarter syntax automatically creates \(G-1\) dummies with the first category as base
  • R: factor() in lm() automatically creates \(G-1\) dummies; use relevel() to change the base
  • Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem: why dropping a dummy is equivalent to partialling it out

docs.title: Lesson M05.L05: Interactions Between Dummies and Continuous Variables
docs.text: Field Detail Module 05 — Functional Forms & Dummy Variables Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Specify and interpret dummy-continuous interaction models; understand slope-shift vs intercept-shift; conduct and interpret the Chow test; apply interaction models in policy evaluation contexts. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 7.3–7.4

docs.title: Dummy × Continuous Interaction: Slope Shifts
docs.text:
In Lesson M05.L03 we allowed a dummy variable to shift the intercept of the regression line (parallel lines with different heights). But what if the dummy variable also changes the slope of the relationship between \(y\) and a continuous variable \(x\)?

The model:

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 x_i + \beta_3 (D_i \cdot x_i) + u_i\]

Expected values by group:

\[E[y_i \mid D_i = 0, x_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_2 x_i \quad \text{(base group: slope } \beta_2\text{)}$$ $$E[y_i \mid D_i = 1, x_i] = (\beta_0 + \beta_1) + (\beta_2 + \beta_3) x_i \quad \text{(dummy group: slope } \beta_2 + \beta_3\text{)}\]

Interpretation of coefficients:

Coefficient Meaning \(\beta_0\) Intercept for base group (\(D=0\)) \(\beta_1\) Intercept difference: group \(D=1\) vs \(D=0\) \(\beta_2\) Slope of \(x\) for base group \(\beta_3\) Slope difference: how much steeper (or flatter) the \(x\)-\(y\) relationship is for the \(D=1\) group

\(\hat{\beta}_3\) is the key parameter: it tells us whether the marginal effect of \(x\) on \(y\) differs between groups.

  • \(\hat{\beta}_3 > 0\): the effect of \(x\) is stronger (larger slope) for the \(D=1\) group
  • \(\hat{\beta}_3 < 0\): the effect of \(x\) is weaker for the \(D=1\) group
  • \(\hat{\beta}_3 = 0\): parallel lines (no slope difference; reduces to the model in M05.L03)

docs.title: The Chow Test
docs.text:
The Chow test is an F-test of whether all regression coefficients differ between two groups, not just the slope.

Full unrestricted model:

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 x_i + \beta_3 (D_i \cdot x_i) + u_i\]

Null hypothesis (no structural break between groups):

\[H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \text{ and } \beta_3 = 0\]

This tests whether both the intercept and the slope are the same for both groups. Rejection means the two groups have different regression functions — you should estimate them separately (or use the interaction model).

F-statistic:

\[F = \frac{(SSR_R - SSR_U)/q}{SSR_U/(n - k - 1)} \sim F_{q,\, n-k-1}\]

where \(q = 2\) (number of restrictions: \(\beta_1 = 0\) and \(\beta_3 = 0\)), \(SSR_R\) is from the restricted model (pooled, no interactions), and \(SSR_U\) is from the unrestricted model.

Alternative formulation (computationally equivalent): Run OLS separately for each group; compute \(SSR_1\) and \(SSR_2\); then:

\[F = \frac{[SSR_{pooled} - (SSR_1 + SSR_2)] / k}{(SSR_1 + SSR_2)/(n - 2k)}\]

where \(k\) is the number of coefficients in each group's model.

docs.title: Policy Evaluation Application
docs.text:
Interactions are central to difference-in-differences (DiD) style analysis:

\[y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Treated_i + \beta_2 Post_t + \beta_3 (Treated_i \times Post_t) + u_{it}\]

Here: - \(Treated_i \in \{0,1\}\): treatment group indicator - \(Post_t \in \{0,1\}\): post-policy period indicator - \(\beta_3\): the DiD estimator — the treatment effect, identifying causal impact under the parallel trends assumption

This is M07 content, but the structural form — dummy × dummy or dummy × continuous interactions — is the same tool introduced here.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Research question: Do women receive lower returns to education than men?

Model:

\[\log(wage_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, female_i + \beta_2\, educ_i + \beta_3\, (female_i \times educ_i) + u_i\]

Estimated (Wooldridge WAGE1, \(n = 526\)):

\[\log(\widehat{wage_i}) = 0.389 - 0.227\, female_i + 0.082\, educ_i - 0.0056\, (female_i \times educ_i)\] Variable Coefficient SE t-stat Intercept 0.389 0.119 3.27 female −0.227 0.168 −1.35 educ 0.082 0.009 9.11 female × educ −0.0056 0.013 −0.43

Interpreting the slope:

  • Men (\(female = 0\)): return to education = \(0.082\) per year ≈ 8.2%
  • Women (\(female = 1\)): return to education = \(0.082 + (-0.0056) = 0.0764\) per year ≈ 7.6%

Test: Is \(\hat{\beta}_3 = -0.0056\) statistically significant? \(t = -0.43\), \(p\)-value large. We cannot reject \(H_0: \beta_3 = 0\) — the evidence does not support a statistically significant difference in the education slope between men and women in this sample.

Chow test (test both intercept and slope differences, \(H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_3 = 0\)):

Compute \(F_{2,522}\). If significant, conclude the entire wage equation differs by gender.

Important caveat: The coefficient on \(female\) (\(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.227\)) is now the effect of being female for workers with zero years of education — not the average gender gap across all workers. When the interaction is present, the "main effect" of the dummy is evaluated at \(x = 0\).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"If the interaction term is significant, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) gives the average effect of being in the dummy group."

Correction: In an interaction model, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is the effect of \(D = 1\) when \(x = 0\) — not the average effect over all values of \(x\). The full effect of the dummy at any given value of \(x\) is:

\[\text{Effect of } D \text{ at value } x = \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3 \cdot x\]

At \(x = 0\), this equals \(\hat{\beta}_1\). At the mean of \(x\), it equals \(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3 \bar{x}\). For a meaningful average effect, you must either evaluate at a substantively interesting value of \(x\) (e.g. \(\bar{x}\)) or compute the marginal effect averaged over the sample distribution of \(x\) using margins in Stata or marginaleffects in R.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Slope interpretation A researcher estimates the effect of training programs on worker productivity:

\[\widehat{output_i} = 15.2 + 4.1\, trained_i + 0.8\, months_i + 0.5\, (trained_i \times months_i)\]

where \(output\) is units produced per day, \(trained \in \{0,1\}\), and \(months\) is months on the job.

(a) What is the slope of experience (months) for untrained workers? (b) What is the slope for trained workers? (c) Interpret the coefficient 0.5 on the interaction. (d) At what level of \(months\) does the productivity of trained workers first exceed that of untrained workers?

Prompt 2 — Chow test A researcher pools data from two countries (A and B) and estimates:

\[\log(GDP_{it}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 countryB_i + \beta_2\, invest_t + \beta_3\, (countryB_i \times invest_t) + u_{it}\]

The restricted model (no interactions, \(\beta_1 = \beta_3 = 0\)) gives \(SSR_R = 412.3\); the unrestricted model gives \(SSR_U = 388.1\); \(n = 200\), \(k = 4\).

(a) Compute the Chow F-statistic. (b) Find the critical value at the 5% level. (c) What do you conclude?

Prompt 3 — Policy evaluation A state introduces a minimum wage increase in 2020. You have quarterly employment data for affected counties (treatment) and unaffected counties (control), 2018–2022.

(a) Write the difference-in-differences regression equation, defining all variables clearly. (b) Which coefficient is the policy effect of interest? (c) What assumption is needed for \(\hat{\beta}_{DiD}\) to be a causal estimate?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §7.3–7.4
  • Stata: gen femXeduc = female * educ then reg lwage female educ femXeduc, or reg lwage female##c.educ
  • R: lm(log(wage) ~ female * educ, data = wage1) — automatically creates main effects and interaction
  • Chow test in Stata: suest or separate regressions with test after seemingly unrelated estimation
  • marginaleffects R package: compute average marginal effects after interactions

docs.title: Lesson M06.L01: The Nature and Consequences of Heteroskedasticity
docs.text: Field Detail Module 06 — Heteroskedasticity Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Define heteroskedasticity precisely; understand which OLS properties are retained and which are lost; identify likely sources in economic data; diagnose heteroskedasticity from residual plots. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 8.1

docs.title: Recall: The Gauss-Markov Assumptions
docs.text:
The classical linear regression model (MLR.1–MLR.6) requires five core assumptions for OLS to be the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE). The assumption relevant to this module is:

MLR.5 (Homoskedasticity):

\[\text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2 \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \ldots, n\]

The variance of the unobserved error is constant across all observations, regardless of the values of the regressors.

docs.title: Definition: Heteroskedasticity
docs.text:
Heteroskedasticity is the violation of MLR.5 — the error variance is not constant:

\[\text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma_i^2\]

where \(\sigma_i^2\) varies across observations. The variance may depend on one or more of the regressors (e.g. \(\sigma_i^2 = \sigma^2 x_i\)), on omitted variables, or on observation-level characteristics.

Etymology: from Greek hetero (different) + skedasis (dispersion). Opposite: homoskedasticity (homo = same).

docs.title: Consequences for OLS
docs.text: Understanding exactly what breaks — and what doesn't — is critical for applied work.

docs.title: What OLS Retains Under Heteroskedasticity
docs.text:
Unbiasedness (\(E[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \boldsymbol{\beta}\)): requires only MLR.1–MLR.4. Since heteroskedasticity is a violation of MLR.5, not MLR.1–MLR.4, OLS estimates remain unbiased.

Consistency (\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol{\beta}\) as \(n \to \infty\)): also requires only MLR.1–MLR.4. OLS is still consistent under heteroskedasticity.

Key takeaway: Heteroskedasticity does not bias your coefficient estimates.

docs.title: What OLS Loses Under Heteroskedasticity
docs.text:
1. Efficiency (Gauss-Markov fails): OLS is no longer BLUE. There exist other linear unbiased estimators (specifically, Weighted Least Squares) with smaller variance. OLS is inefficient.

  2. Standard errors are wrong: The standard OLS formula for the variance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\):

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}_{OLS}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \hat{\sigma}^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

assumes \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}\). Under heteroskedasticity, \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \neq \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}\). The OLS standard errors are therefore biased and inconsistent — they may be too large or too small.

  1. t-tests and F-tests are invalid: Since \(t\)-statistics and \(F\)-statistics are constructed from OLS standard errors, they no longer have the correct sampling distributions. Confidence intervals are misleading. Hypothesis tests have incorrect size (rejection rates).

docs.title: Common Sources of Heteroskedasticity
docs.text:
Heteroskedasticity arises naturally in many economic datasets:

Context Why heteroskedasticity arises Household expenditure data Higher-income households have more discretion over spending → more variable expenditure patterns. Firm-level cross-sectional data Larger firms have larger absolute errors (revenue, employment); the scale of "noise" grows with firm size. Wage data Higher earners have more variable wages due to bonuses, commissions, equity compensation. Country-level panel data Larger, more diverse economies have more variable macroeconomic outcomes. Aggregated data When individual observations are averages over groups of different sizes, the variance of the group mean is \(\sigma^2/n_g\), which varies with group size \(n_g\).

docs.title: Visual Detection: Residual Plots
docs.text:
The primary diagnostic tool is a plot of OLS residuals \(\hat{u}_i\) (or \(\hat{u}_i^2\)) against:

  • Fitted values \(\hat{y}_i\): should show a random scatter with roughly constant spread. A fan shape (spread increases with \(\hat{y}\)) indicates heteroskedasticity.
  • A suspected regressor \(x_j\): if \(\text{Var}(u_i)\) depends on \(x_j\), the residual spread will widen or narrow systematically with \(x_j\).

Patterns to look for:

  • Fan shape (left to right): variance increases with \(x\) or \(\hat{y}\) — classic heteroskedasticity.
  • Funnel shape (right to left): variance decreases with \(x\) — less common.
  • Butterfly shape: variance peaks at intermediate values of \(x\).

Residual plots are informal but essential. Formal tests (Breusch-Pagan, White) follow in M06.L02.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setting: Household expenditure on food (\(food\_exp_i\), $/month) regressed on monthly income (\(income_i\), $/month).

\[\widehat{food\_exp_i} = 83.4 + 0.109\, income_i \quad (n = 40)\]

Residual plot description:

At low incomes (\(income < \$500\)/month), residuals cluster tightly around zero (spread ≈ ±$30). At high incomes (\(income > \$2000\)/month), residuals are dispersed widely (spread ≈ ±$200). The residual plot shows a clear fan shape opening to the right.

Interpretation:

\(\text{Var}(u_i \mid income_i)\) increases with \(income_i\). This makes economic sense: low-income households must spend a relatively fixed amount on food (basic subsistence); high-income households have much more discretion (gourmet vs. budget food, eating out, etc.), generating higher variance in food expenditure.

Consequence: OLS standard error on the income coefficient (\(SE = 0.032\)) is unreliable. The \(t\)-statistic (\(t = 0.109/0.032 = 3.41\)) may be inflated or deflated depending on the direction of the bias in the SE. Inference based on the naive OLS SE is not trustworthy.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Heteroskedasticity biases the OLS coefficient estimates."

Correction: This is false. Heteroskedasticity violates MLR.5 but leaves MLR.1–MLR.4 intact. Unbiasedness depends only on MLR.1–MLR.4. Your \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) estimates are still unbiased and consistent — they are just inefficient (larger variance than necessary) and they come with incorrect standard errors. The problem is with inference (t-tests, F-tests, confidence intervals), not with the point estimates. A student who writes "heteroskedasticity biases my slope estimates" has misidentified the problem; the correct statement is "heteroskedasticity invalidates my standard errors and hypothesis tests."

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Identification Which of the following datasets would you most suspect of exhibiting heteroskedasticity, and why?

(a) A time-series dataset of monthly inflation rates in Australia, 1990–2023. (b) A cross-sectional dataset of 500 manufacturing firms with revenue as the dependent variable and employment as the regressor. (c) An experimental dataset of test scores from 30 students in a randomised controlled study with identical class sizes.

Prompt 2 — Consequences A researcher estimates a model of household savings using OLS and obtains the coefficient on income as \(\hat{\beta}_{income} = 0.18\) with \(SE = 0.04\) (\(t = 4.5\)). A diagnostician then detects significant heteroskedasticity in the residuals.

(a) Is the researcher's estimate \(\hat{\beta}_{income} = 0.18\) still reliable? Why or why not? (b) Is the \(t\)-statistic of 4.5 still reliable? Why or why not? (c) What should the researcher do next?

Prompt 3 — Residual plot Describe what you would expect to see in a residual plot (\(\hat{u}_i\) vs \(\hat{y}_i\)) if:

(a) The model is correctly specified and homoskedastic. (b) Variance increases with fitted values. (c) Variance is large at intermediate fitted values and small at extremes.

In each case, what would you conclude?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §8.1
  • Stata: rvfplot after regress draws residual vs. fitted plot; rvpplot varname plots residuals vs a specific variable
  • R: plot(lm_object, which = 1) draws residual vs. fitted plot; plot(lm_object, which = 3) draws scale-location plot
  • Greene, Econometric Analysis (8th ed.), Ch 9 — for a more rigorous treatment of the GLS framework

docs.title: Lesson M06.L02: Testing for Heteroskedasticity
docs.text: Field Detail Module 06 — Heteroskedasticity Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Execute and interpret the Breusch-Pagan LM test and the White test for heteroskedasticity; understand the intuition behind regressing squared residuals; know the limitations of formal tests. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 8.3

docs.title: Why Test Formally?
docs.text: Residual plots (M06.L01) provide informal visual evidence of heteroskedasticity. Formal tests provide a decision rule with a known significance level. However, both tools have limitations: formal tests depend on functional form assumptions, and all tests have low power in small samples.

docs.title: The Breusch-Pagan (BP) Test
docs.text: The Breusch-Pagan test is the most widely used formal test for heteroskedasticity. It tests whether the error variance is a linear function of the regressors.

docs.title: Null and Alternative Hypotheses
docs.text:
\[H_0: \text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2 \quad \text{(homoskedasticity)}$$ $$H_1: \text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2 h(\delta_0 + \delta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \delta_k x_{ik})\]

The test is equivalent to:

\[H_0: \delta_1 = \delta_2 = \cdots = \delta_k = 0\]

Under \(H_0\), the variance of \(u_i\) does not depend on any of the \(x\)'s.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Step 1: Estimate the original model by OLS; save the residuals \(\hat{u}_i\).

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik} + u_i\]

Step 2: Compute squared residuals \(\hat{u}_i^2\) and regress them on all regressors:

\[\hat{u}_i^2 = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \delta_k x_{ik} + v_i\]

Step 3: Compute the LM statistic (Lagrange Multiplier):

\[LM = n \cdot R_{\hat{u}^2}^2\]

where \(R_{\hat{u}^2}^2\) is the \(R^2\) from the auxiliary regression in Step 2.

Step 4: Under \(H_0\), the LM statistic has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution:

\[LM \sim \chi^2_k\]

where \(k\) is the number of slope regressors (the number of \(x\)'s) in the original model.

Step 5: Reject \(H_0\) if \(LM > \chi^2_{k,\alpha}\) (the critical value at significance level \(\alpha\)).

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: The key idea: if the error variance is homoskedastic (\(\sigma_i^2 = \sigma^2\) for all \(i\)), then knowing the values of \(x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ik}\) tells you nothing about \(\hat{u}_i^2\). The auxiliary regression would have \(R^2 \approx 0\) and \(n \cdot R^2 \approx 0\). If \(x\)'s predict \(\hat{u}_i^2\) well (high \(R^2\)), it suggests the variance depends on the \(x\)'s — evidence against homoskedasticity.

docs.title: The White Test
docs.text: The White test is a more general alternative to BP. Instead of regressing \(\hat{u}_i^2\) only on the original \(x\)'s, it also includes squares and cross-products of the regressors.

docs.title: Auxiliary Regression (for \(k = 2\) regressors, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)):
docs.text: \[\hat{u}_i^2 = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_{i1} + \delta_2 x_{i2} + \delta_3 x_{i1}^2 + \delta_4 x_{i2}^2 + \delta_5 x_{i1} x_{i2} + v_i\]

docs.title: Test Statistic
docs.text:
\[LM = n \cdot R_{\hat{u}^2}^2 \sim \chi^2_{p}\]

where \(p\) is the number of regressors in the auxiliary regression (here \(p = 5\)).

docs.title: BP vs White
docs.text:
Feature Breusch-Pagan White Null Variance linear in \(x\)'s Any form of heteroskedasticity Auxiliary regressors \(x_1, \ldots, x_k\) \(x\)'s, \(x^2\)'s, cross-products Degrees of freedom \(k\) Up to \(k(k+3)/2\) Power against linear het. Higher Lower (loses df) Power against non-linear het. May miss it Higher Preferred when Model for het. is known You want a general check

Practical rule: Run BP first as a quick check. If you suspect non-linear heteroskedasticity or have no prior model, follow with White.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Dataset: Wooldridge WAGE1, \(n = 526\). Original model:

\[\log(wage_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, educ_i + \beta_2\, exper_i + \beta_3\, exper_i^2 + u_i\]

Step 1: Run OLS, obtain residuals \(\hat{u}_i\).

Step 2: Compute \(\hat{u}_i^2\). Run auxiliary regression:

\[\hat{u}_i^2 = \delta_0 + \delta_1\, educ_i + \delta_2\, exper_i + \delta_3\, exper_i^2 + v_i\]

Results: \(R^2 = 0.0286\) (the \(x\)'s explain 2.86% of variation in squared residuals).

Step 3: Compute LM statistic:

\[LM = 526 \times 0.0286 = 15.04\]

Step 4: Compare to \(\chi^2_3\) (three slope regressors: \(educ\), \(exper\), \(exper^2\)). Critical value at 5%: \(\chi^2_{3,0.05} = 7.815\).

Step 5: Since \(15.04 > 7.815\), reject \(H_0\). There is statistically significant evidence of heteroskedasticity in the log-wage equation.

Interpretation: The squared residuals are partially explained by the regressors, indicating that the error variance varies with education and/or experience. The OLS standard errors reported by default software are not reliable; use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (M06.L03).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"If the Breusch-Pagan test fails to reject, homoskedasticity holds and I can use OLS standard errors."

Correction: Failing to reject \(H_0\) means we lack sufficient statistical evidence of heteroskedasticity — it does not prove homoskedasticity. The test may lack power in small samples or against non-linear forms of heteroskedasticity. There is no cost to using heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors regardless of test results — they are valid under both homoskedasticity and heteroskedasticity. The modern consensus in applied econometrics is to always use robust standard errors in cross-sectional work, without relying on a pre-test. If you only use robust SEs after a significant BP test, you introduce a pre-test bias: your choice of SE depends on a noisy inference step.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — BP test computation A researcher estimates a model with \(k = 3\) regressors, \(n = 200\) observations. The auxiliary regression of \(\hat{u}_i^2\) on the three regressors yields \(R^2 = 0.052\).

(a) Compute the Breusch-Pagan LM statistic. (b) What is the chi-squared critical value at the 5% significance level? (c) Do you reject or fail to reject homoskedasticity? What should the researcher do next?

Prompt 2 — White test vs BP A researcher suspects that the error variance in a firm-level dataset depends on the square of firm revenue, not just its level. The BP test (using revenue levels) fails to reject at 5%. The White test (adding revenue² and other cross products) rejects at 1%.

(a) Why might BP fail to detect this heteroskedasticity? (b) What does the White test result imply? (c) What is the researcher's recommended next step?

Prompt 3 — Interpretation of auxiliary R² In the Breusch-Pagan auxiliary regression, a researcher obtains \(R^2 = 0.001\) with \(n = 1000\) and \(k = 5\).

(a) Compute the LM statistic. Is it significant at 5%? (b) Does a low \(R^2\) in the auxiliary regression mean heteroskedasticity is not economically important? Explain. (c) Why can even a very small \(R^2\) lead to rejection with a large sample?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §8.3
  • Stata: estat hettest (Breusch-Pagan after regress); estat imtest, white (White test)
  • R: bptest(lm_object) from the lmtest package; bptest(lm_object, studentize = FALSE) for classical BP
  • Original paper: Breusch & Pagan (1979), "A Simple Test for Heteroscedasticity and Random Coefficient Variation", Econometrica, 47(5), 1287–1294
  • White (1980), "A Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator and a Direct Test for Heteroskedasticity", Econometrica, 48(4), 817–838

docs.title: Lesson M06.L03: Heteroskedasticity-Robust Standard Errors
docs.text: Field Detail Module 06 — Heteroskedasticity Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand the sandwich estimator for heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; apply robust SEs in Stata and R; correctly interpret the effect on inference; understand why robust SEs do not fix coefficient estimates. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 8.2

docs.title: Motivation: Fixing Inference Without Changing Estimates
docs.text: We established in M06.L01 that heteroskedasticity leaves OLS estimates unbiased and consistent but corrupts the standard errors — and therefore all t-tests, F-tests, and confidence intervals. The robust standard error approach provides a way to obtain valid inference under heteroskedasticity without changing the coefficient estimates and without needing to know the exact form of heteroskedasticity.

docs.title: The OLS Variance Estimator (Homoskedastic Case)
docs.text:
Under homoskedasticity, the variance-covariance matrix of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

Estimated by replacing \(\sigma^2\) with \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = SSR/(n-k-1)\):

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}_{OLS}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \hat{\sigma}^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

This formula is only valid if \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{u} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}\).

docs.title: The Heteroskedasticity-Robust (Sandwich) Estimator
docs.text:
Under heteroskedasticity, the true variance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i^2 \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i' \right) (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is the \(i\)th row of \(\mathbf{X}\) (as a column vector). Since \(\sigma_i^2\) is unknown, White (1980) proposed replacing \(\sigma_i^2\) with \(\hat{u}_i^2\):

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}_{HC}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i^2 \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i' \right) (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

This is the Huber-Eicker-White (HEW) sandwich estimator. The name comes from its structure: the outer two factors \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) are the "bread," and the middle sum \(\sum \hat{u}_i^2 \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i'\) is the "meat."

Key property: This estimator is consistent for \(\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\) regardless of whether the errors are homoskedastic or heteroskedastic. It requires no assumptions about the form of \(\sigma_i^2\).

docs.title: Heteroskedasticity Corrections (HC0–HC3)
docs.text:
Several finite-sample corrections to the basic HC estimator exist:

Estimator Formula for meat Notes HC0 \(\hat{u}_i^2\) White's original; can be biased in small samples HC1 \(\frac{n}{n-k-1}\hat{u}_i^2\) Degrees-of-freedom correction; Stata's default HC2 \(\frac{\hat{u}_i^2}{1 - h_{ii}}\) Adjusts for leverage; \(h_{ii}\) = hat matrix diagonal HC3 \(\frac{\hat{u}_i^2}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}\) More conservative; preferred in small samples

In large samples, all four give essentially the same answer. Stata's vce(robust) uses HC1. R's sandwich package offers all four.

docs.title: Effect on t-statistics and Confidence Intervals
docs.text:
Robust SEs are typically (though not always) larger than the corresponding OLS SEs when heteroskedasticity is present:

  • Larger robust SE → smaller t-statistic → wider confidence interval → more conservative inference
  • Smaller robust SE (less common, when OLS SEs are upward biased) → larger t-statistic → narrower CI

This means some variables that appeared significant under OLS standard errors may not be significant with robust SEs — a real cost of ignoring heteroskedasticity in the original OLS analysis.

docs.title: Practical Guidance: When to Use Robust SEs
docs.text:
Rule of thumb: Use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors by default in all cross-sectional applied work.

Rationale:

  • If heteroskedasticity is present: robust SEs give valid inference; OLS SEs do not.
  • If errors are actually homoskedastic: robust SEs are still valid (consistent), just slightly less efficient than OLS SEs.
  • The cost of using robust SEs when unnecessary is negligible (very slight loss of efficiency in large samples).
  • The cost of not using robust SEs when heteroskedasticity is present is incorrect inference.

Asymmetric risk → always use robust SEs in cross-sectional work.

Caveat: Robust SEs rely on asymptotic (large-sample) theory. In very small samples (\(n < 50\)), they can be unreliable. HC3 is more conservative and preferred in small samples.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Dataset: Wooldridge WAGE1, \(n = 526\).

Model: \(\log(wage_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ_i + \beta_2 exper_i + u_i\)

Comparison of OLS vs Robust Standard Errors:

Variable \(\hat{\beta}\) OLS SE Robust SE OLS \(t\) Robust \(t\) Intercept 0.584 0.101 0.108 5.78 5.41 educ 0.083 0.008 0.009 10.38 9.22 exper 0.025 0.005 0.006 5.00 4.17

Observations:

  1. Coefficient estimates are identical — robust SEs change only the SEs, not \(\hat{\beta}\).
  2. Robust SEs are slightly larger than OLS SEs, consistent with the presence of mild heteroskedasticity.
  3. Both \(educ\) and \(exper\) remain strongly significant under robust SEs (\(t > 4\)). The qualitative conclusions do not change here, but the magnitude of \(t\)-statistics is reduced.
  4. Confidence intervals widen slightly. For example, the 95% CI for \(\beta_{educ}\):
  5. OLS: \(0.083 \pm 1.96 \times 0.008 = [0.067, 0.099]\)
  6. Robust: \(0.083 \pm 1.96 \times 0.009 = [0.065, 0.101]\)

Stata code: 

regress lwage educ exper, vce(robust)

R code: 

library(sandwich); library(lmtest)
m <- lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = wage1)
coeftest(m, vcov = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors fix the biased coefficient estimates caused by heteroskedasticity."

Correction: Robust standard errors only fix the standard errors (and therefore \(t\)-statistics, \(F\)-statistics, and confidence intervals). They do not change the point estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). As established in M06.L01, OLS estimates are unbiased and consistent under heteroskedasticity — so there is nothing to fix in the coefficients. The sandwich estimator addresses only the inference problem, not an estimation problem. If a student reports "I corrected for heteroskedasticity by using robust standard errors, which fixed my biased estimates," that statement is incorrect on two counts: (a) the estimates were not biased, and (b) robust SEs don't change estimates.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — OLS vs robust SEs A researcher estimates a model of house prices with \(n = 800\) observations. OLS gives:

Variable \(\hat{\beta}\) OLS SE Robust SE Intercept 85,000 12,000 18,500 sqft 120 15 22 bedrooms 8,000 3,500 2,800

(a) For which variable does heteroskedasticity most increase the SE? What does this imply about OLS inference for that variable? (b) For the bedrooms coefficient, the OLS SE is larger than the robust SE. What does this imply about OLS inference for bedrooms? (c) Does the difference between OLS and robust SEs change the researcher's estimate of the effect of square footage on price?

Prompt 2 — Correct statement A student writes in their research paper: "We detected heteroskedasticity using the Breusch-Pagan test (\(p = 0.003\)). We therefore corrected for heteroskedasticity by re-estimating the model with robust standard errors. Our corrected coefficient estimates are now unbiased."

Identify and correct any errors in this statement.

Prompt 3 — Small sample concern A researcher has \(n = 35\) observations and detects possible heteroskedasticity. She plans to use HC1 robust standard errors.

(a) Why might HC1 be unreliable in this small sample? (b) What alternative correction would you recommend? (c) Is there any other approach she should consider?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §8.2
  • White (1980), "A Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator", Econometrica, 48(4), 817–838
  • MacKinnon & White (1985) — HC2 and HC3 small-sample corrections
  • Stata: regress y x1 x2, vce(robust) or regress y x1 x2, robust
  • R: coeftest(m, vcov = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1")) — sandwich + lmtest packages
  • Angrist & Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch 8 — practical motivation for always using robust SEs

docs.title: Lesson M06.L04: Weighted Least Squares
docs.text: Field Detail Module 06 — Heteroskedasticity Level Graduate Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand when and how to apply Weighted Least Squares (WLS); distinguish GLS from Feasible GLS; interpret WLS as a variance-stabilising transformation; recognise the risks of misspecified weights. Provenance Wooldridge Introductory Econometrics, Ch 8.4

docs.title: Motivation: Exploiting Known Variance Structure
docs.text: Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (M06.L03) are the default remedy when the form of heteroskedasticity is unknown. But in some settings, economic theory or data structure gives us information about how the error variance varies across observations. In these cases, we can do better: Weighted Least Squares (WLS) exploits this structure to produce estimates that are more efficient than OLS (with or without robust SEs).

docs.title: The Setup: Known Variance Structure
docs.text:
Assume the error variance takes the form:

\[\text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2 h(\mathbf{x}_i) \equiv \sigma^2 h_i\]

where \(h_i > 0\) is a known function of the regressors (or other observable characteristics). The parameter \(\sigma^2\) is unknown but constant; only \(h_i\) varies across observations.

Examples:

  • \(h_i = x_i\) (variance proportional to a regressor, e.g. income)
  • \(h_i = x_i^2\) (standard deviation proportional to \(x_i\))
  • \(h_i = 1/n_g\) (for group averages with group size \(n_g\))

docs.title: The WLS Transformation
docs.text:
Define the weight \(w_i = 1/\sqrt{h_i}\). Multiply through every term in the regression by \(w_i\):

\[\frac{y_i}{\sqrt{h_i}} = \frac{\beta_0}{\sqrt{h_i}} + \beta_1 \frac{x_{i1}}{\sqrt{h_i}} + \cdots + \beta_k \frac{x_{ik}}{\sqrt{h_i}} + \frac{u_i}{\sqrt{h_i}}\]

Let \(y_i^* = y_i/\sqrt{h_i}\), \(x_{ij}^* = x_{ij}/\sqrt{h_i}\), \(u_i^* = u_i/\sqrt{h_i}\).

Transformed error variance:

\[\text{Var}(u_i^* \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\text{Var}(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)}{h_i} = \frac{\sigma^2 h_i}{h_i} = \sigma^2\]

The transformed model is homoskedastic. Applying OLS to the transformed model is equivalent to WLS on the original model.

WLS objective function: WLS minimises the weighted sum of squared residuals:

\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{h_i} (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \cdots - \beta_k x_{ik})^2\]

Observations with larger variance (\(h_i\) large) receive smaller weights — they are less informative and should contribute less to estimation. Observations with smaller variance receive larger weights — they are more precise.

docs.title: GLS vs Feasible GLS
docs.text:
Generalised Least Squares (GLS): If \(h_i\) is exactly known, WLS = GLS. By the Gauss-Markov theorem applied to the transformed model, GLS is BLUE — the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator. It dominates OLS in efficiency whenever heteroskedasticity is present.

Feasible GLS (FGLS): In practice, \(h_i\) is almost never exactly known. We estimate it from the data, typically by:

  1. Run OLS; save residuals \(\hat{u}_i\).
  2. Regress \(\log(\hat{u}_i^2)\) on the \(x\)'s (or posited determinants of variance): \(\log(\hat{u}_i^2) = \delta_0 + \delta_1 z_i + \text{error}\).
  3. Obtain fitted values \(\hat{g}_i\) from this auxiliary regression.
  4. Compute estimated weights: \(\hat{h}_i = e^{\hat{g}_i}\).
  5. Run WLS with weights \(1/\hat{h}_i\).

Properties of FGLS: Consistent and asymptotically more efficient than OLS. Not exactly BLUE in finite samples because \(\hat{h}_i\) is estimated. If the model for \(h_i\) is correct, FGLS gains over OLS in large samples. If the model is misspecified, FGLS can be worse (see Common Misconception).

docs.title: When WLS Is Appropriate
docs.text: WLS is most natural and defensible in two settings:

docs.title: 1. Aggregated/Group-Average Data
docs.text:
When each observation is an average over a group of \(n_g\) individuals, and the individual errors are homoskedastic and independent, the group-average error has variance \(\sigma^2/n_g\). The appropriate weight is \(n_g\) (weight each group by its size).

Example: County-level crime rates, where each county is an average over \(n_g\) residents. Counties with more residents provide more precise estimates of the true crime rate.

docs.title: 2. Known Variance from Theory or Data Structure
