docs.text: When the form of \(h_i\) is known from economic theory (e.g. variance proportional to income in an Engel curve), WLS with \(w_i = 1/income_i\) is the natural estimator.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
• Unknown \(h_i\) (the common case): Use OLS + robust standard errors. This is simpler, more robust to misspecification, and asymptotically valid.
  • Known or well-motivated \(h_i\): Use WLS for efficiency gains.
  • Group data with known group sizes: Always weight by group size.
  • After WLS estimation: use WLS-robust standard errors (weight-adjusted sandwich), not OLS-standard errors on the weighted model.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setting: County-level data on crime rates and unemployment (\(n_c = 90\) counties).

  • \(crime_c\): county crime rate (crimes per 100,000)
  • \(unemp_c\): county unemployment rate (%)
  • \(pop_c\): county population (thousands)

Each county observation is an average across \(pop_c\) individuals. The variance of the county-level error is inversely proportional to population: \(h_c = 1/pop_c\).

WLS model (weight each county by \(pop_c\)):

\[crime_c = \beta_0 + \beta_1 unemp_c + u_c\]

Step 1 — OLS (unweighted):

\[\widehat{crime_c} = 128.4 + 4.7\, unemp_c, \quad SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = 1.8, \quad R^2 = 0.183\]

Step 2 — WLS (weighted by population):

\[\widehat{crime_c}^{WLS} = 115.2 + 5.9\, unemp_c, \quad SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = 1.2, \quad R^2 = 0.261\]

Comparison:

OLS WLS \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (unemployment) 4.7 5.9 SE 1.8 1.2 \(t\)-statistic 2.61 4.92
  • WLS gives a different point estimate (5.9 vs 4.7) because high-population counties (more precise) get more weight — and if they happen to show a stronger unemployment-crime relationship, WLS upweights that.
  • WLS SE is smaller (more efficient): we exploit the known variance structure.
  • Both estimators are consistent, but WLS is more efficient if the variance model is correct.

Stata: 

regress crime unemp [aweight = pop]

R: 

lm(crime ~ unemp, data = counties, weights = pop)

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"WLS always gives better estimates than OLS."

Correction: WLS is more efficient than OLS only if the assumed variance function \(h_i\) is correctly specified. If you assume \(h_i = x_i\) but the true variance structure is \(h_i = x_i^2\), your weights are wrong. Misspecified WLS:

  • Is still consistent (as long as the mean function is correctly specified), but
  • Can be less efficient than OLS, or even yield misleading inference if the misspecification is severe.

Moreover, WLS with misspecified weights does not produce homoskedastic errors in the transformed model — so the standard WLS standard errors are also incorrect, and you would need to further apply robust SEs. This is why the practical default in applied work is OLS + robust SEs: it requires no assumption about the form of \(\sigma_i^2\) and is protected by the sandwich estimator regardless.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt 1 — Weighted by group size A researcher has state-level data on average hourly wages (the average of individual wages within each state). There are \(G = 50\) states, with state sizes \(n_s\) ranging from 500,000 to 8,000,000 workers.

(a) Why is the error variance in a state-level regression likely to vary across states? (b) What weights would you apply in WLS, and why? (c) If you applied equal weights (OLS), what would be the consequence for efficiency?

Prompt 2 — FGLS procedure A researcher suspects \(\text{Var}(u_i \mid x_i) = \sigma^2 x_i^2\). Outline the FGLS procedure step by step:

(a) What is the implied weight \(w_i = 1/\sqrt{h_i}\)? (b) How would you transform the regression equation? (c) Describe the two-step estimation procedure if \(h_i\) were not known exactly but you wanted to estimate it from the residuals.

Prompt 3 — OLS vs WLS comparison In the worked example above, OLS gives \(\hat{\beta}_{unemp} = 4.7\) and WLS gives \(\hat{\beta}_{unemp} = 5.9\).

(a) Why are the two estimates different? What does the difference tell you about the data? (b) Which estimate would you report in a policy memo? Justify your answer. (c) If you discovered the population data was measured with substantial error, how would this affect your confidence in the WLS results?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), §8.4
  • Stata: regress y x [aweight = w] for analytic weights (WLS); [pweight = w] for probability weights (survey data)
  • R: lm(y ~ x, weights = w, data = d) for WLS
  • For FGLS with unknown form: glm(y ~ x, family = quasi(var = "mu^2"), data = d) in R models multiplicative heteroskedasticity
  • Greene, Econometric Analysis (8th ed.), §9.5–9.6 — matrix treatment of GLS and FGLS
  • Angrist & Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, §3.4 — when WLS is and isn't the right tool

docs.title: Lesson M07.L01: Specification Errors and Model Selection
docs.text: Field Detail Module 07 — Specification Issues Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand functional form misspecification, apply the RESET test, and use information criteria to compare non-nested models; distinguish the consequences of under- versus over-specification. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 9.1

docs.title: 1. Functional Form Misspecification
docs.text:
A model is functionally misspecified when the assumed relationship between regressors and the dependent variable does not match the true data-generating process. The most common version: imposing linearity when the true relationship is nonlinear.

Suppose the true model is:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + u\]

but you estimate only:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\]

The omitted \(x^2\) term is correlated with \(x\), so by the OVB formula (recall M03.L04), \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is biased and inconsistent. Functional form misspecification is therefore a special case of omitted variable bias where the omitted variable is a transformation of an included regressor.

Other common functional form errors: - Using a linear model when a log–linear (or log–log) form is more appropriate. - Omitting interaction terms when the marginal effect of one variable depends on another. - Fitting a straight line through a relationship that curves back.

docs.title: 2. The RESET Test (Ramsey Regression Equation Specification Error Test)
docs.text:
The RESET test provides a general diagnostic for functional form misspecification. The idea: if the model is correctly specified, adding powers of the fitted values \(\hat{y}\) to the regression should not significantly improve fit—because \(\hat{y}\) is already a linear combination of the regressors.

Procedure:

Step 1. Estimate the original (restricted) model by OLS:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u\]

Obtain fitted values \(\hat{y}_i\).

Step 2. Construct an augmented (unrestricted) model:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + \delta_1 \hat{y}^2 + \delta_2 \hat{y}^3 + \text{error}\]

Step 3. Test the null hypothesis:

\[H_0: \delta_1 = 0,\; \delta_2 = 0\]

using an F-test (joint significance of the added powers). The test statistic:

\[F = \frac{(SSR_r - SSR_{ur})/2}{SSR_{ur}/(n - k - 3)}\]

follows an \(F_{2,\, n-k-3}\) distribution under \(H_0\).

Step 4. Interpret the outcome: - Reject \(H_0\) → evidence of functional form misspecification; consider transformations, interactions, or polynomial terms. - Fail to reject \(H_0\) → no evidence detected by this test (but see Common Misconception).

Why \(\hat{y}^2\) and \(\hat{y}^3\)? These are smooth nonlinear functions of all included regressors. If any nonlinear combination of the \(x\)'s belongs in the model, it will likely be correlated with \(\hat{y}^2\) or \(\hat{y}^3\).

docs.title: 3. Non-Nested Model Selection: Adjusted R², AIC, BIC
docs.text:
When two models are non-nested (neither is a restricted version of the other), standard F-tests do not apply. Example:

  • Model A: \(\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{exper} + u\)
  • Model B: \(\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{tenure} + u\)

Use information criteria to compare:

Criterion Formula Preference Adjusted R² \(\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)}\) Higher is better AIC \(\ln(\hat{\sigma}^2) + \frac{2(k+1)}{n}\) Lower is better BIC \(\ln(\hat{\sigma}^2) + \frac{(k+1)\ln n}{n}\) Lower is better

BIC vs AIC: BIC penalises complexity more heavily (via \(\ln n\) vs \(2\)), so it tends to select more parsimonious models, especially for large samples.

Caution: Information criteria compare models on the same sample and same dependent variable. You cannot use R² (or AIC/BIC in the standard form) to compare a model with \(y\) as dependent variable against one with \(\log(y)\)—different scales.

docs.title: 4. Under-Specification (Omitted Variable Bias)
docs.text:
Covered in depth in M03.L04. Brief recap:

If the true model is \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\) but you omit \(x_2\):

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \tilde{\delta}_1\]

where \(\tilde{\delta}_1\) is the coefficient from regressing \(x_2\) on \(x_1\). Unless \(\beta_2 = 0\) or \(x_1 \perp x_2\), OLS is biased and inconsistent — the most serious specification error.

docs.title: 5. Over-Specification (Irrelevant Variables)
docs.text:
Suppose the true model has \(k\) regressors but you include an irrelevant variable \(x_{k+1}\) (whose true coefficient \(\beta_{k+1} = 0\)). OLS is:

  • Still unbiased and consistent for all coefficients (including \(\hat{\beta}_{k+1} \approx 0\) in expectation).
  • Less efficient: including an irrelevant variable inflates the variance of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) for the other regressors (via multicollinearity), producing wider confidence intervals.

There is thus an asymmetry in the cost of specification errors:

Error type Bias? Efficiency? Omit a relevant variable (correlated with \(x\)) Yes — biased, inconsistent — Include an irrelevant variable No — still unbiased Worse — higher variance

The practical implication: omitting a relevant variable is almost always worse. But over-specification is not free—if you include many irrelevant controls you may lose the precision needed to detect true effects.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. Consider a wage equation estimated on \(n = 526\) observations from Wooldridge's wage1 dataset:

\[\widehat{\log(\text{wage})} = 0.284 + 0.092\,\text{educ} + 0.041\,\text{exper} - 0.0007\,\text{exper}^2 + 0.022\,\text{tenure}\]

RESET Test Application.

  1. Save \(\hat{y}_i = \widehat{\log(\text{wage})}_i\) from OLS.
  2. Add \(\hat{y}^2\) and \(\hat{y}^3\) as additional regressors.
  3. Run F-test for their joint significance.

Suppose the resulting F-statistic is \(F = 4.67\) with \(p\text{-value} = 0.010\).

Interpretation.

At the 5% level, we reject \(H_0\): there is evidence of functional form misspecification in this specification. The significant F-statistic suggests a nonlinear function of the regressors (or an omitted interaction) is correlated with \(\hat{y}^2\) or \(\hat{y}^3\).

Follow-up actions: - Test whether \(\text{exper}^2\) or \(\text{tenure}^2\) should be added. - Consider whether interactions (e.g. educ × tenure) improve fit. - Re-run RESET after augmenting the model; if \(p > 0.10\), the new specification passes.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Passing the RESET test means the model is correctly specified."

This is false. The RESET test is a necessary check, not a sufficient one. It has power only against misspecifications that cause \(\hat{y}^2\) or \(\hat{y}^3\) to be significant — a particular class of functional form errors. It will not detect:

  • Omitted variables that are uncorrelated with \(\hat{y}^2, \hat{y}^3\) (e.g. a purely additive shift from an omitted dummy).
  • Heteroskedasticity.
  • Endogeneity or reverse causality.
  • Wrong choice of sample or incorrect coding.

Think of RESET as a smoke alarm: silence means no smoke detected, not that there's no fire.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. RESET mechanics. You estimate \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\) with \(n = 200\). The restricted SSR is 450 and the unrestricted SSR (after adding \(\hat{y}^2, \hat{y}^3\)) is 420. Compute the RESET F-statistic and state your conclusion at the 5% significance level. (Use \(F_{2,195}\) critical value ≈ 3.04.)

  2. Non-nested model comparison. Model A (\(k = 3\)): \(\hat{\sigma}^2_A = 0.85\), \(n = 150\). Model B (\(k = 5\)): \(\hat{\sigma}^2_B = 0.80\), \(n = 150\). Compute AIC and BIC for each model. Which does AIC prefer? Which does BIC prefer? Explain why they may differ.

  3. Under- vs over-specification. A researcher estimates a salary model. True model: \(\text{salary} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{ability} + u\). She cannot observe ability. (a) What happens to \(\hat{\beta}_1\) if ability is positively correlated with educ and positively affects salary? (b) Separately, she adds an irrelevant variable (respondent's shoe size). What happens to \(\hat{\beta}_1\) now? Is it biased? What changes?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7e), §9.1 — Functional Form Misspecification; RESET test.
  • Ramsey, J.B. (1969). "Tests for specification errors in classical linear least squares regression analysis." Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 31(2), 350–371.
  • Davidson, R. & MacKinnon, J.G. (1993). Estimation and Inference in Econometrics, Ch 3 — model specification and non-nested tests.
  • See also: M03.L04 (Omitted Variable Bias) for the formal OVB derivation.

docs.title: Lesson M07.L02: Proxy Variables and Measurement Error
docs.text: Field Detail Module 07 — Specification Issues Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand how proxy variables can partially address OVB; derive the attenuation bias formula for classical measurement error in a regressor; distinguish measurement error consequences in \(y\) versus \(x\). Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 9.2–9.3

docs.title: 1. Proxy Variables
docs.text:
In many economic applications the true variable of interest is unobservable. The classic case is ability in a wage equation:

\[\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{ability} + u\]

We cannot directly measure ability, so we substitute an observable proxy — a variable that is highly correlated with the unobservable concept. Common proxies for ability:

  • IQ test score
  • GPA (grade point average)
  • Armed Forces Qualifying Test (AFQT) score

docs.title: Formal Requirement for a Valid Proxy
docs.text:
Let \(q\) denote the unobservable variable and \(x_3^*\) the proposed proxy. The proxy is valid if, once we condition on \(x_3^*\), the original unobservable \(q\) provides no additional information about the outcome:

\[E(u \mid x_1, x_2, q) = E(u \mid x_1, x_2, x_3^*)\]

This means: conditioning on the proxy is as good as conditioning on the truth. Equivalently, \(q\) and the outcome are mean-independent given \((x_1, x_2, x_3^*)\).

In the wage example: once we include IQ in the regression, ability itself (beyond IQ) should not directly affect \(\log(\text{wage})\). This is a strong assumption—IQ is an imperfect proxy for ability.

docs.title: Proxy Variables Reduce but May Not Eliminate OVB
docs.text:
Even with an imperfect proxy:

\[E(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{proxy}}) = \beta_1 + \text{bias}^{\text{proxy}}\]

The remaining bias satisfies \(|\text{bias}^{\text{proxy}}| \leq |\text{bias}^{\text{no proxy}}|\), so including a proxy almost always moves us closer to the truth. But if the proxy condition fails—if \(q\) affects \(y\) beyond what \(x_3^*\) captures—some OVB remains.

docs.title: 2. Measurement Error in the Dependent Variable (\(y\))
docs.text:
Suppose the true outcome is \(y^*\) but we observe \(y = y^* + e_0\), where \(e_0\) is classical measurement error satisfying:

  • \(E(e_0) = 0\)
  • \(\text{Cov}(e_0, x_j) = 0\) for all regressors \(x_j\)
  • \(\text{Cov}(e_0, u) = 0\)

Substituting \(y^* = y - e_0\) into the true model \(y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + (u + e_0)\]

The composite error \((u + e_0)\) still satisfies zero mean and is uncorrelated with \(x\). Therefore:

OLS remains unbiased and consistent when classical measurement error is in the dependent variable.

The only consequence is reduced efficiency: the error variance \(\text{Var}(u + e_0) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_{e_0}^2 > \sigma_u^2\), so standard errors are inflated and estimates are less precise.

docs.title: 3. Measurement Error in an Explanatory Variable (\(x\)): Attenuation Bias
docs.text:
Now suppose the true regressor is \(x^*\) but we observe \(x = x^* + e\), where \(e\) is classical measurement error:

  • \(E(e) = 0\)
  • \(\text{Cov}(e, x^*) = 0\) (error is independent of true value)
  • \(\text{Cov}(e, u) = 0\)

The true model is \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^* + u\). Substituting \(x^* = x - e\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + (u - \beta_1 e)\]

The problem: the composite error \((u - \beta_1 e)\) is correlated with \(x = x^* + e\), because \(x\) contains \(e\). Specifically:

\[\text{Cov}(x,\; u - \beta_1 e) = \text{Cov}(x^* + e,\; -\beta_1 e) = -\beta_1 \sigma_e^2 \neq 0\]

OLS is therefore biased and inconsistent. The probability limit of the OLS estimator is:

\[\text{plim}(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{\sigma_{x^*}^2}{\sigma_{x^*}^2 + \sigma_e^2}\]

where \(\sigma_{x^*}^2 = \text{Var}(x^*)\) and \(\sigma_e^2 = \text{Var}(e)\).

docs.title: The Attenuation Bias Formula
docs.text:
\[\boxed{E(\tilde{\beta}_1) \approx \beta_1 \cdot \frac{\sigma_{x^*}^2}{\sigma_{x^*}^2 + \sigma_e^2}}\]

Equivalently, writing \(\sigma_x^2\) for the variance of the true regressor:

\[E(\tilde{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{\sigma_x^2}{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_e^2}\]

The multiplier \(\dfrac{\sigma_{x^*}^2}{\sigma_{x^*}^2 + \sigma_e^2}\) is the reliability ratio, often denoted \(\lambda \in (0,1)\).

Since \(\lambda < 1\):

  • If \(\beta_1 > 0\): \(\tilde{\beta}_1 < \beta_1\) — OLS understates the true positive effect.
  • If \(\beta_1 < 0\): \(\tilde{\beta}_1 > \beta_1\) — OLS understates the true negative effect in magnitude.
  • In both cases: \(|\tilde{\beta}_1| < |\beta_1|\) — the estimated effect is attenuated toward zero.

This is called attenuation bias or errors-in-variables bias.

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text: As measurement error grows (\(\sigma_e^2 \to \infty\)), the reliability ratio \(\to 0\) and \(\tilde{\beta}_1 \to 0\): the estimate is completely swamped by noise. As \(\sigma_e^2 \to 0\), \(\lambda \to 1\) and we recover the true \(\beta_1\).

docs.title: 4. Solution: Instrumental Variables
docs.text:
The standard remedy for measurement error in \(x\) is instrumental variables (IV) estimation. An instrument \(z\) must:

  1. Be correlated with the true regressor \(x^*\) (relevance).
  2. Be uncorrelated with the measurement error \(e\) and with \(u\) (exogeneity).

Then IV/2SLS consistently estimates \(\beta_1\) despite the measurement error. This will be covered in M10.

docs.title: Part A — Ability Proxy in a Wage Equation
docs.text:
True model:

\[\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{ability} + u\]

Since ability is unobservable, consider two specifications:

Specification OLS estimate of \(\beta_1\) No proxy for ability \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.107\) (likely upward bias if educ and ability are positively correlated) IQ score as proxy \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.094\) (closer to true return to education)

Interpretation: Including IQ as a proxy for ability reduces the estimated return to education from 10.7% to 9.4% per year of schooling. If IQ is a valid proxy, the 9.4% estimate better isolates the causal effect of education itself.

Caveat: If IQ is an imperfect proxy (ability affects wages beyond what IQ captures), residual OVB remains, and the 9.4% estimate is still biased—just less so.

docs.title: Part B — Measurement Error in Self-Reported Income
docs.text:
Researchers often measure income via survey self-reports. Suppose true income is \(x^* = \text{annual income}\) but the survey records \(x = x^* + e\) where \(e \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)\).

Suppose \(\sigma_{x^*}^2 = 40{,}000\) (AUD²) and \(\sigma_e^2 = 10{,}000\) (AUD²). The reliability ratio is:

\[\lambda = \frac{40{,}000}{40{,}000 + 10{,}000} = 0.80\]

If the true slope (effect of income on some outcome \(y\)) is \(\beta_1 = 0.50\), OLS on the mismeasured regressor yields approximately:

\[\tilde{\beta}_1 \approx 0.50 \times 0.80 = 0.40\]

Conclusion: A 20% downward bias. The true effect is understated by one fifth. Survey-based income regressions will systematically find smaller effects than the truth.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Measurement error in \(y\) is benign, and measurement error in \(x\) is also fine if the error is random."

The first part is true (classical ME in \(y\) does not bias OLS), but the second is false.

Classical (random, zero-mean) measurement error in an explanatory variable \(x\) causes systematic attenuation bias. "Random" does not mean "harmless" here—even pure random noise in \(x\) creates a correlation between \(x\) and the composite error, violating the OLS exogeneity assumption.

The intuition: observed \(x\) contains signal (\(x^*\)) plus noise (\(e\)). When we regress \(y\) on noisy \(x\), part of the variation in \(x\) is pure noise that has no relationship with \(y\), pulling the estimated slope toward zero.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Proxy validity. A researcher uses mother's education as a proxy for parental ability in a child-outcome study. Under what conditions is this a valid proxy? What would have to be true about the relationship between mother's education and parental ability beyond what mother's education captures? If the condition fails, in which direction do you expect the remaining bias to go?

  2. Attenuation bias calculation. A true model has \(\beta_1 = 2.5\). The true regressor has variance \(\sigma_{x^*}^2 = 16\) and measurement error variance \(\sigma_e^2 = 4\). (a) Compute the reliability ratio \(\lambda\). (b) Compute the expected OLS estimate \(E(\tilde{\beta}_1)\). (c) By what percentage is the true effect understated?

  3. ME in \(y\) vs ME in \(x\). A model explains test scores using hours studied. Suppose:

  4. Scenario A: Test scores are recorded with random rounding error (ME in \(y\)).
  5. Scenario B: Hours studied are self-reported with random error (ME in \(x\)).

For each scenario: (a) Is OLS biased? (b) Is OLS consistent? (c) What happens to standard errors? Compare the two scenarios and explain why they have different implications for OLS.

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7e), §9.2 (Proxy Variables) and §9.3 (Measurement Error).
  • Griliches, Z. (1977). "Estimating the returns to schooling: Some econometric problems." Econometrica, 45(1), 1–22. — Classic paper on ability bias and proxies.
  • Carroll, R.J., Ruppert, D., Stefanski, L.A. & Crainiceanu, C.M. (2006). Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models. — Comprehensive reference.
  • See also: M03.L04 (OVB) and M10 (Instrumental Variables — remedy for ME in \(x\)).

docs.title: Lesson M07.L03: Missing Data, Sample Selection, and Outliers
docs.text: Field Detail Module 07 — Specification Issues Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Classify missing data mechanisms and understand when listwise deletion is valid; recognise sample selection bias; distinguish truncation from censoring; identify outliers using leverage and Cook's distance. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 9.4

docs.title: 1. Missing Data Mechanisms
docs.text: Missing data is pervasive in applied work. The consequences for OLS depend critically on why observations are missing. Rubin's (1976) taxonomy identifies three mechanisms:

docs.title: MCAR — Missing Completely At Random
docs.text:
Missingness is unrelated to any variable in the dataset, observed or unobserved:

\[P(\text{missing} \mid y, x_1, \ldots, x_k) = P(\text{missing})\]

Example: A survey firm loses 5% of questionnaires due to a server failure unrelated to respondents' characteristics.

Consequence: The observed sample is a random sub-sample of the full population. OLS on complete cases is unbiased and consistent — you just have a smaller \(n\) (and thus larger standard errors).

docs.title: MAR — Missing At Random
docs.text:
Missingness depends on observed variables but not on the missing value itself, conditional on observables:

\[P(\text{missing} \mid y, x_1, \ldots, x_k) = P(\text{missing} \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k)\]

Example: Higher-income respondents are less likely to report their wealth (income is observed; wealth is missing), but the probability of missing wealth does not further depend on the actual (unobserved) wealth level conditional on income.

Consequence: Complete-case OLS may be biased but modern methods (multiple imputation, inverse probability weighting) can recover consistent estimates.

docs.title: MNAR — Missing Not At Random
docs.text:
Missingness depends on the unobserved value itself:

\[P(\text{missing} \mid y, x_1, \ldots, x_k) \text{ depends on } y \text{ even conditional on } x_1, \ldots, x_k\]

Example: People with very high (or very low) income refuse to disclose it — the missingness is driven by the income value itself.

Consequence: Complete-case OLS is biased and inconsistent. This is the hardest case; requires strong modelling assumptions or additional data.

docs.title: 2. Complete-Case Analysis (Listwise Deletion)
docs.text:
Listwise deletion (dropping all rows with any missing value) is the default in most software. It is:

  • Valid (unbiased) under MCAR.
  • Potentially valid but inefficient under MAR (if you don't model the selection).
  • Biased under MNAR.

Practical guidance: Before dropping rows, test whether missingness is correlated with observed \(y\) or \(x\) variables. Regress a missingness indicator on the covariates; significant coefficients suggest MAR or MNAR, not MCAR.

docs.title: 3. Sample Selection Problem
docs.text:
Sample selection bias arises when the observed sample is systematically different from the population of interest, and this selection is correlated with the outcome.

Classic example — wage data:

We observe wages only for workers who are currently employed. But the decision to work (the selection equation) may be correlated with the wage itself: high-ability individuals are both more likely to be employed and to earn higher wages. The observed wage distribution is therefore not a random draw from the full population distribution.

If we regress \(\log(\text{wage})\) on education using only employed workers:

\[E(\log(\text{wage}) \mid \text{employed}) \neq E(\log(\text{wage}) \mid \text{all workers})\]

OLS on the selected sample may overstate or understate the population return to education depending on the nature of the selection.

Formal model (Heckman two-step): The workhorse solution is Heckman's (1979) selection model, which jointly models: 1. Selection equation: \(P(\text{employed} = 1 \mid z)\) — probit. 2. Outcome equation: \(\log(\text{wage}) = x'\beta + \lambda(\hat{\alpha}'z) + \epsilon\) — OLS with an added inverse Mills ratio \(\lambda(\cdot)\) to correct for selection.

(Advanced; covered in ECMT6002. Here, recognise the problem and understand what drives it.)

docs.title: 4. Truncation vs Censoring
docs.text:
These terms are often confused:

Concept Definition Example Truncation The entire observation (including \(x\)) is excluded from the sample when \(y\) falls outside a range. Study of high earners: everyone earning below $200k is entirely excluded from the dataset. Censoring The observation is in the dataset, but \(y\) is only partially observed (recorded as a limit value). Top-coded income: everyone earning above $200k has income recorded as "≥$200k".

In both cases, OLS on the observed data is biased because the sample no longer represents the full distribution.

Tobit model: For censored data (e.g. hours worked, which is 0 for non-workers), the Tobit estimator correctly accounts for the censoring mechanism:

\[y^* = x'\beta + u, \quad u \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$ $$y = \max(0,\; y^*)\]

OLS on the censored sample produces estimates biased toward zero (because many observations are piled at the boundary). Tobit recovers the latent \(\beta\) consistently.

docs.title: 5. Outliers: Leverage, Influence, and Cook's D
docs.text:
Outliers can severely distort OLS estimates. Two distinct concepts:

Leverage — how unusual is observation \(i\)'s position in \(x\)-space:

\[h_{ii} = x_i'(X'X)^{-1}x_i\]

High-leverage observations (\(h_{ii} > 2(k+1)/n\)) have the potential to distort estimates, but do not necessarily do so.

Cook's Distance — the actual influence of observation \(i\) on all estimated coefficients:

\[D_i = \frac{(\hat{\beta}_{(-i)} - \hat{\beta})'(X'X)(\hat{\beta}_{(-i)} - \hat{\beta})}{(k+1)\hat{\sigma}^2}\]

Rule of thumb: \(D_i > 4/n\) warrants investigation; \(D_i > 1\) is often considered highly influential.

Remedies: - Inspect the flagged observation for data entry errors. - Use robust regression (e.g. M-estimation, least trimmed squares) which downweights high-influence observations. - Report results with and without the outlier to demonstrate sensitivity.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup. Suppose we use the Wooldridge mroz dataset, which contains labour market data for 753 married women, of whom only 428 are employed (report a positive wage).

Naive OLS: Regress \(\log(\text{wage})\) on education, experience, and experience² using only the 428 employed women.

Problem: Women with lower wages are more likely to be out of the labour force entirely (their potential wage is below their reservation wage). The employed subsample is therefore positively selected — we see the upper portion of the wage distribution.

Direction of bias: - If low-ability/low-wage women are excluded, the observed average wage is above the population average. - The estimated return to education may be understated if higher-education women are disproportionately likely to work regardless, so there is less variation in education among the selected group. - In practice, the Heckman correction for the mroz data typically shows that the selection-corrected return to education is higher than the naive OLS estimate.

Practical takeaway: Always ask "What determines whether I observe \(y\) for this unit?" If the answer involves variables correlated with \(y\) itself, you have a sample selection problem.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Just drop rows with missing data and proceed — the data are probably missing at random."

This is one of the most dangerous casual assumptions in applied econometrics.

Dropping observations is only valid under MCAR, which is the strongest (and least common) assumption. In most real datasets, missingness is related to the outcome or covariates (MAR or MNAR). Simply deleting missing rows in those cases introduces selection bias that is invisible to standard diagnostic tests — your regression runs, produces plausible-looking coefficients, and you have no warning that the estimates are systematically wrong.

Always investigate the missingness pattern: 1. Tabulate missingness rates by key subgroups. 2. Regress a missingness indicator on observed covariates. 3. Compare means of \(y\) and \(x\) between complete and incomplete cases.

Only after this should you decide whether listwise deletion, imputation, or a selection model is appropriate.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Missing data classification. A researcher studies the effect of class size on student test scores. In 30% of schools, test scores are not reported because the schools opted out of standardised testing. Low-performing schools are more likely to opt out. (a) Which missing data mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) best describes this situation? Justify your answer. (b) What is the likely direction of bias if the researcher drops schools with missing test scores?

  2. Truncation vs censoring. A bank studies the determinants of loan repayment amounts. Repayment is recorded as: (i) the actual dollar amount for amounts between $0 and $500,000; (ii) "$500,000+" for any repayment at or above the cap. (a) Is this truncation or censoring? Explain. (b) What model would you use to recover unbiased estimates of the effect of borrower characteristics on repayment?

  3. Outlier diagnostics. You estimate a consumption function with \(n = 200\) and \(k = 4\) regressors. Observation 17 has Cook's D = 0.85 and leverage \(h_{17,17} = 0.18\). (a) Is observation 17 high-leverage? (Use the \(2(k+1)/n\) rule of thumb.) (b) Is it influential by Cook's D? (Use the \(4/n\) rule.) (c) Outline the steps you would take before deciding whether to exclude observation 17.

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7e), §9.4 — Missing Data and Nonrandom Samples.
  • Rubin, D.B. (1976). "Inference and missing data." Biometrika, 63(3), 581–592. — Original taxonomy of MCAR/MAR/MNAR.
  • Heckman, J.J. (1979). "Sample selection bias as a specification error." Econometrica, 47(1), 153–161. — Nobel Prize–winning correction model.
  • Little, R.J.A. & Rubin, D.B. (2002). Statistical Analysis with Missing Data (2nd ed.). — Comprehensive reference.
  • Tobin, J. (1958). "Estimation of relationships for limited dependent variables." Econometrica, 26(1), 24–36. — Original Tobit paper.

docs.title: Lesson M08.L01: The Nature of Time Series Data
docs.text: Field Detail Module 08 — Time Series Basics Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand how time series data differ from cross-sections; define strict vs contemporaneous exogeneity; introduce the finite distributed lag model and lag operator notation. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 10.1

docs.title: 1. What Is Time Series Data?
docs.text:
A time series is a sequence of observations on one or more variables taken at equally spaced points in time:

\[\{y_t\}_{t=1}^{T} = \{y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_T\}\]

Examples from economics and finance:

Series Frequency Key feature Australian GDP growth (%) Quarterly Mean-reverting, business-cycle fluctuations RBA cash rate (%) Monthly Persistent, slow-moving CPI inflation (%) Monthly Some persistence; mean-shifts over policy regimes Unemployment rate (%) Monthly Persistent; rises fast, falls slowly ASX 200 daily returns Daily Near-serially-uncorrelated, volatility clustering

docs.title: 2. Key Difference from Cross-Sectional Data
docs.text:
In a cross-section, observations are drawn independently from a population: knowing respondent \(i\)'s income tells us nothing about respondent \(j\)'s income.

In a time series, observations are temporally ordered and dependent: today's GDP growth, interest rate, and inflation all depend on yesterday's values. This serial dependence (autocorrelation) is the defining feature of time series, and it fundamentally changes what assumptions are required for valid OLS inference.

Formally, for a stationary time series we expect:

\[\text{Cov}(y_t, y_{t-h}) \neq 0 \quad \text{for small } h\]

This means the i.i.d. assumption that underlies cross-sectional OLS asymptotics does not hold for time series without additional structure.

docs.title: 3. Strict Exogeneity
docs.text:
In cross-sectional OLS, the key assumption is contemporaneous exogeneity: \(E(u_i \mid x_i) = 0\).

For time series, the stronger assumption of strict exogeneity requires that the error at time \(t\) is uncorrelated with every regressor at every time period — past, present, and future:

\[E(u_t \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T) = 0 \quad \text{for all } t\]

This means: - \(u_t\) is uncorrelated with current \(x_t\) (contemporaneous). - \(u_t\) is uncorrelated with past regressors \(x_{t-1}, x_{t-2}, \ldots\) (no feedback from past errors to current regressors). - \(u_t\) is uncorrelated with future regressors \(x_{t+1}, x_{t+2}, \ldots\) — the most demanding part.

Why is strict exogeneity so strong? Future regressors must be unaffected by current errors. This rules out: - Feedback systems: If \(y\) affects \(x\) in subsequent periods (e.g. income today affects savings next period, which affects income next period), strict exogeneity fails. - Lagged dependent variables as regressors: \(y_{t-1}\) as a regressor automatically violates strict exogeneity because \(u_{t-1}\) affects \(y_{t-1}\), which is a regressor at time \(t\).

Under strict exogeneity, OLS is unbiased for finite \(T\). Under weaker (contemporaneous) exogeneity, OLS is consistent as \(T \to \infty\) but not unbiased in finite samples.

docs.title: 4. Economic Time Series: Autocorrelation Is the Norm
docs.text:
Consider the RBA cash rate (\(r_t\)). After the RBA sets the rate in period \(t\), it tends to keep it at a similar level next period — changing rates by 25 basis points at a time, infrequently. Correlation between \(r_t\) and \(r_{t-1}\) is typically above 0.95. This is not noise — it reflects the persistence of monetary policy.

Similarly, Australian GDP growth (\(g_t\)) is positively autocorrelated at short lags (expansions last multiple quarters) but can show negative autocorrelation at business-cycle frequency.

The practical implication: regressing one time series on another without accounting for this persistence can produce misleading results (see M08.L03 on spurious regression).

docs.title: 5. Finite Distributed Lag (FDL) Models — Preview
docs.text:
A finite distributed lag model allows current and past values of a regressor \(z\) to affect the current outcome \(y\):

\[y_t = \alpha + \delta_0 z_t + \delta_1 z_{t-1} + \delta_2 z_{t-2} + \cdots + \delta_q z_{t-q} + u_t\]

This is natural in economics: a change in the interest rate today affects consumption over the next several quarters, not just this quarter. The subscripts on \(\delta_j\) represent the lag — how many periods back the effect applies.

Full treatment of FDL models is in M08.L02.

docs.title: 6. The Lag Operator
docs.text:
The lag operator \(L\) (also written \(B\) in some textbooks) is a convenient notation for time-shifted series:

\[L y_t = y_{t-1}$$ $$L^2 y_t = y_{t-2}$$ $$L^j y_t = y_{t-j}\]

The first difference operator \(\Delta\):

\[\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} = (1 - L) y_t\]

Using lag operator notation, the FDL model becomes:

\[y_t = \alpha + (\delta_0 + \delta_1 L + \delta_2 L^2 + \cdots + \delta_q L^q) z_t + u_t = \alpha + \delta(L) z_t + u_t\]

where \(\delta(L) = \sum_{j=0}^q \delta_j L^j\) is a lag polynomial.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setting up an Australian monetary policy time series model.

Suppose we want to model Australian headline CPI inflation (\(\pi_t\), %) as a function of the RBA cash rate (\(r_t\), %). Using monthly RBA data (January 2000 – December 2023):

Static model:

\[\pi_t = \alpha + \beta_0 r_t + u_t\]

Problem with the static model: Rate changes take time to filter through the economy (via bank lending rates, mortgage repayments, business investment, etc.). The contemporaneous relationship alone is insufficient.

FDL model (12 lags):

\[\pi_t = \alpha + \sum_{j=0}^{12} \delta_j r_{t-j} + u_t\]

Here: - \(\delta_0\): immediate effect of a 1 pp rate rise on inflation this month. - \(\delta_3\): effect 3 months later. - \(\sum_{j=0}^{12} \delta_j\): total (long-run) effect after one year.

Strict exogeneity concern: Does the RBA set \(r_t\) partly in response to past inflation errors \(u_{t-1}\)? Almost certainly yes — the RBA targets inflation. This means strict exogeneity is likely violated; OLS may still be consistent (under sequential exogeneity), but finite-sample properties are less clean.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"OLS works the same for time series as for cross-sectional data."

This is false in several important ways:

  1. Temporal dependence invalidates i.i.d.-based inference. Standard errors computed assuming i.i.d. errors are incorrect in the presence of serial correlation. You need HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) standard errors or GLS.

  2. Strict exogeneity is a much stronger assumption than contemporaneous exogeneity and often fails in feedback models common in macroeconomics.

  3. Non-stationarity creates entirely new problems (spurious regressions, invalid t-statistics, diverging variance) that do not arise in cross-sections. See M08.L03 and M08.L04.

  4. Finite-sample distributions of OLS estimators may differ from their cross-sectional counterparts even when asymptotic properties hold.

Time series econometrics requires its own toolkit: HAC SEs, unit root tests, cointegration, ARIMA/VAR models.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Strict vs contemporaneous exogeneity. An analyst estimates a model where quarterly retail sales (\(y_t\)) are regressed on the consumer sentiment index (\(x_t\)). (a) What does strict exogeneity require of the error \(u_t\) relative to all values of \(x\)? (b) Explain why strict exogeneity might be violated if the RBA uses retail sales data to set interest rates, which in turn affect consumer sentiment. (c) Is OLS necessarily inconsistent if strict exogeneity fails? What weaker assumption would still give consistency?

  2. Lag operator practice. Let \(y_t = 2 + 0.6 y_{t-1} + e_t\) (an AR(1) process). (a) Express this model using the lag operator \(L\). (b) Write out \(\Delta y_t\) using \(L\). (c) If \(y_{100} = 5.0\) and \(e_{101} = 0.2\), compute \(y_{101}\).

  3. FDL interpretation. A researcher estimates a quarterly FDL model of the unemployment rate (\(u_t\)) on GDP growth (\(g_t\)) with 4 lags:

$\(u_t = 6.1 - 0.3 g_t - 0.5 g_{t-1} - 0.4 g_{t-2} - 0.2 g_{t-3} + \text{error}\)$

(a) Interpret \(\delta_0 = -0.3\). (b) Interpret \(\delta_2 = -0.4\). (c) Compute the long-run propensity (LRP). What does it mean?

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7e), Ch 10 — Basic Regression Analysis with Time Series Data.
  • RBA Statistical Tables (available at rba.gov.au) — for Australian cash rate, CPI, and GDP series.
  • Hamilton, J.D. (1994). Time Series Analysis. Princeton University Press. — Graduate-level reference.
  • Stock, J.H. & Watson, M.W. (2020). Introduction to Econometrics (4e), Ch 14–16 — complementary time series treatment.

docs.title: Lesson M08.L02: Static and Finite Distributed Lag Models
docs.text: Field Detail Module 08 — Time Series Basics Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Distinguish static from FDL models; interpret impact effects, lagged effects, and the long-run propensity; apply FDL reasoning to monetary policy transmission. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 10.2

docs.title: 1. Static Model
docs.text:
A static model assumes that the effect of \(z_t\) on \(y_t\) is entirely contemporaneous — there are no lagged effects:

\[y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z_t + u_t\]

When appropriate: - The adjustment from \(z\) to \(y\) is instantaneous (financial markets: asset prices react within the period to information). - You have no reason to believe past values of \(z\) matter independently.

When inappropriate: - Economic processes take time: investment responds to interest rates over quarters; wages adjust to inflation with a lag; exchange rate changes pass through to import prices gradually.

In most macroeconomic applications, the static model is a restrictive special case of the FDL model.

docs.title: 2. Finite Distributed Lag (FDL) Model
docs.text:
A finite distributed lag model of order \(q\) allows \(q\) past values of \(z\) to independently affect \(y\):

\[\boxed{y_t = \alpha + \delta_0 z_t + \delta_1 z_{t-1} + \delta_2 z_{t-2} + \cdots + \delta_q z_{t-q} + u_t}\]

The coefficients \(\{\delta_0, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_q\}\) are called the lag distribution or distributed lag weights.

Interpretation of each coefficient:

Suppose \(z\) increases by one unit in period \(t\) and remains at the new level forever (a permanent change). Then:

  • In period \(t\): \(y\) changes by \(\delta_0\) (the impact effect or impact multiplier).
  • In period \(t+1\): additional change is \(\delta_1\) (beyond what already happened).
  • In period \(t+j\): additional change is \(\delta_j\).

Alternatively, if \(z\) increases by one unit in period \(t\) only (a temporary change, a pulse), then:

  • Period \(t\): \(y\) changes by \(\delta_0\).
  • Period \(t+1\): \(y\) changes by \(\delta_1\).
  • Period \(t+j\): \(y\) changes by \(\delta_j\).
  • Period \(t+q+1\): effect is zero (the pulse has worked through all lags).

docs.title: 3. Impact Effect
docs.text:
\[\delta_0 = \frac{\partial y_t}{\partial z_t}\]

The impact effect is the immediate response of \(y\) to a one-unit change in \(z\) in the same period, holding all other lags constant. It is the coefficient on the contemporaneous value of the regressor.

docs.title: 4. Lagged Effects
docs.text:
\[\delta_j = \frac{\partial y_{t+j}}{\partial z_t}, \quad j = 1, 2, \ldots, q\]

The \(j\)-period lagged effect measures how much \(y\) changes \(j\) periods after a one-unit change in \(z\). These capture the delayed transmission of shocks through the economy.

Lag distribution shape: The pattern of \(\{\delta_j\}\) over \(j\) traces out the impulse response function — how \(y\) responds over time to a one-time shock in \(z\).

docs.title: 5. Long-Run Propensity (LRP)
docs.text:
The long-run propensity (or long-run multiplier) is the total cumulative effect on \(y\) after all lag effects have worked through:

\[\boxed{LRP = \sum_{j=0}^{q} \delta_j = \delta_0 + \delta_1 + \cdots + \delta_q}\]

Economic interpretation: The LRP tells us the long-run equilibrium change in \(y\) for a sustained one-unit increase in \(z\). It is the sum of all immediate and delayed effects.

Graphically: The LRP is the area under the lag distribution plot (coefficients vs lag length).

docs.title: 6. Monetary Policy Example: Money Supply and Inflation
docs.text:
Quantity theory motivation. In the long run, sustained growth in the money supply (\(m_t\), %) drives inflation (\(\pi_t\), %), but the transmission operates with a lag: - Banks receive reserves, expand credit. - Firms and households spend more. - Producers raise prices. - Wage negotiations adjust. - Import prices react.

A simple FDL model:

\[\pi_t = \alpha + \delta_0 \Delta m_t + \delta_1 \Delta m_{t-1} + \delta_2 \Delta m_{t-2} + \cdots + \delta_q \Delta m_{t-q} + u_t\]

Friedman's hypothesis: in the long run, a sustained 1% increase in money growth raises inflation by approximately 1%, so \(LRP \approx 1\). But the impact effect \(\delta_0\) may be small — prices don't respond immediately.

docs.title: 7. Australian Example: RBA Rate Changes and Inflation
docs.text:
The RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) adjusts the cash rate to control inflation. A classic stylised fact of monetary policy is the "long and variable lags" (Friedman, 1961):

  • Rate changes take roughly 12–18 months to fully affect inflation in Australia.
  • Early effects (0–3 months): mainly exchange rate channel — AUD appreciates, import prices fall.
  • Medium-term (3–12 months): credit channel — higher rates reduce borrowing, cool demand.
  • Long-term (12–18+ months): aggregate demand falls, labour market softens, wage growth slows, inflation falls.

A quarterly FDL of inflation on the cash rate change (\(\Delta r_t\)) with \(q = 6\) lags (18 months) would capture this:

\[\pi_t = \alpha + \sum_{j=0}^{6} \delta_j \Delta r_{t-j} + u_t\]

The LRP = \(\sum_{j=0}^6 \delta_j\) should be negative (higher rates → lower inflation) and its magnitude reveals the total disinflationary power of a 1 pp rate hike sustained over 18 months.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Given FDL coefficients from a quarterly model of Australian unemployment (\(u_t\), %) on GDP growth (\(g_t\), %):

\[u_t = 5.8 - 0.2\, g_t - 0.4\, g_{t-1} - 0.3\, g_{t-2} - 0.1\, g_{t-3} + \text{error}\]

Q1. What is the impact effect of a 1 pp increase in GDP growth on unemployment?

\[\delta_0 = -0.2\]

A 1 percentage point rise in GDP growth this quarter is associated with a 0.2 pp fall in unemployment this quarter.

Q2. What is the effect 2 quarters later?

\[\delta_2 = -0.3\]

Two quarters after the 1 pp GDP growth increase, unemployment falls by an additional 0.3 pp (cumulative change from the pulse: \(\delta_0 + \delta_1 + \delta_2 = -0.2 - 0.4 - 0.3 = -0.9\) pp).

Q3. Compute the LRP.

\[LRP = -0.2 + (-0.4) + (-0.3) + (-0.1) = -1.0\]

Interpretation: A sustained 1 pp increase in GDP growth is associated with a 1 percentage point permanent fall in the unemployment rate over 3 quarters. This is close to an Okun's Law relationship — a rule of thumb widely used in macroeconomics.

Q4. Where is the largest single-period effect?

The lag with the largest \(|\delta_j|\) is \(j=1\) (\(\delta_1 = -0.4\)): the biggest unemployment response occurs one quarter after the GDP growth shock, not immediately.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"The long-run effect equals the sum of all lagged coefficients — regardless of how many lags I've included."

This requires an important caveat: the LRP formula \(\sum_{j=0}^q \delta_j\) is only valid if you have included enough lags to capture the full distributed lag response.

If the true model has \(q^* = 8\) lags but you estimate with \(q = 3\), your "LRP" is \(\sum_{j=0}^3 \delta_j\), which underestimates the true long-run effect. The remaining effects (lags 4–8) are omitted, causing omitted variable bias in all estimated coefficients and a biased LRP.

How to choose \(q\)? - Use economic theory (e.g. monetary policy lags are roughly 4–6 quarters in Australia). - Start with a long lag length and use AIC/BIC to select the optimal \(q\). - Verify that the \(\delta_j\)'s become small and statistically insignificant at long lags (indicating the distributed lag has been captured).

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. LRP and impact effect. A researcher estimates the following quarterly FDL model for Australian housing starts (\(h_t\)) on the mortgage rate (\(r_t\)):

$\(h_t = 120 - 5.0\, r_t - 8.0\, r_{t-1} - 6.0\, r_{t-2} - 3.0\, r_{t-3} - 1.0\, r_{t-4} + u_t\)$

(a) Interpret the impact effect \(\delta_0 = -5.0\). (b) Compute the LRP. Interpret it in economic terms. (c) At which lag does the largest effect on housing starts occur?

  1. Lag selection. You estimate two FDL models of inflation on money growth: one with \(q = 4\) lags (AIC = −3.42, BIC = −3.18) and one with \(q = 8\) lags (AIC = −3.51, BIC = −3.09). (a) Which model does AIC prefer? BIC? (b) Explain intuitively why AIC and BIC can disagree. (c) If the true lag length is 8, what is the consequence of selecting \(q = 4\) for the estimated LRP?

  2. Policy interpretation. The RBA increases the cash rate by 50 basis points (0.5 pp) in a single meeting. Using the lag distribution below, compute the cumulative effect on quarterly inflation after 1, 2, and 4 quarters. Plot (sketch) the impulse response.

Lag \(j\) \(\delta_j\) 0 −0.03 1 −0.08 2 −0.10 3 −0.09 4 −0.07

(Multiply each \(\delta_j\) by the shock size of 0.5 pp.)

docs.text:

  • Friedman, M. (1961). "The lag in effect of monetary policy." Journal of Political Economy, 69(5), 447–466. — Original "long and variable lags" reference.
  • RBA (2020). "Monetary Policy Transmission in Australia." RBA Bulletin, March 2020. — Australian policy transmission lags evidence.
  • Stock, J.H. & Watson, M.W. (2020). Introduction to Econometrics (4e), §14.2 — FDL and distributed lag models.

docs.title: Lesson M08.L03: Serial Correlation and Spurious Regression
docs.text: Field Detail Module 08 — Time Series Basics Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Define serial correlation and its consequences for OLS; derive why spurious regression occurs with non-stationary series; apply diagnostic checks for both problems. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 10.5, 11.1

docs.title: 1. Serial Correlation (Autocorrelation)
docs.text:
Serial correlation (autocorrelation) exists when the error terms at different time periods are correlated:

\[ ext{Corr}(u_t, u_s) eq 0 \quad ext{for some } t eq s\]

This violates Gauss-Markov assumption MLR.5 (no serial correlation in errors), which assumes:

\[ ext{Cov}(u_t, u_s) = 0 \quad orall\; t eq s\]

Serial correlation is the norm, not the exception, in economic time series — residuals that reflect omitted cyclical forces, adjustment costs, habit formation, or policy persistence will be correlated over time.

docs.title: 2. The AR(1) Error Process
docs.text:
The most common model for serial correlation is the AR(1) (first-order autoregressive) process:

\[\boxed{u_t = \rho u_{t-1} + e_t}\]

where: - \(\rho\) is the autocorrelation coefficient, \(|\rho| < 1\) for covariance stationarity. - \(e_t \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, \sigma_e^2)\) is white noise (serially uncorrelated). - When \(\rho > 0\): positive serial correlation — positive errors tend to follow positive errors (smooth, persistent residuals). - When \(\rho < 0\): negative serial correlation — errors alternate in sign (oscillating residuals, less common in macro).

Under this AR(1) process, the error variance and autocovariances are:

\[\text{Var}(u_t) = \frac{\sigma_e^2}{1 - \rho^2}, \quad \text{Cov}(u_t, u_{t-h}) = \rho^h \cdot \frac{\sigma_e^2}{1 - \rho^2}\]

docs.title: 3. Consequences of Serial Correlation for OLS
docs.text:
If the regressors satisfy strict exogeneity, OLS remains:

  • Unbiased: \(E(\hat{\beta}) = \beta\) — serial correlation in errors does not bias the coefficient estimates.
  • Consistent: \(\text{plim}(\hat{\beta}) = \beta\).

However, OLS is:

  • Inefficient: GLS (or FGLS) with the correct error structure is more efficient.
  • Invalid standard errors: The OLS variance formula \(\hat{V}(\hat{\beta}) = \hat{\sigma}^2(X'X)^{-1}\) is incorrect when errors are serially correlated. This means t-statistics, F-statistics, and confidence intervals are all invalid.

The direction of standard error bias with positive serial correlation (\(\rho > 0\)):

OLS standard errors are typically understated (too small), leading to over-rejection of \(H_0\) and spuriously significant t-statistics.

Remedies: 1. HAC standard errors (Newey-West): correct the variance-covariance matrix to account for serial correlation (and heteroskedasticity) without modelling the specific error structure. 2. FGLS / Cochrane-Orcutt: estimate \(\rho\) from residuals, transform data to remove AR(1) correlation, run OLS on the transformed model. 3. Include lagged regressors / lagged \(y\) to absorb the serial correlation structurally.

docs.title: 4. Testing for Serial Correlation
docs.text:
Visual inspection: Plot OLS residuals against time. Positive serial correlation: runs of positive residuals followed by runs of negative residuals. Negative: alternating patterns.

Breusch-Godfrey (BG) LM test: Regress OLS residuals \(\hat{u}_t\) on \(\hat{u}_{t-1}, \ldots, \hat{u}_{t-p}\) and all original regressors. Test \(H_0\): \(\rho_1 = \cdots = \rho_p = 0\) using LM statistic \(\sim \chi^2_p\).

Durbin-Watson statistic (for AR(1) only, no lagged \(y\) in the model):

\[DW = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^T (\hat{u}_t - \hat{u}_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^T \hat{u}_t^2} \approx 2(1 - \hat{\rho})\]

Interpretation: \(DW \approx 2\) (no AC), \(DW < 2\) (positive AC), \(DW > 2\) (negative AC).

docs.title: 5. Spurious Regression
docs.text:
Spurious regression is one of the most dangerous traps in time series econometrics. It occurs when two unrelated time series, each exhibiting a trend or unit root (non-stationarity), are regressed on each other:

The result: Very high \(R^2\), highly significant t-statistics, and large coefficients — even though the two series have no genuine economic relationship.

Classic example:

Regress Australian GDP (in levels, \(A\)) on US population (in millions, \(P\)):

\[A_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 P_t + u_t\]

Both series trend upward over time. OLS may find \(R^2 > 0.95\) and a highly significant \(\hat{\beta}_1\) — but this is entirely spurious. Australian GDP is not caused by US population size; both simply trend upward over the 20th century.

Formal explanation (Granger and Newbold, 1974):

When \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) are independent random walks (unit root processes):

\[y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t, \quad x_t = x_{t-1} + v_t \quad (e_t \perp v_t)\]

The true slope is \(\beta_1 = 0\), but the OLS \(t\)-statistic for \(\hat{\beta}_1\) does not follow a \(t\)-distribution. It diverges as \(T \to \infty\):

\[t \to \pm\infty \text{ in distribution as } T \to \infty\]

In finite samples, you will almost always reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) even when the truth is \(\beta_1 = 0\). The standard critical values (e.g. ±1.96) are entirely wrong.

The residuals are highly serially correlated (DW statistic near 0) — this is in fact the telltale sign of a spurious regression.

Rule: Always check for spurious regression when working with non-stationary time series: 1. Plot the series: do they trend? 2. Compute DW on the regression residuals: if DW ≪ 2, suspect spurious regression. 3. Test each series for a unit root (ADF test — see M08.L04). 4. If both series have unit roots and are not cointegrated, do not run OLS in levels. First-difference the series instead.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Identifying a Spurious Regression

Data: Australian nominal GDP (\(A_t\), billions AUD) and US population (\(P_t\), millions), annual 1960–2023.

Step 1. Estimate OLS in levels:

\[\hat{A}_t = -2{,}850 + 72.4\, P_t, \quad R^2 = 0.98, \quad t_{\hat{\beta}} = 54.3, \quad DW = 0.12\]

Step 2. Red flags:

Indicator Value Interpretation \(R^2\) 0.98 Unusually high — both series trend \(t\)-statistic 54.3 Enormous — but invalid DW statistic 0.12 Extremely low → severe positive serial correlation → spurious regression

Step 3. Why R² is misleading here.

The high \(R^2\) reflects a shared trend, not economic causation. If we fit a common time trend \(t\) to both series and remove it, the residuals would have near-zero correlation. The regression is capturing "both things went up over time", nothing more.

Step 4. Solution — use growth rates (first differences).

\[\Delta A_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \Delta P_t + u_t\]

After differencing, \(R^2\) drops dramatically and the t-statistic becomes insignificant (\(p > 0.5\)), correctly indicating no relationship between Australian GDP growth and US population growth.

Conclusion: The original regression was entirely spurious. The DW statistic near zero was the critical warning sign.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"A high R² in a time series regression indicates a strong causal relationship."

This is false, especially when the series are non-stationary (trending or have a unit root).

In a spurious regression, \(R^2\) can approach 1 even when the two series are completely independent random walks. The high \(R^2\) reflects nothing more than common trending behaviour — both series are moving in the same direction over time, driven by their own dynamics, not by each other.

The correct interpretation of \(R^2\) in time series requires: 1. Checking that both series are stationary (or cointegrated if non-stationary). 2. Confirming that regression residuals show no severe serial correlation (DW not near 0). 3. Economic plausibility — does theory support the relationship?

High \(R^2\) is a necessary but far-from-sufficient condition for a valid time series relationship.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Consequences of AR(1) errors. A regression of quarterly consumer spending on disposable income yields an OLS \(\hat{\rho} = 0.72\) from the residuals. (a) Is OLS biased? Justify your answer (assume strict exogeneity holds). (b) What is the consequence for the reported t-statistics? (c) Describe two approaches to obtain valid inference despite the serial correlation.

  2. Spurious regression detection. You regress monthly Australian house prices on monthly global oil prices over 1990–2023. Results: \(R^2 = 0.91\), \(DW = 0.18\), \(t\)-statistic on oil price = 38.7. (a) Is this likely a spurious regression? List the evidence. (b) What would you test next, and what would you do if the test confirms your suspicion? (c) If both series are I(1), under what condition could you still run OLS in levels without it being spurious?

  3. DW statistic interpretation. Three regressions on different time series datasets yield DW statistics of 0.24, 1.95, and 3.61. (a) For each DW value, state whether it suggests positive autocorrelation, no autocorrelation, or negative autocorrelation. (b) For the regression with DW = 0.24, what is the approximate estimated \(\hat{\rho}\) (using the approximation \(DW \approx 2(1-\hat{\rho})\))? (c) What follow-up steps would you take for the regression with DW = 0.24?

docs.text:

  • Granger, C.W.J. & Newbold, P. (1974). "Spurious regressions in econometrics." Journal of Econometrics, 2(2), 111–120. — Foundational paper on spurious regression.
  • Newey, W.K. & West, K.D. (1987). "A simple, positive semi-definite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix." Econometrica, 55(3), 703–708. — HAC standard errors.
  • Hamilton, J.D. (1994). Time Series Analysis, Ch 8 — Serial correlation and GLS.
  • See also: M08.L04 (Stationarity and Unit Root Tests — solution to the spurious regression problem).

docs.title: Lesson M08.L04: Stationarity, Trends, and Unit Root Tests
docs.text: Field Detail Module 08 — Time Series Basics Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Define covariance stationarity; distinguish deterministic from stochastic trends; understand the ADF unit root test; know when to detrend versus first-difference. Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 10.4–10.5

docs.title: 1. Stationarity
docs.text:
A time series \(\{y_t\}\) is covariance stationary (weakly stationary) if its first two moments are time-invariant:

\[\begin{aligned} E(y_t) &= \mu \quad &&\text{(constant mean)} \\ \text{Var}(y_t) &= \sigma^2 < \infty \quad &&\text{(constant, finite variance)} \\ \text{Cov}(y_t, y_{t-h}) &= \gamma(h) \quad &&\text{(depends only on lag } h\text{, not on } t\text{)} \end{aligned}\]

Covariance stationarity is also called weak stationarity (as opposed to strict stationarity, which requires the entire joint distribution to be time-invariant).

Why does stationarity matter? - Standard asymptotic theory (LLN, CLT) for time series requires stationarity or near-stationarity. - Non-stationary series have moments that change over time, making the past a poor guide to the future and standard inference invalid. - Spurious regressions (M08.L03) arise from regressing non-stationary series on each other.

Examples: - Stationary: stock returns, GDP growth rate (%), CPI inflation (if in a stable policy regime). - Non-stationary: GDP level, stock prices, nominal wages — all trend upward over time.

docs.title: 2. Deterministic Trend (Trend-Stationary Process)
docs.text:
A deterministic trend model:

\[y_t = \alpha + \beta t + u_t, \quad u_t \sim \text{stationary}\]

Here the mean changes linearly over time (\(E(y_t) = \alpha + \beta t\)), but the variance is constant (\(\text{Var}(y_t) = \sigma_u^2\)). The series "wanders" above and below the trend line but always reverts to it.

This series is NOT stationary (non-constant mean), but it is trend-stationary: once you remove the linear time trend, the residuals \(u_t\) are stationary.

Solution: include \(t\) as a regressor (detrending):

  1. Regress \(y_t\) on a constant and \(t\): \(y_t = \hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta} t + \hat{u}_t\).
  2. Use the detrended residuals \(\hat{u}_t\) (or the detrended \(y\)) in subsequent regressions.

Alternatively, simply include \(t\) as a control variable in the regression of interest. This soaks up the common trend and avoids spurious correlation between \(y_t\) and other trending series.

docs.title: 3. Stochastic Trend / Unit Root
docs.text:
A random walk (the canonical stochastic trend model):

\[y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t, \quad e_t \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, \sigma_e^2)\]

Starting from \(y_0\):

\[y_t = y_0 + \sum_{s=1}^t e_s\]

Key properties: $\(E(y_t) = y_0 \quad \text{(constant mean)}\)$ $\(\text{Var}(y_t) = t \sigma_e^2 \quad \text{(grows without bound)}\)$

The variance increases linearly with \(t\) — this series has a stochastic trend: it wanders further and further from its starting point over time, with no tendency to revert. The shocks are permanent: a shock \(e_t\) shifts the level of \(y\) permanently.

Why "unit root"? Express the random walk as:

\[y_t = \rho y_{t-1} + e_t\]

with \(\rho = 1\). In the AR(1) representation, the autoregressive coefficient equals 1 (the "unit root"). For \(|\rho| < 1\), the process is stationary (mean-reverting). For \(\rho = 1\), the process is non-stationary.

Random walk with drift:

\[y_t = \mu + y_{t-1} + e_t\]

Now \(E(y_t) = y_0 + \mu t\) — trending upward (or downward) on average, with a variance still growing as \(t\sigma_e^2\). Most economic levels (GDP, price indices) follow a random walk with positive drift.

docs.title: 4. Contrast: Deterministic vs Stochastic Trend
docs.text:
Feature Deterministic Trend Stochastic Trend (Unit Root) Mean \(\alpha + \beta t\) (non-constant) \(y_0\) (random walk) or \(y_0 + \mu t\) (drift) Variance Constant \(\sigma_u^2\) Grows: \(t \sigma_e^2\) Shock persistence Temporary (shocks decay) Permanent (shocks accumulate) Remedy Detrend (subtract \(\hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta} t\)) First-difference (\(\Delta y_t\)) After remedy Stationary Stationary (if one unit root)

Critical point: If a series has a unit root, detrending does not make it stationary — you must first-difference. Applying the wrong remedy leaves you with a non-stationary series and invalid inference.

docs.title: 5. Integrated Processes
docs.text:
A process \(y_t\) that becomes stationary after \(d\) first-differences is said to be integrated of order \(d\), written \(y_t \sim I(d)\):

  • \(I(0)\): already stationary.
  • \(I(1)\): one unit root; \(\Delta y_t \sim I(0)\).
  • \(I(2)\): two unit roots; \(\Delta^2 y_t \sim I(0)\) (rare in economics).

Most macroeconomic levels (GDP, prices, nominal wages) are \(I(1)\). Their growth rates (log differences) are \(I(0)\).

docs.title: 6. Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test
docs.text:
The ADF test is the standard formal test for a unit root.

Null hypothesis: \(H_0\): \(y_t\) has a unit root (is non-stationary, \(I(1)\)). Alternative: \(H_1\): \(y_t\) is stationary (\(I(0)\)).

Regression form:

\[\Delta y_t = \alpha + \theta y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^p \gamma_j \Delta y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t\]

The augmentation terms \(\sum_{j=1}^p \gamma_j \Delta y_{t-j}\) absorb any serial correlation in the errors (the Dickey-Fuller test without augmentation assumes i.i.d. errors; the ADF is more general).

Test statistic: \(t_\theta = \hat{\theta} / SE(\hat{\theta})\)

Decision rule: - Reject \(H_0\) (conclude stationary) if \(t_\theta < \text{ADF critical value}\) (e.g. \(-2.89\) at 5% for no trend; \(-3.45\) at 5% with trend). - The ADF critical values are not standard normal — they are more negative (require a larger magnitude to reject) because the distribution shifts under the unit-root null. - Fail to reject \(H_0\) → conclude \(I(1)\); take first differences.

Lag length selection for \(p\): Use AIC/BIC or start with a long lag and drop insignificant ones.

Specification choices: - No constant, no trend (rarely appropriate in economics). - With constant (most common for stationary-around-mean series). - With constant and linear trend (for potentially trend-stationary series).

docs.title: 7. Solution: First Differencing
docs.text:
If a series is \(I(1)\), first-differencing produces a stationary \(I(0)\) series:

\[\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\]

Examples: - \(\ln(\text{GDP}_t)\) is \(I(1)\) → \(\Delta \ln(\text{GDP}_t) \approx g_t\) (GDP growth rate) is \(I(0)\). - \(\ln(\text{CPI}_t)\) is \(I(1)\) → \(\Delta \ln(\text{CPI}_t) \approx \pi_t\) (inflation rate) is \(I(0)\). - Nominal interest rate \(r_t\) is often \(I(1)\) → \(\Delta r_t\) is \(I(0)\).

Trade-off of differencing: You lose information about long-run levels. If you suspect a long-run cointegrating relationship between two \(I(1)\) series, first-differencing discards that relationship — you should instead use a vector error correction model (VECM) (advanced topic).

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Is Australian GDP stationary? Levels vs. growth rates.

Setup. Consider quarterly Australian real GDP (\(Y_t\)) and the quarterly GDP growth rate (\(g_t = 100 \times \Delta \ln Y_t\)), 1960Q1–2023Q4 (\(T = 256\)).

Step 1. Visual inspection.

  • \(Y_t\) (level): trends steadily upward from ~$100bn to ~$600bn (2015 AUD). Clearly non-constant mean.
  • \(g_t\) (growth rate): fluctuates around approximately 0.8% per quarter with no obvious trend. Plausible stationarity.

Step 2. ADF test — GDP level (\(Y_t\)).

Specification: with constant and linear trend (because \(Y_t\) trends upward).

\[\Delta Y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \theta Y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^4 \gamma_j \Delta Y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t\]

Suppose \(t_\theta = -1.85\). ADF 5% critical value (with trend) = \(-3.45\).

Since \(-1.85 > -3.45\): fail to reject \(H_0\). Conclude \(Y_t\) has a unit root — it is \(I(1)\).

Step 3. ADF test — GDP growth rate (\(g_t\)).

Specification: with constant only (growth rate fluctuates around a positive mean).

\[\Delta g_t = \alpha + \theta g_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^4 \gamma_j \Delta g_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t\]

Suppose \(t_\theta = -5.42\). ADF 5% critical value (with constant) = \(-2.89\).

Since \(-5.42 < -2.89\): reject \(H_0\). Conclude \(g_t\) is stationary — it is \(I(0)\).

Step 4. Conclusion and implication.

Series ADF stat 5% CV Decision Order \(Y_t\) (level) −1.85 −3.45 Fail to reject \(H_0\) \(I(1)\) \(g_t\) (growth) −5.42 −2.89 Reject \(H_0\) \(I(0)\)

Implication: Regressions using GDP levels are at risk of spurious regression unless the other variable is also \(I(1)\) and the two series are cointegrated. Regressions using GDP growth rates are valid under standard OLS asymptotics (given stationarity).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Detrending (removing a linear time trend) removes all non-stationarity."

This is false. Detrending (subtracting \(\hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta} t\)) only works if the series is trend-stationary — i.e. non-stationary only because of a deterministic trend, with stationary errors.

If the series has a stochastic trend (unit root), detrending does not produce a stationary series. The detrended series will still have a variance that grows over time (because the unit-root shocks accumulate even around a linear trend). You must first-difference, not detrend.

How to tell which applies: Use the ADF test. Include a time trend in the ADF regression. If you reject the unit-root null, the series is trend-stationary (detrend). If you fail to reject, it has a unit root (first-difference).

Practical cost of the wrong remedy: - First-differencing a trend-stationary series: over-differencing → introduces unnecessary moving-average structure in errors. - Detrending a unit-root series: fails to achieve stationarity → spurious regression, invalid inference.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Stationarity check. Consider three time series:
  2. \(A_t\): Australian CPI level (1990–2023, monthly).
  3. \(B_t\): Australian CPI inflation rate (monthly change in log CPI).
  4. \(C_t\): 10-year government bond yield (%).

(a) For each series, state whether you would expect it to be stationary or non-stationary, and why. (b) For any non-stationary series, suggest the appropriate transformation to induce stationarity. (c) What specification (no trend, constant only, constant + trend) would you use in the ADF test for each series? Justify.

  1. ADF test interpretation. A researcher tests whether the monthly Australian unemployment rate (\(U_t\)) is stationary using an ADF test with constant and no trend. She finds \(t_\theta = -2.31\) and the 5% ADF critical value is \(-2.89\). (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses of the ADF test. (b) What is the conclusion at the 5% level? (c) What should she do before running a regression of \(U_t\) on other economic variables? Give two specific steps.

  2. Random walk properties. A random walk is defined by \(y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t\), \(e_t \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, 4)\), \(y_0 = 0\). (a) Compute \(\text{Var}(y_{25})\). (b) Explain why this series is not covariance stationary. (c) Show that \(\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\) is stationary. What are its mean and variance? (d) Explain in words what it means for shocks to be "permanent" in a random walk, vs "transitory" in a stationary AR(1).
