docs.title: Lesson M09.L01: OLS and Serial Correlation
docs.text: Field Detail Module M09 — Serial Correlation and Time Series Inference Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Understand why OLS remains consistent under contemporaneous exogeneity but produces invalid standard errors when errors are serially correlated; quantify the direction of the bias in OLS SEs under AR(1) errors Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 12.1

docs.title: Time Series Assumptions: TS.1′–TS.5′
docs.text:
In cross-section, OLS requires strict exogeneity (MLR.4): \(E(u_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n) = 0\). In time series, strict exogeneity is often implausible — it rules out lagged dependent variables and feedback from \(y\) to future \(x\). The relaxed assumptions TS.1′–TS.5′ replace strict with contemporaneous exogeneity:

Assumption Statement TS.1′ Linearity in parameters (same as before) TS.2′ No perfect collinearity among regressors TS.3′ Contemporaneous exogeneity: \(E(u_t \mid \mathbf{x}_t) = 0\) — the error is mean-zero given current regressors only TS.4′ Homoskedasticity: \(\text{Var}(u_t \mid \mathbf{x}_t) = \sigma^2\) TS.5′ No serial correlation: \(\text{Cov}(u_t, u_s \mid \mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{x}_s) = 0\) for \(t \neq s\)

Under TS.1′–TS.3′ alone, OLS is consistent for \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Under TS.1′–TS.5′, OLS is BLUE and standard \(t\)- and \(F\)-statistics are valid.

Key distinction: - Strict exogeneity → OLS unbiased (stronger, harder to satisfy) - Contemporaneous exogeneity → OLS consistent (weaker, sufficient for large-sample validity if TS.5′ also holds)

docs.title: What Happens When TS.5′ Fails?
docs.text:
When \(\text{Cov}(u_t, u_s) \neq 0\), serial correlation is present. Under TS.1′–TS.3′ (contemporaneous exogeneity), OLS is still consistent — the coefficient estimates converge to the true \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) as \(n \to \infty\). But the OLS standard errors are wrong because their derivation assumes TS.5′.

Serial correlation does NOT bias OLS estimates (under contemporaneous exogeneity). It only invalidates inference.

docs.title: AR(1) Error Process
docs.text:
The simplest and most common serial correlation structure is the first-order autoregressive process:

\[u_t = \rho\, u_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, \sigma_e^2), \quad |\rho| < 1\]
  • \(\rho\) is the autocorrelation coefficient of the errors
  • \(e_t\) is a white-noise innovation — uncorrelated with everything up to period \(t-1\)
  • Stationarity requires \(|\rho| < 1\)

The variance and autocovariances of \(u_t\) under AR(1):

\[\text{Var}(u_t) = \frac{\sigma_e^2}{1 - \rho^2}, \qquad \text{Cov}(u_t, u_{t-s}) = \rho^s \cdot \frac{\sigma_e^2}{1 - \rho^2}\]

The autocorrelations decay geometrically:

\[\text{Corr}(u_t, u_{t-s}) = \rho^s\]

docs.title: Effect of Serial Correlation on OLS Variance
docs.text:
Consider a simple time-series regression \(y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + u_t\) with AR(1) errors. The true asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}}\) is larger than the standard OLS formula assumes.

Under positive serial correlation (\(\rho > 0\)):

\[\text{True Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}}) > \text{Computed Var}_{\text{OLS}}(\hat{\beta}_1)\]

Intuition: Positively correlated errors mean consecutive observations carry less independent information than \(n\) i.i.d. draws. The "effective sample size" is smaller than \(n\), but the standard OLS SE formula pretends it equals \(n\) — so it understates the true variance.

Consequences of understated SEs when \(\rho > 0\):

Statistic Effect Standard errors Too small \(t\)-statistics Too large (inflated) Confidence intervals Too narrow Hypothesis tests Over-reject \(H_0\) — spurious significance

docs.title: Why Positive Serial Correlation is Common in Economics
docs.text:
Economic time series exhibit persistence for structural reasons:

  • Technology shocks take time to diffuse through the economy
  • Policy changes (monetary, fiscal) have lagged multiplier effects
  • Demand shocks (oil prices, consumer confidence) propagate through supply chains
  • Habit formation in consumption: \(c_t\) depends on \(c_{t-1}\)

Positive \(\rho\) is the rule rather than the exception in macro time series.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: Consider a monthly model of consumer spending on income:

\[\text{cons}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{income}_t + u_t\]

Suppose the true error process is AR(1) with \(\rho = 0.6\), \(\sigma_e^2 = 1\), \(n = 120\), and \(\text{Var}(x) = 4\).

Step 1: True error variance

\[\text{Var}(u_t) = \frac{\sigma_e^2}{1-\rho^2} = \frac{1}{1-0.36} = \frac{1}{0.64} = 1.5625\]

Step 2: OLS-computed variance of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (incorrectly assuming i.i.d. errors)

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}_{\text{OLS}}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sum(x_t - \bar{x})^2} \approx \frac{1.5625}{n \cdot \text{Var}(x)} = \frac{1.5625}{120 \times 4} = 0.003255\] \[\widehat{\text{SE}}_{\text{OLS}}(\hat{\beta}_1) \approx 0.057\]

Step 3: True asymptotic variance (accounting for AR(1) correlation)

The true variance involves a correction factor. For a simple illustration, the ratio of true to OLS variance under AR(1) is approximately:

\[\frac{\text{True Var}}{\text{OLS Var}} \approx 1 + 2\rho \cdot r_x\]

where \(r_x = \text{Corr}(x_t, x_{t-1})\). If \(r_x = 0.5\) (income is also persistent):

\[\text{Inflation factor} \approx 1 + 2(0.6)(0.5) = 1.6\] \[\text{True SE} \approx 0.057 \times \sqrt{1.6} = 0.057 \times 1.265 \approx 0.072\]

Step 4: Interpret

The OLS standard error (0.057) is 21% smaller than the true standard error (0.072). If the true \(t\)-statistic were \(0.072/\text{s.e.} = 1.8\), the OLS procedure would report \(t = 0.057^{-1} \times \hat{\beta}_1\) and classify it as significant at 5% when it should not be. This is the mechanism of spurious significance due to serial correlation.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Serial correlation biases OLS coefficient estimates."

This is false under contemporaneous exogeneity. If \(E(u_t \mid \mathbf{x}_t) = 0\) (TS.3′), OLS is consistent regardless of serial correlation in \(u_t\). The coefficients converge to the true \(\beta\) in large samples. The only problem is that the OLS standard errors are computed under the false assumption that errors are uncorrelated — so inference (t-tests, confidence intervals, F-tests) is invalid.

The correct statement: Serial correlation leaves OLS point estimates consistent but renders inference unreliable. The fix is corrected standard errors (HAC) or GLS — not a new estimation strategy to unbias \(\hat{\beta}\).

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. A researcher estimates a quarterly GDP growth regression and finds \(\hat{\rho} = 0.7\) from the residuals. The OLS \(t\)-statistic on the lagged policy variable is 2.4. Should the researcher conclude the policy variable is significant at the 5% level? Explain your reasoning in terms of what \(\hat{\rho} = 0.7\) implies for the OLS SE.

  2. Under AR(1) errors with \(\rho = -0.4\) (negative serial correlation), in which direction are OLS standard errors biased — understated or overstated? What does this imply for Type I and Type II errors in hypothesis testing?

  3. Consider the regression \(\log(\text{wage}_t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{edu}_t + u_t\) estimated on annual panel data. Explain why contemporaneous exogeneity (TS.3′) is a more defensible assumption than strict exogeneity for this model. Does contemporaneous exogeneity alone guarantee valid OLS \(t\)-statistics?

docs.title: Lesson M09.L02: Testing for Serial Correlation
docs.text: Field Detail Module M09 — Serial Correlation and Time Series Inference Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Apply the Durbin-Watson and Breusch-Godfrey tests for serial correlation; understand the limitations of each and when to prefer BG over DW Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 12.2

docs.title: 1. The Durbin-Watson Test
docs.text:
The Durbin-Watson (DW) statistic is the classical test for first-order serial correlation in OLS residuals:

\[\text{DW} = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{n}(\hat{u}_t - \hat{u}_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}\hat{u}_t^2}\]

Relationship to the sample autocorrelation \(\hat{\rho}\):

Expanding the numerator and simplifying:

\[\text{DW} \approx 2(1 - \hat{\rho})\]

where \(\hat{\rho} = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^n \hat{u}_t \hat{u}_{t-1}}{\sum_{t=1}^n \hat{u}_t^2}\) is the first-order sample autocorrelation of the residuals.

Interpretation:

DW value \(\hat{\rho}\) implied Conclusion \(\approx 2\) \(\approx 0\) No serial correlation \(< 2\) (e.g., 0.8) \(> 0\) Positive serial correlation \(> 2\) (e.g., 3.2) \(< 0\) Negative serial correlation \(\approx 0\) \(\approx 1\) Strong positive SC \(\approx 4\) \(\approx -1\) Strong negative SC

Critical values: The DW test compares the computed statistic against lower (\(d_L\)) and upper (\(d_U\)) bounds from the DW table (which depend on \(n\), \(k\), and significance level):

\[\begin{cases} \text{Reject } H_0 \text{ (pos. SC)} & \text{if } \text{DW} < d_L \\ \text{Inconclusive} & \text{if } d_L \leq \text{DW} \leq d_U \\ \text{Fail to reject } H_0 & \text{if } \text{DW} > d_U \end{cases}\]

docs.title: Limitations of the DW Test
docs.text:
1. Strict exogeneity required: DW is only valid when no lagged dependent variables appear as regressors. If \(y_{t-1} \in \mathbf{x}_t\), the DW statistic is biased toward 2 (under-rejects).

  2. Inconclusive region: There is a range \([d_L, d_U]\) where the test gives no answer. This is the most frustrating feature for practitioners.

  3. Only tests AR(1): DW is not designed to detect higher-order serial correlation, e.g., AR(2) or seasonal patterns.

  4. Doesn't test for negative SC by default: Most tables are set up for positive SC; negative SC test requires comparing \((4 - \text{DW})\) to the same critical values.

docs.title: 2. The Breusch-Godfrey Test
docs.text:
The Breusch-Godfrey (BG) LM test addresses all three DW limitations. It: - Allows lagged dependent variables in the regression - Tests for serial correlation up to any pre-specified order \(p\) - Has a clean \(\chi^2\) distribution under \(H_0\) (no inconclusive region)

Hypotheses:

\[H_0: \rho_1 = \rho_2 = \cdots = \rho_p = 0 \quad \text{(no serial correlation up to order } p\text{)}$$ $$H_1: \text{at least one } \rho_j \neq 0\]

Steps for the BG Test:

Step 1: Estimate the original model by OLS and save the residuals \(\hat{u}_t\):

\[y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1t} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{kt} + u_t \quad \Rightarrow \quad \hat{u}_t = y_t - \hat{y}_t\]

Step 2: Run the auxiliary regression: regress \(\hat{u}_t\) on the original regressors and \(p\) lags of the residuals:

\[\hat{u}_t = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_{1t} + \cdots + \delta_k x_{kt} + \gamma_1 \hat{u}_{t-1} + \gamma_2 \hat{u}_{t-2} + \cdots + \gamma_p \hat{u}_{t-p} + \text{error}\]

The regressors \(\mathbf{x}_t\) are included to partial out the effect of the design matrix.

Step 3: Compute the LM statistic:

\[\text{LM} = n \cdot R^2_{\text{aux}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_p \quad \text{under } H_0\]

where \(R^2_{\text{aux}}\) is from the auxiliary regression and \(n\) is the usable sample size.

Step 4: Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\) if \(\text{LM} > \chi^2_{p,\alpha}\).

Key advantage: The BG test only requires contemporaneous exogeneity (TS.3′) — it is valid even with \(y_{t-1}\) in the model.

docs.title: Comparison: DW vs BG
docs.text:
Feature Durbin-Watson Breusch-Godfrey Requires strict exogeneity Yes No (contemporaneous sufficient) Valid with \(y_{t-1}\) as regressor No Yes Tests higher-order SC No (AR(1) only) Yes (up to order \(p\)) Inconclusive region Yes No Null distribution Non-standard (DW tables) \(\chi^2_p\) (simple) Sample requirement Moderate Larger samples preferred

Bottom line: In most applied work, prefer the BG test. DW is still reported in many software outputs but should not be your primary diagnostic when lagged \(y\) is present.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Data: Annual data on retail sales (in $bn) regressed on GDP and a trend, \(n = 80\) observations.

\[\text{sales}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{GDP}_t + \beta_2 t + u_t\]

After OLS estimation, the researcher computes:

  • \(\text{DW} = 1.12\)
  • First-order residual autocorrelation: \(\hat{\rho}_1 = (2 - 1.12)/2 = 0.44\)

Step 1: DW check

From DW tables with \(n=80\), \(k=2\), \(\alpha = 5\%\): \(d_L = 1.59\), \(d_U = 1.73\).

Since \(\text{DW} = 1.12 < d_L = 1.59\) → reject \(H_0\), evidence of positive AR(1) serial correlation.

Step 2: BG test (order \(p = 2\))

Run auxiliary regression:

\[\hat{u}_t = \delta_0 + \delta_1 \text{GDP}_t + \delta_2 t + \gamma_1 \hat{u}_{t-1} + \gamma_2 \hat{u}_{t-2} + \text{error}\]

Results: \(R^2_{\text{aux}} = 0.21\), effective \(n = 78\) (lost 2 observations for lags).

\[\text{LM} = 78 \times 0.21 = 16.38\]

Critical value: \(\chi^2_{2, 0.05} = 5.99\).

Since \(16.38 > 5.99\) → reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level. There is significant serial correlation up to order 2.

Step 3: Interpret and compare

Both tests reject \(H_0\). However, the BG test additionally tells us that the serial correlation extends beyond AR(1) (the AR(2) lag is also significant). DW would have missed this nuance.

Software note (Stata): estat bgodfrey, lags(2) after regress; in Python: statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.acorr_breusch_godfrey(result, nlags=2).

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"DW ≈ 2 guarantees there is no serial correlation."

This is false on two counts:

  1. DW ≈ 2 means no evidence of AR(1) serial correlation — it says nothing about higher-order patterns. An AR(2) process with \(\rho_1 = 0\) and \(\rho_2 = 0.5\) can produce DW ≈ 2 while BG(p=2) clearly rejects.

  2. Even for AR(1), the DW has an inconclusive region. DW in \([d_L, d_U]\) means the test is uninformative, not that \(H_0\) is true.

Always use BG as the primary test, and choose \(p\) based on the data frequency (e.g., \(p = 4\) for quarterly data, \(p = 12\) for monthly) or economic reasoning.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. An analyst regresses log(employment) on log(output) and one lag of log(employment), obtaining DW = 1.85. They conclude "no serial correlation." Explain why this conclusion is unreliable. What test should they use instead?

  2. You run a BG test with \(p = 4\) on monthly data and compute \(\text{LM} = 9.3\). At the 5% level, do you reject \(H_0\)? (Recall \(\chi^2_{4,0.05} = 9.49\).) Interpret the result carefully — what can and cannot you conclude?

  3. A time-series regression produces \(\hat{\rho}_1 = -0.35\) from OLS residuals. Compute the approximate DW statistic. What direction of serial correlation does this suggest, and is it more or less common in macroeconomic data than positive serial correlation?

  • Godfrey, L.G. (1978), "Testing Against General Autoregressive and Moving Average Error Models," Econometrica

docs.title: Lesson M09.L03: Correcting for Serial Correlation
docs.text: Field Detail Module M09 — Serial Correlation and Time Series Inference Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Apply HAC standard errors and feasible GLS to obtain valid inference when serial correlation is present; understand when each approach is appropriate and what each changes Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 12.3

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Once serial correlation is detected, two broad remedies exist:

  1. Keep OLS, fix the standard errors → HAC (Newey-West)
  2. Change the estimator → GLS / feasible GLS (Cochrane-Orcutt, Prais-Winsten)

docs.title: 1. HAC (Newey-West) Standard Errors
docs.text:
HAC stands for Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent. It corrects OLS standard errors for both heteroskedasticity and serial correlation simultaneously, analogous to White (robust) standard errors in cross-section settings.

Key property: HAC SEs adjust the variance-covariance matrix of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\text{OLS}}\) without changing the point estimates.

The HAC estimator replaces the usual \(\hat{\sigma}^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) with a sandwich estimator:

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}_{\text{HAC}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \hat{\mathbf{S}} (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{S}}\) is the Newey-West long-run variance estimator that uses a kernel to weight autocovariances of the score:

\[\hat{S} = \hat{\Gamma}_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{L} w_j \left(\hat{\Gamma}_j + \hat{\Gamma}_j'\right)\]

with \(\hat{\Gamma}_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=j+1}^{n} \hat{u}_t \hat{u}_{t-j} \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{x}_{t-j}'\) and Bartlett kernel weights \(w_j = 1 - j/(L+1)\).

Bandwidth choice: The lag truncation \(L\) is typically chosen as \(L = \lfloor 4(n/100)^{2/9} \rfloor\) (Newey-West rule of thumb) or \(L = \lfloor 0.75 \cdot n^{1/3} \rfloor\).

Practical recommendation: Use HAC SEs as the default for any time-series regression. They are valid under very general conditions — you don't need to know the exact form of the serial correlation.

docs.title: 2. GLS with AR(1) Errors: Quasi-Differencing
docs.text:
When the error process is known (or assumed) to be AR(1), Generalized Least Squares (GLS) eliminates the serial correlation by transforming the model.

Population model:

\[y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + u_t, \qquad u_t = \rho u_{t-1} + e_t, \quad e_t \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, \sigma_e^2)\]

Quasi-differencing transformation: Subtract \(\rho\) times the lagged equation from the current equation:

\[y_t - \rho y_{t-1} = \beta_0(1-\rho) + \beta_1(x_t - \rho x_{t-1}) + e_t\]

Define the quasi-differenced variables:

\[\tilde{y}_t = y_t - \rho y_{t-1}, \qquad \tilde{x}_t = x_t - \rho x_{t-1}, \qquad \tilde{\beta}_0 = \beta_0(1-\rho)\]

Then the transformed model is:

\[\tilde{y}_t = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \beta_1 \tilde{x}_t + e_t\]

where \(e_t\) is i.i.d. — so OLS on the quasi-differenced model is BLUE (Gauss-Markov applies).

Note on the first observation: Under Prais-Winsten, the first observation is transformed as \(\tilde{y}_1 = \sqrt{1-\rho^2} \cdot y_1\) (preserves it). Under Cochrane-Orcutt, the first observation is dropped.

docs.title: 3. Feasible GLS (FGLS)
docs.text:
In practice \(\rho\) is unknown and must be estimated. The Feasible GLS (or FGLS) procedure:

Step 1: Estimate the original model by OLS, obtain residuals \(\hat{u}_t\).

Step 2: Estimate \(\rho\) by regressing \(\hat{u}_t\) on \(\hat{u}_{t-1}\) (without intercept):

\[\hat{\rho} = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{n} \hat{u}_t \hat{u}_{t-1}}{\sum_{t=1}^{n-1} \hat{u}_t^2}\]

Step 3: Form quasi-differenced variables using \(\hat{\rho}\):

\[\tilde{y}_t = y_t - \hat{\rho}\, y_{t-1}, \qquad \tilde{x}_t = x_t - \hat{\rho}\, x_{t-1}\]

Step 4: Regress \(\tilde{y}_t\) on \(\tilde{x}_t\) by OLS — these are the Cochrane-Orcutt estimates.

Iterative Cochrane-Orcutt repeats Steps 2–4 until \(\hat{\rho}\) converges.

docs.title: 4. First Differencing as a Special Case
docs.text:
If \(\rho \approx 1\) (the process is near a unit root), quasi-differencing with \(\hat{\rho} \approx 1\) becomes first differencing:

\[\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} = \beta_1 \Delta x_t + \Delta u_t\]

First differencing removes any I(1) non-stationarity and eliminates AR(1) serial correlation when \(\rho = 1\). It is common practice for trending macro series (GDP, price levels, employment). The cost: the constant \(\beta_0\) is absorbed, and you lose one observation.

docs.title: Comparing HAC vs GLS
docs.text: Feature HAC SEs (OLS + corrected SEs) FGLS (Cochrane-Orcutt) Point estimates change? No — only SEs change Yes — both \(\hat{\beta}\) and SEs change Requires knowing error structure? No Yes (assumes AR(1)) Efficiency Less efficient if AR(1) is correct More efficient under correct specification Robustness More robust to mis-specification Sensitive to wrong \(\rho\) or wrong order Practical recommendation Default choice Use only with strong AR(1) evidence

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: Annual data on interest rates and inflation, \(n = 50\) years.

\[\text{rate}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{inflation}_t + u_t\]

OLS estimates (with standard SEs):

Coeff Std Err \(t\) Intercept 1.42 0.38 3.74 inflation 0.81 0.12 6.75

Diagnostics: BG test (p=1) gives LM = 8.3 > \(\chi^2_{1,0.05} = 3.84\) → serial correlation confirmed. \(\hat{\rho} = 0.52\).

Step 1: Apply Cochrane-Orcutt

Quasi-differenced variables (\(t = 2, \ldots, 50\)):

\[\widetilde{\text{rate}}_t = \text{rate}_t - 0.52\,\text{rate}_{t-1}, \quad \widetilde{\text{infl}}_t = \text{infl}_t - 0.52\,\text{infl}_{t-1}\]

Step 2: OLS on transformed model — FGLS estimates:

Coeff Std Err \(t\) \(\tilde{\beta}_0\) (intercept) 0.68 0.24 2.83 inflation 0.74 0.16 4.63

Step 3: OLS with HAC SEs (Newey-West, \(L = 3\)):

Coeff Std Err (HAC) \(t\) Intercept 1.42 0.52 2.73 inflation 0.81 0.19 4.26

Comparison:

Method \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (inflation) SE \(t\)-stat OLS (naive) 0.81 0.12 6.75 OLS + HAC 0.81 0.19 4.26 FGLS (CO) 0.74 0.16 4.63

Conclusions: - HAC keeps the OLS coefficient (0.81) but widens the SE from 0.12 to 0.19 — the \(t\)-stat falls from 6.75 to 4.26. Still significant but less dramatically so. - FGLS changes the coefficient estimate (0.81 → 0.74) and widens the SE. Different interpretation: the estimated effect of inflation on interest rates is smaller under FGLS. - Naive OLS \(t = 6.75\) is inflated — the true evidence is weaker.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Correcting for serial correlation changes the coefficient estimates."

This is only partially true — it depends on the method:

  • HAC SEs: The OLS point estimates are unchanged. Only the standard errors (and hence \(t\)-stats and confidence intervals) change. This is the most common and recommended correction.
  • GLS/FGLS (Cochrane-Orcutt): Both the coefficient estimates and the standard errors change, because the estimator itself changes — it minimises a different (weighted) objective function.

The key distinction: HAC is a correction to inference, not estimation. GLS is a correction to both.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. A researcher estimates a wage-inflation model and finds \(\hat{\rho} = 0.65\) from OLS residuals. They apply Cochrane-Orcutt. After transformation, the coefficient on inflation changes from 0.52 to 0.39 and the standard error increases from 0.08 to 0.13. Compute the \(t\)-statistic for the OLS and FGLS estimates. Which should the researcher report, and why?

  2. For a monthly financial time series with \(n = 240\), compute the Newey-West bandwidth \(L\) using the rule \(L = \lfloor 4(n/100)^{2/9} \rfloor\). How does this bandwidth affect the bias-variance tradeoff in the HAC estimator?

  3. A researcher has annual GDP data and suspects the error process may be AR(1) with \(\rho\) close to 1. They apply Cochrane-Orcutt with \(\hat{\rho} = 0.97\). Explain why first differencing might be more appropriate than Cochrane-Orcutt in this case, and what additional diagnostic (unit root test) they should run first.

docs.title: Lesson M10.L01: Endogeneity and Causality
docs.text: Field Detail Module M10 — Instrumental Variables Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Identify the three sources of endogeneity; derive the probability limit of OLS under endogeneity; explain why increasing sample size cannot fix the problem Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 15 (introduction)

docs.title: Why Causality Matters
docs.text: The goal of most applied econometrics is not prediction but causal inference: what is the effect of a policy, treatment, or variable \(x\) on an outcome \(y\)? OLS recovers causal effects only under MLR.4 — zero conditional mean: \(E(u \mid \mathbf{x}) = 0\). When this fails, we have endogeneity, and OLS does not estimate causal parameters even in very large samples.

docs.title: Definition: Endogeneity
docs.text:
A regressor \(x_j\) is endogenous if:

\[\text{Cov}(x_j, u) \neq 0\]

This violates MLR.4 and means OLS is biased and inconsistent — the estimates do not converge to the true causal parameter even as \(n \to \infty\).

docs.title: Source 1: Omitted Variables
docs.text:
The true model is:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 q + u\]

but \(q\) is unobserved and omitted. The estimated model is:

\[y = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x + v, \qquad v = \beta_2 q + u\]

If \(\text{Cov}(x, q) \neq 0\), then \(\text{Cov}(x, v) \neq 0\) → \(x\) is endogenous. The omitted variable bias formula (from M03) shows:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\alpha}_1 = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \frac{\text{Cov}(x,q)}{\text{Var}(x)}\]

Classic example: Wage regressed on education alone. Ability (\(q\)) is omitted. Since ability is positively correlated with education and positively affects wages, the OLS coefficient on education is upward biased.

docs.title: Source 2: Simultaneity (Reverse Causality)
docs.text:
Both \(y\) and \(x\) are jointly determined by a system of equations. The causal arrow runs in both directions:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u \quad \text{(demand equation)}$$ $$x = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 y + v \quad \text{(supply equation)}\]

Classic example: Price (\(x\)) and quantity (\(y\)) in a market. Price affects demand (quantity), but quantity demanded also affects price through market clearing. Since \(x\) is partly determined by \(y\), \(\text{Cov}(x, u) \neq 0\) — OLS on either equation gives biased estimates of structural parameters.

Another example: Returns to schooling. Do smarter people go to school longer, or does school make people smarter? Both directions may be present, creating a simultaneous relationship between education and wages.

docs.title: Source 3: Measurement Error in \(x\)
docs.text:
Suppose the true model has the true regressor \(x^*\) but we observe a mismeasured \(x = x^* + \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon\) is classical measurement error (\(\text{Cov}(\epsilon, x^*) = 0\), \(\text{Cov}(\epsilon, u) = 0\)).

The estimated model uses \(x\) instead of \(x^*\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + (u - \beta_1 \epsilon)\]

The composite error is \((u - \beta_1 \epsilon)\), which is correlated with \(x = x^* + \epsilon\) through \(\epsilon\). This creates attenuation bias:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{\text{Var}(x^*)}{\text{Var}(x^*) + \text{Var}(\epsilon)} = \beta_1 \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\text{Var}(\epsilon)}{\text{Var}(x)}\right) < \beta_1 \text{ (if } \beta_1 > 0\text{)}\]

OLS is attenuated toward zero — underestimates the true effect. This is the errors-in-variables problem.

docs.title: Probability Limit of OLS Under Endogeneity
docs.text:
For the simple regression \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\), the probability limit of \(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}}\) is:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}} = \beta_1 + \frac{\text{Cov}(x, u)}{\text{Var}(x)}\]

The bias is:

\[\text{Inconsistency} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, u)}{\text{Var}(x)}\]

Key properties:

  • If \(\text{Cov}(x,u) > 0\): OLS overestimates \(\beta_1\) (upward inconsistency)
  • If \(\text{Cov}(x,u) < 0\): OLS underestimates \(\beta_1\) (downward inconsistency)
  • If \(\text{Cov}(x,u) = 0\): OLS is consistent (even if \(u\) is not zero-mean, as long as the intercept absorbs it)

docs.title: Classic Examples of Endogeneity
docs.text: Model Endogenous variable Source Direction of OLS bias Wage = f(education) education Ability in \(u\) (omitted) Upward Test scores = f(class size) class size School resources (omitted); richer schools have smaller classes AND better outcomes Downward (class size coefficient is biased toward zero or negative) Crime = f(police) police More crime → more police (simultaneity) Upward (more police appear to increase crime) Earnings = f(health) health Income enables better health (simultaneity) Upward Sales = f(price) price Demand and supply simultaneous Ambiguous

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Estimate the effect of class size on student test scores.

\[\text{score}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{class\_size}_t + u_t\]

Why is class size endogenous?

Wealthy school districts tend to: 1. Have smaller class sizes (more per-pupil spending) 2. Have students from higher-income families → higher scores

The omitted variable "school district wealth" is positively correlated with scores and negatively correlated with class size (\(\text{Cov}(\text{class\_size}, u) < 0\)). The bias:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \frac{\text{Cov}(\text{class\_size}, u)}{\text{Var}(\text{class\_size})} = \beta_1 + \text{negative number}\]

OLS will overstate the negative effect of class size (i.e., make smaller classes look more beneficial than they truly are). This is a case of negative bias when the true \(\beta_1 < 0\).

Magnitude illustration:

Suppose the true causal effect of a 1-student increase in class size on scores is \(\beta_1 = -0.5\) points. If \(\text{Cov}(\text{class\_size}, u)/\text{Var}(\text{class\_size}) = -0.8\):

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.5 + (-0.8) = -1.3\]

OLS reports \(-1.3\) — class size appears 2.6× more harmful than it truly is. A policy maker who reduces class size by 10 students would predict a 13-point gain, but the true causal gain is only 5 points.

Implication: Any study that doesn't account for school wealth/resources in the error term will give misleading policy guidance.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Using a large sample fixes endogeneity — the law of large numbers takes care of it."

This is false. Consistency requires \(\text{Cov}(x, u) = 0\), not just a large \(n\). If \(\text{Cov}(x, u) = c \neq 0\), the OLS estimator converges as \(n \to \infty\) to:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \frac{c}{\text{Var}(x)} \neq \beta_1\]

A larger sample narrows the confidence interval around a wrong estimate. With \(n = 1{,}000{,}000\) and endogeneity, you get a very precise, very wrong answer. The law of large numbers ensures convergence — it just converges to the wrong limit.

Analogy: A scale that reads 2 kg too heavy is biased. Weighing yourself 10,000 times averages to "2 kg too heavy" — you don't get the correct weight, you just confirm the wrong answer with great precision.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. A researcher estimates returns to schooling using OLS with \(n = 50{,}000\) observations, obtaining \(\hat{\beta} = 0.12\) (12% wage increase per year of school). They argue that with such a large sample, endogeneity concerns are irrelevant. Critique this argument using the probability limit formula.

  2. Consider the model \(\text{crime}_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{police}_{it} + u_{it}\) estimated by OLS. Explain the simultaneity problem. Is the expected OLS bias positive or negative relative to the true effect of police on crime? (Hint: what does city government do when crime rises?)

  3. A firm measures employee productivity \(y\) using self-reported hours worked \(x\), which suffers from classical measurement error. If the true elasticity is \(\beta_1 = 0.8\) and the reliability ratio \(\text{Var}(x^*)/\text{Var}(x) = 0.7\), compute the probability limit of the OLS estimator. Is this attenuation bias economically significant?

docs.text:

  • Angrist, J.D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch 4 — Instrumental Variables
  • Card, D. (1999), "The Causal Effect of Education on Earnings," Handbook of Labor Economics
  • Angrist, J.D. & Krueger, A.B. (1991), "Does Compulsory School Attendance Affect Schooling and Earnings?" QJE

docs.title: Lesson M10.L02: Instrumental Variable Estimation
docs.text: Field Detail Module M10 — Instrumental Variables Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective State and verify the two IV conditions; derive the IV estimator; compute IV estimates from summary statistics; understand the efficiency cost of IV relative to OLS Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 15.1–15.2

docs.title: The IV Strategy
docs.text: When \(\text{Cov}(x, u) \neq 0\), OLS is inconsistent. The instrumental variables (IV) strategy identifies a variable \(z\) — the instrument — that is related to \(x\) but not directly related to \(y\) except through \(x\). This allows us to recover the causal effect \(\beta_1\) by using only the "clean" (exogenous) variation in \(x\) that comes from \(z\).

docs.title: IV Requirements
docs.text: A valid instrument \(z\) must satisfy two conditions:

docs.title: Condition 1: Relevance
docs.text:
\[\text{Cov}(z, x) \neq 0\]

The instrument must be correlated with the endogenous regressor \(x\). Without this, \(z\) carries no information about \(x\) and the IV estimator is undefined (or very poorly behaved).

Testable: Relevance can be tested with a first-stage \(F\)-test (see M10.L04 on weak instruments).

docs.title: Condition 2: Exogeneity (Exclusion Restriction)
docs.text:
\[\text{Cov}(z, u) = 0\]

The instrument affects \(y\) only through \(x\) — not through any other channel. This means \(z\) does not belong in the structural equation as a direct determinant of \(y\).

Not directly testable (in the exactly identified case): This is an assumption that must be justified on theoretical or institutional grounds. It is the central credibility condition for any IV strategy.

Mnemonic: A valid instrument is relevant (talks to \(x\)) and exogenous (doesn't talk to \(u\)).

docs.title: The IV Estimator
docs.text:
For the simple model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\) with instrument \(z\), the IV estimator is:

\[\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, y)}{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, x)} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_i - \bar{z})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_i - \bar{z})(x_i - \bar{x})}\]

Derivation of consistency:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(z, y)}{\text{Cov}(z, x)} = \frac{\text{Cov}(z, \beta_1 x + u)}{\text{Cov}(z, x)} = \beta_1 + \frac{\text{Cov}(z, u)}{\text{Cov}(z, x)}\]

Under exogeneity (\(\text{Cov}(z, u) = 0\)) and relevance (\(\text{Cov}(z, x) \neq 0\)):

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \beta_1 \checkmark\]

Intuition: The IV estimator divides the "reduced form" (effect of \(z\) on \(y\)) by the "first stage" (effect of \(z\) on \(x\)). If \(z\) only affects \(y\) through \(x\), then the ratio recovers the causal effect of \(x\) on \(y\).

docs.title: Connection to OLS
docs.text:
Compare IV and OLS:

\[\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(x, y)}{\widehat{\text{Var}}(x)}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, y)}{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, x)}\]

OLS uses the sample covariance of \(x\) with \(y\) (all variation in \(x\)). IV uses only the variation in \(x\) that is "explained by \(z\)" — discarding the endogenous variation.

docs.title: 1. Card (1993) — Proximity to College
docs.text:
• Structural equation: \(\log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + u\)
  • Endogeneity: Ability is in \(u\), correlated with education
  • Instrument (\(z\)): Whether the individual grew up near a 4-year college
  • Relevance: People near colleges attend more schooling (lower cost of access)
  • Exogeneity: Living near a college doesn't directly affect wages except through education

docs.title: 2. Angrist & Krueger (1991) — Quarter of Birth
docs.text:
• Instrument (\(z\)): Quarter of birth (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4)
  • Relevance: US compulsory schooling laws mean Q1 babies reach school-leaving age earlier → get less education on average
  • Exogeneity: Birth quarter is essentially random with respect to ability/wages (debated)

docs.title: 3. Rainfall as Instrument for Agricultural Income
docs.text:
• Structural equation: \(\text{consumption} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{income} + u\)
  • Instrument: Rainfall (affects agricultural output and hence income in farming communities)
  • Relevance: Rainfall → crop yields → income
  • Exogeneity: Rainfall doesn't directly affect consumption except through income

docs.title: IV vs OLS: Efficiency Trade-off
docs.text:
Property OLS (if exogenous) IV (endogenous \(x\)) Unbiasedness Unbiased Biased in finite samples (consistent) Consistency Consistent Consistent Efficiency BLUE Less efficient (larger SE) SE formula \(\sigma^2 / \text{Var}(x)\) Larger (see below)

Approximate IV variance (large \(n\)):

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}}) \approx \frac{\sigma_u^2}{n \cdot \text{Var}(x) \cdot R^2_{x,z}}\]

where \(R^2_{x,z}\) is the R² from regressing \(x\) on \(z\). Since \(R^2_{x,z} \leq 1\):

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}}) \geq \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}}) = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{n \cdot \text{Var}(x)}\]

The stronger the instrument (higher \(R^2_{x,z}\)), the smaller the efficiency loss. A perfect instrument (\(R^2_{x,z} = 1\)) makes IV as efficient as OLS — but such instruments don't exist in practice. The larger SE of IV is the price of addressing endogeneity.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Estimate the return to schooling in a wage equation.

\[\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ}_i + u_i\]

Instrument: Proximity to college (binary: \(z_i = 1\) if grew up within 25 miles of a 4-year college).

Summary statistics (hypothetical, from \(n = 3{,}010\) observations):

Statistic Value \(\overline{\log(\text{wage})}\) 6.26 \(\overline{\text{educ}}\) 13.17 \(\bar{z}\) 0.68 \(\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, \log(\text{wage}))\) 0.0514 \(\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, \text{educ})\) 0.3851 \(\widehat{\text{Cov}}(\text{educ}, \log(\text{wage}))\) 0.3022 \(\widehat{\text{Var}}(\text{educ})\) 7.513

Step 1: OLS estimate

\[\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(\text{educ}, \log(\text{wage}))}{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\text{educ})} = \frac{0.3022}{7.513} = 0.0402\]

OLS says one extra year of education raises wages by approximately 4.0%.

Step 2: IV estimate

\[\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, \log(\text{wage}))}{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, \text{educ})} = \frac{0.0514}{0.3851} = 0.1335\]

IV says one extra year of education raises wages by approximately 13.4%.

Step 3: Interpret the gap

\(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = 0.134 > \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{OLS}} = 0.040\)

The higher IV estimate is consistent with: (a) ability bias pulling OLS down (if high-ability people go to school and earn more, OLS should be upward biased — but Card found upward IV, suggesting ability bias is not dominant here); OR (b) IV estimates a Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) — the return for "compliers" (those induced into more education by proximity to college) may differ from the average return. This is the LATE interpretation, studied in M10 extension topics.

Step 4: Compare relevance

\(\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z, \text{educ}) = 0.385 > 0\) — people near colleges get significantly more education. Relevance is supported.

Exogeneity — we must argue that proximity to college does not affect wages through any channel other than education (e.g., urban/rural location, peer effects). Card controls for additional covariates to bolster this assumption.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"Any variable that is correlated with \(x\) makes a valid instrument."

Only Condition 1 (relevance) is satisfied. Relevance alone is insufficient — the instrument must also satisfy exogeneity: \(\text{Cov}(z, u) = 0\). If \(z\) has a direct effect on \(y\) or is correlated with omitted variables in \(u\), the IV estimator is also inconsistent:

\[\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \beta_1 + \frac{\text{Cov}(z, u)}{\text{Cov}(z, x)}\]

Even a small violation of exogeneity can cause substantial bias when the instrument is weak (small \(\text{Cov}(z,x)\)). This is why instrument validity is the most contested part of any IV analysis — finding a relevant instrument is easy; finding an exogenous one is hard.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. Card (1993) uses proximity to college as an instrument for education. A critic argues that "people who grow up near colleges live in urban areas, and urban areas have higher wages for reasons unrelated to education." How does this critique threaten the exogeneity condition? How might Card's paper address this?

  2. Using the data in the worked example, verify the IV formula by computing: \((a)\) the reduced-form coefficient \(\hat{\pi}_{\text{RF}} = \widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,y)/\widehat{\text{Var}}(z)\) and \((b)\) the first-stage coefficient \(\hat{\pi}_{\text{FS}} = \widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,x)/\widehat{\text{Var}}(z)\). Confirm that \(\hat{\pi}_{\text{RF}}/\hat{\pi}_{\text{FS}} = \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}}\) (Wald estimator). [Assume \(\widehat{\text{Var}}(z) = 0.218\).]

  3. In the wage–education example, OLS gives \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.040\) and IV gives \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.134\). Under what two scenarios could IV be higher than OLS? (Hint: think about the direction of ability bias and the LATE interpretation.)

docs.title: Further Resources
docs.text:
• Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.), Ch 15.1–15.2
  • Card, D. (1993), "Using Geographic Variation in College Proximity to Estimate the Return to Schooling," NBER Working Paper 4483
  • Angrist, J.D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch 4
  • Imbens, G. & Angrist, J.D. (1994), "Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects," Econometrica

docs.title: Lesson M10.L03: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
docs.text: Field Detail Module M10 — Instrumental Variables Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 35 min Learning Objective Implement 2SLS with multiple instruments; understand over-, under-, and exact-identification; correctly interpret first- and second-stage output; avoid the SEs mistake from naive two-step OLS Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 15.3–15.4

docs.title: Why 2SLS?
docs.text:
The simple IV estimator from M10.L02 handles one endogenous variable with one instrument. In practice, we often have:

  • Multiple instruments for one endogenous variable (over-identified)
  • Multiple endogenous variables requiring multiple instruments
  • Exogenous control variables that must be included in both stages

Two-stage least squares (2SLS) is the general framework that handles all these cases efficiently, combining all instruments optimally.

docs.title: The 2SLS Procedure
docs.text:
Setup: Structural model with one endogenous regressor \(x\), exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\), and instruments \(\mathbf{z}\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \boldsymbol{\beta}_w' \mathbf{w} + u\]

where \(\text{Cov}(x, u) \neq 0\), \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{w}, u) = 0\), \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{z}, u) = 0\).

docs.title: Stage 1: First-Stage Regression
docs.text:
Regress the endogenous variable \(x\) on all instruments \(\mathbf{z}\) and all exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\):

\[x = \pi_0 + \boldsymbol{\pi}_z' \mathbf{z} + \boldsymbol{\pi}_w' \mathbf{w} + v\]

Save the fitted values \(\hat{x}\) from this OLS regression. The fitted values represent the "clean" (exogenous) variation in \(x\) — the part driven by instruments.

Important: Include all exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\) in Stage 1, even though they're already exogenous. Omitting them leads to misspecification.

docs.title: Stage 2: Second-Stage Regression
docs.text:
Regress \(y\) on \(\hat{x}\) (from Stage 1) and the exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\):

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{x} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_w' \mathbf{w} + \text{error}\]

The OLS coefficients from this second regression are the 2SLS estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\text{2SLS}}\).

Intuition: Stage 2 uses only the variation in \(x\) that is explained by the instruments — the part uncorrelated with \(u\). The endogenous variation (correlated with \(u\)) is "projected out" in Stage 1.

docs.title: Equivalence to Simple IV
docs.text:
With one instrument and one endogenous variable, 2SLS = IV.

Stage 1: \(\hat{x} = \hat{\pi}_0 + \hat{\pi}_z z\) Stage 2 coefficient on \(\hat{x}\): \(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{2SLS}} = \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{IV}} = \widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,y)/\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,x)\) ✓

The advantage of 2SLS is that it generalises to multiple instruments by projecting \(x\) onto the instrument subspace optimally.

docs.title: Identification: Under-, Exact-, and Over-Identification
docs.text:
Let: - \(m\) = number of endogenous regressors - \(\ell\) = number of instruments (excluded from structural equation)

Case Condition Implication Under-identified \(\ell < m\) Cannot identify all endogenous coefficients; 2SLS not feasible Exactly identified \(\ell = m\) Unique 2SLS solution; cannot test instrument validity Over-identified \(\ell > m\) Multiple instruments; 2SLS uses them efficiently; can test exogeneity

Over-identification is a gift — it provides testable restrictions (Sargan-Hansen \(J\)-test) on instrument validity, and the extra instruments improve efficiency.

docs.title: The Sargan-Hansen J-Test (Over-Identified Case)
docs.text:
When \(\ell > m\), we can test whether the instruments are jointly exogenous.

\[H_0: \text{all } \ell \text{ instruments are exogenous (i.e., } \text{Cov}(\mathbf{z}, u) = 0\text{)}\]

Steps:

  1. Estimate by 2SLS and save residuals \(\hat{u}_t^{\text{2SLS}}\)
  2. Regress \(\hat{u}_t^{\text{2SLS}}\) on all instruments \(\mathbf{z}\) and exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\)
  3. \(J = n \cdot R^2_{\text{aux}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{\ell - m}\) under \(H_0\)
  4. Reject \(H_0\) if \(J > \chi^2_{\ell-m, \alpha}\)

Limitation: The \(J\)-test requires the model to be over-identified (\(\ell > m\)). In the exactly-identified case (\(\ell = m\)), \(J = 0\) identically — you cannot test instrument validity. This is why finding multiple valid instruments is valuable.

Caution: Failing to reject \(H_0\) does NOT confirm instrument validity — it only says the over-identifying restrictions are not rejected. All instruments could be endogenous if they are endogenous in the same direction.

docs.title: 2SLS Standard Errors
docs.text:
2SLS SEs are always larger than OLS SEs — this is the efficiency cost of using IV.

The asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{2SLS}}\) (simplified for one endogenous variable):

\[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{2SLS}}) \approx \frac{\sigma_u^2}{n \cdot \text{Var}(\hat{x})} = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{n \cdot R^2_{1} \cdot \text{Var}(x)}\]

where \(R^2_1\) is the R² from the first-stage regression. Since \(R^2_1 \leq 1\), \(\text{Var}^{\text{2SLS}} \geq \text{Var}^{\text{OLS}}\).

Use robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) SEs in 2SLS — most software does this by default. Stata: ivregress 2sls ... , robust.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: Estimate the return to education with two instruments.

\[\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ}_i + \beta_2 \text{exper}_i + u_i\]

where exper (work experience) is exogenous. Two instruments: - \(z_1\): proximity to 4-year college (binary) - \(z_2\): proximity to 2-year college (binary)

Since \(m = 1\) (one endogenous variable: education) and \(\ell = 2\) (two instruments), this is over-identified (\(\ell - m = 1\) degree of freedom for J-test).

Stage 1: Regress educ on exper, \(z_1\), \(z_2\):

\[\text{educ}_i = \pi_0 + \pi_1 \text{exper}_i + \pi_2 z_{1i} + \pi_3 z_{2i} + v_i\] Variable \(\hat{\pi}\) SE \(t\) Intercept 14.32 0.58 24.7 exper −0.073 0.018 −4.1 near4yr (\(z_1\)) 0.442 0.107 4.13 near2yr (\(z_2\)) 0.312 0.098 3.18

First-stage F-statistic (joint test of \(\pi_2 = \pi_3 = 0\)): \(F = 12.4 > 10\) → instruments are relevant (not weak).

Stage 2: Regress \(\log(\text{wage})\) on \(\hat{\text{educ}}\), exper:

\[\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{\text{educ}}_i + \beta_2 \text{exper}_i + \text{error}\] Variable \(\hat{\beta}^{\text{2SLS}}\) SE (robust) \(t\) Intercept 3.41 0.72 4.74 educ 0.129 0.047 2.74 exper 0.032 0.011 2.91

Second-stage interpretation: Each additional year of education raises wages by approximately 12.9% (2SLS), compared to an OLS estimate of 4.0%. The 2SLS SE (0.047) is larger than the hypothetical OLS SE, reflecting the efficiency cost.

Sargan-Hansen J-test:

Regress 2SLS residuals on all instruments and controls; \(n \cdot R^2_{\text{aux}} = 2.14\). Critical value \(\chi^2_{1,0.05} = 3.84\).

Since \(2.14 < 3.84\) → fail to reject \(H_0\). Over-identifying restriction not rejected — instruments appear jointly exogenous.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"2SLS is just running two separate OLS regressions and plugging in predicted values from the first — you can do it manually in two steps."

This gives wrong standard errors. If you manually run Stage 2 with \(\hat{x}\) as a regressor, the Stage 2 residuals are computed as:

\[\hat{e}_i = y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 \hat{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}}_w' \mathbf{w}_i\]

These residuals are based on \(\hat{x}\), not \(x\). The Stage 2 OLS formula uses \(\hat{e}\) to estimate \(\sigma^2\), but \(\hat{e}\) is not the correct structural residual \(u = y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x - \boldsymbol{\beta}_w' \mathbf{w}\). The proper 2SLS variance formula corrects for this substitution — manual two-step OLS does not. Always use a proper 2SLS command (ivregress 2sls in Stata, IV2SLS in statsmodels or linearmodels.IV2SLS in Python).

The coefficient estimates from manual two-step OLS and proper 2SLS are identical; only the SEs differ.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. A researcher has two endogenous variables (education and experience) and three instruments (proximity to college, quarter of birth, and state compulsory schooling laws). Is the model under-, exactly-, or over-identified? How many degrees of freedom does the Sargan-Hansen J-test have?

  2. In the worked example, the Sargan-Hansen J-statistic is 2.14. Interpret this result carefully: does it confirm that both instruments are valid? If one instrument were endogenous but both instruments were endogenous in the same direction, would the test detect this?

  3. Explain why 2SLS standard errors are always at least as large as OLS standard errors, using the formula \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{2SLS}}) \approx \sigma_u^2 / (n \cdot R^2_1 \cdot \text{Var}(x))\). Under what limiting condition would 2SLS be equally efficient as OLS, and why can that condition never hold in practice for a truly endogenous regressor?

docs.title: Lesson M10.L04: Weak Instruments
docs.text: Field Detail Module M10 — Instrumental Variables Level Graduate (ECMT5001 S1 2027) Duration 30–35 min Learning Objective Diagnose weak instruments using the first-stage F-statistic; understand why weak instruments cause bias and poor inference; apply the Stock-Yogo rule of thumb and interpret the Sargan-Hansen J-test in overidentified models Provenance Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch 15.5

docs.title: The Weak Instrument Problem
docs.text: Even if an instrument \(z\) is technically relevant (\(\text{Cov}(z,x) \neq 0\)) and exogenous (\(\text{Cov}(z,u) = 0\)), it may be weakly correlated with the endogenous variable. Weak instruments cause severe problems in finite samples:

docs.title: Problem 1: Bias Toward OLS
docs.text:
In finite samples, the IV estimator is biased. The direction and magnitude of the finite-sample bias depends on the correlation between the instrument and the endogenous variable. When the instrument is weak:

\[\text{Bias}(\hat{\beta}^{\text{IV}}) \approx \frac{1}{F_1 - 1} \cdot \text{Bias}(\hat{\beta}^{\text{OLS}})\]

where \(F_1\) is the first-stage \(F\)-statistic. As \(F_1 \to 1\) (essentially no first stage), IV bias \(\to\) OLS bias — the IV estimator provides no improvement over the biased OLS.

Interpretation: A weak instrument yields an IV estimate that is contaminated by the same endogeneity it is supposed to cure. You've gone to the trouble of finding an instrument and the inference is nearly as bad as OLS.

docs.title: Problem 2: Large Standard Errors
docs.text: From M10.L02, \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}^{\text{2SLS}}) \propto 1/R^2_1\) where \(R^2_1\) is the first-stage R². A weak instrument means small \(R^2_1\) → enormous SEs → very wide confidence intervals.

docs.title: Problem 3: Size Distortions
docs.text: Standard 2SLS \(t\)-tests dramatically over-reject the null when instruments are weak. Staiger and Stock (1997) showed that even when the null is true, \(t\)-tests at the 5% level can reject at rates of 30–40% when \(F_1 \approx 3\). Nominal 5% tests become 40% tests — a catastrophic failure.

docs.title: First-Stage F-Statistic: The Rule of Thumb
docs.text:
The Stock-Yogo (2005) rule of thumb provides a simple diagnostic:

\[\boxed{F_1 > 10 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{instrument is sufficiently strong}}\]

where \(F_1\) is the \(F\)-statistic for the joint hypothesis that all instruments are excluded from the first stage (\(H_0: \pi_2 = \pi_3 = \cdots = 0\)).

Derivation context: Stock & Yogo derived critical values such that, if \(F > c^*\), the worst-case relative bias of 2SLS over OLS is less than 10%. The rule \(F > 10\) corresponds approximately to this 10% maximal bias criterion.

docs.title: The Staiger-Stock Rule (One Instrument)
docs.text:
For the special case of one instrument and one endogenous variable, the first-stage is a simple regression with \(t\)-statistic \(t_z\) on the instrument coefficient. The rule:

\[|t_z| > 3.2 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad F_1 = t_z^2 > 10.24 \approx 10\]

A \(t\)-statistic of 2.0 (significant at 5% in a standard test) implies \(F_1 = 4 < 10\) — the instrument is weak even though the first-stage coefficient is conventionally significant!

docs.title: The Stock-Yogo Weak Instrument Test
docs.text:
More formally, Stock & Yogo (2005) tabulate critical values \(c^*(\ell, m, b)\) where: - \(\ell\) = number of instruments - \(m\) = number of endogenous variables - \(b\) = maximal acceptable relative bias (typically 10%)

\(\ell\) instruments (one endogenous) \(c^*\) (10% max bias) 1 16.38 2 19.93 3 22.30

With one instrument, the formal threshold is actually \(F > 16.38\) for 10% maximal relative bias — the rule of thumb \(F > 10\) is a lower bound. Many practitioners use \(F > 10\) as a screening threshold and \(F > 16\) as a stronger standard.

docs.title: The Sargan-Hansen J-Test (Revisited)
docs.text:
In the over-identified case (\(\ell > m\)), the Sargan-Hansen J-test tests instrument exogeneity:

\[H_0: \text{Cov}(\mathbf{z}, u) = 0 \quad \text{(all instruments are exogenous)}\]

Procedure: 1. Estimate by 2SLS; save residuals \(\hat{u}_i^{\text{2SLS}}\) 2. Regress \(\hat{u}_i^{\text{2SLS}}\) on all instruments \(\mathbf{z}\) and exogenous controls \(\mathbf{w}\) 3. \(J = n \cdot R^2_{\text{aux}} \sim \chi^2_{\ell - m}\) under \(H_0\) 4. Reject \(H_0\) if \(J > \chi^2_{\ell-m,\alpha}\)

Important caveats: - J-test is not available in exactly identified models (\(\ell = m\)) - Rejecting \(H_0\) means at least one instrument is endogenous — but the test doesn't tell you which - Failing to reject is not confirmation of exogeneity — just insufficient evidence against it - J-test has low power when instruments are weak

docs.title: Remedies for Weak Instruments
docs.text: Remedy Description Find stronger instruments Return to theory/institutional knowledge for better \(z\) Anderson-Rubin confidence sets Weak-instrument robust inference (AR intervals) Conditional Likelihood Ratio (CLR) Moreira (2003); optimal weak-instrument-robust test LIML (Limited Info Maximum Likelihood) Less biased than 2SLS in weak instrument settings Report OLS as benchmark When instruments are too weak, OLS bias may be preferable to IV variance

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Setup: Wage regression with quarter of birth (Q1–Q3) as instruments for education (Angrist-Krueger design).

\[\log(\text{wage}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ}_i + \beta_2 \text{age}_i + u_i\]

Three instruments: \(z_1 = \mathbf{1}[\text{Q1 birth}]\), \(z_2 = \mathbf{1}[\text{Q2 birth}]\), \(z_3 = \mathbf{1}[\text{Q3 birth}]\) (Q4 is the omitted category).

So \(\ell = 3\), \(m = 1\) → over-identified (J-test has 2 df).

First-stage results:

\[\text{educ}_i = \pi_0 + \pi_1 \text{age}_i + \pi_2 z_{1i} + \pi_3 z_{2i} + \pi_4 z_{3i} + v_i\] Variable \(\hat{\pi}\) SE \(t\) Intercept 16.72 0.41 40.8 age −0.082 0.008 −10.3 Q1 birth (\(z_1\)) −0.091 0.032 −2.84 Q2 birth (\(z_2\)) −0.052 0.032 −1.63 Q3 birth (\(z_3\)) −0.024 0.032 −0.75

Joint F-test (H₀: \(\pi_2 = \pi_3 = \pi_4 = 0\)): \(F = 3.4\)

Weak instrument diagnosis: \(F = 3.4 < 10\) → instruments are weak. Despite Q1 birth having a borderline significant first-stage coefficient (\(t = -2.84\)), the joint \(F\) falls well below the Stock-Yogo threshold.

Consequences: - 2SLS estimates will be biased toward OLS estimates - Standard errors are unreliable; confidence intervals are misleading - Nominal 5% tests may reject at rates far above 5%

Comparing weak vs strong instrument estimates:

Method \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (educ) SE \(t\) OLS 0.067 0.003 22.3 2SLS (weak, \(F=3.4\)) 0.074 0.052 1.42 2SLS (strong, \(F=12.4\)) 0.129 0.047 2.74

The weak-instrument 2SLS estimate (0.074) is close to the OLS estimate (0.067) — consistent with bias toward OLS. The strong-instrument estimate (0.129, from the proximity-to-college design) differs substantially. Standard errors for weak IV are enormous (0.052 vs 0.047 for strong IV).

Sargan-Hansen J-test (over-identified, \(\ell - m = 2\)):

\(J = 4.12\). Critical value \(\chi^2_{2,0.05} = 5.99\). Fail to reject → over-identifying restrictions not violated.

docs.title: Common Misconception
docs.text:
"A significant first-stage coefficient guarantees a strong instrument — if the \(t\)-stat on \(z\) is above 2, the instrument is fine."

This is false. Statistical significance at the 5% level (\(|t| > 1.96\) or equivalently \(F > 3.84\)) does not imply instrument strength. The Stock-Yogo rule of thumb requires \(F > 10\) (equivalently, \(|t| > 3.16\) for a single instrument). A \(t\)-statistic of 2.5 is statistically significant but implies \(F = 6.25 < 10\) — the instrument may still be "weak" in the sense that 2SLS suffers substantial bias and size distortions.

The rule to remember: - Conventional significance test: \(F > 3.84\) (5% critical value for 1 df) - Stock-Yogo weak instrument threshold: \(F > 10\) (rule of thumb) or \(F > 16\) (10% max bias criterion)

These are very different thresholds. Always report the first-stage F-statistic in any IV paper or assignment.

docs.title: Practice Prompts
docs.text:
1. A researcher uses a single instrument \(z\) with a first-stage coefficient estimate of \(\hat{\pi} = 0.18\) and standard error \(0.08\). Compute the first-stage \(t\)-statistic and \(F\)-statistic. Is the instrument strong by the Stock-Yogo rule of thumb? What maximal relative bias does Stock-Yogo associate with \(F \approx 5\)?

  2. In the Angrist-Krueger design above, all three quarter-of-birth indicators have first-stage \(t\)-statistics below 3.2. A student argues: "We should drop Q2 and Q3, since they're individually insignificant, and keep only Q1 as the instrument — that solves the weak instrument problem." Critique this selection strategy. Does dropping weak instruments necessarily solve the problem?

  3. A researcher finds \(J = 6.8\) with two over-identifying restrictions (df = 2). At the 5% level, do they reject the null of instrument exogeneity? (Recall \(\chi^2_{2,0.05} = 5.99\).) What does rejection imply about their instrument set? Can the researcher determine which instrument is endogenous from this test alone?
